legends.name: Atlantis
legends.summary: Plato describes a great island power beyond the Pillars of Heracles that attacked ancient Athens and sank into the sea in a single day and night. The story appears only in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias, and no earlier text mentions it. Most classicists read it as a philosophical fiction that Plato invented, and no proposed location has archaeological support.
legends.when: Set by Plato about 9,000 years before Solon (about 9600 BCE); written about 360 BCE

origin.text: Plato, Timaeus 24e-25d and Critias 113c-121c

legends.look_for: Plato describes rings of land and water around a central island, canals, harbour works and a large plain cut by ditches, which would leave straight, regular walls and channels in seafloor depth data or lidar. Every site tested so far has turned out to be natural rock or a much later ruin.

places.name: Helike
places.claim: The Greek city of Helike was destroyed by an earthquake and wave in 373 BCE, within Plato's lifetime, and some scholars think the disaster gave him the image of a city swallowed in one night. Its buried remains were located in 2001.
places.against: Helike was a small city near Athens, not a distant empire; the link is to the manner of destruction only.

tests.who: Katsonopoulou, Soter and the Helike Project
tests.result: An Early Bronze Age settlement and a Classical site were found buried under 3 to 5 m of lagoon mud; the Classical site may be the city destroyed in 373 BCE. The buried city was found, not drowned, which differs from a sunken island.

places.name: Santorini (Thera)
places.claim: Spyridon Marinatos argued in 1939 that the Bronze Age eruption of Thera wrecked Minoan Crete, and later writers tied that disaster to Plato. The eruption, about 1600 BCE, buried the town of Akrotiri and is the real event most often named behind the story.
places.against: The date, place and size do not fit Plato: he puts Atlantis beyond the Pillars of Heracles, 9,000 years before Solon, and Minoan Crete did not end with the eruption.

places.event_date: Plato's 9,600 BCE as inherited from the dialogues

beyond-pillars.label: The island lay in the Atlantic, in front of the strait the Greeks call the Pillars of Heracles.

atlantic-navigable-then.label: At that time the ocean beyond the strait could be sailed.

larger-than-libya-and-asia.label: The island was larger than Libya and Asia together.

islands-and-opposite-continent.label: From the island one could pass to other islands, and from them to the whole continent on the far side of the true ocean.

mediterranean-is-a-harbour.label: The sea inside the strait is only a harbour with a narrow entrance; the outer sea is the real ocean, and the land around it a true continent.

gadeirus-end-of-island.label: The twin of Atlas, Gadeirus, got the far end of the island toward the Pillars of Heracles, in the region now called Gadeira.

atlantic-named-for-atlas.label: The island and the Atlantic sea were both named after Atlas, the first king.

nine-thousand-years.label: The war with Athens and the sinking happened 9,000 years before the time of the telling.

claimed-true-story.label: The speakers say the story is true, not an invented tale.

republic-city-made-real.label: Critias says he will treat the ideal city Socrates described yesterday as the ancient Athens of the priest's story.

names-translated-by-solon.label: Solon found the Egyptian names had been translated into Egyptian, and rendered each into Greek; the writings were kept in Critias' family.

empire-to-egypt-and-tyrrhenia.label: Atlantis ruled Libya as far as Egypt and Europe as far as Tyrrhenia.

war-with-athens.label: The Atlantean power, gathered into one, tried to enslave Europe and Asia inside the strait, and Athens defeated it.

sank-in-a-day-and-night.label: Violent earthquakes and floods came; in one grievous day and night the Athenian warriors were swallowed by the earth and the island sank under the sea.

impassable-mud.label: The sea at that spot is now impassable and unsearchable because of a shoal of mud left by the sinking island.

periodic-catastrophes.label: The Egyptian priest says mankind is destroyed again and again, mostly by fire and by water, and that Egypt is spared by the Nile.

attica-eroded-after-deluges.label: Critias says many great deluges in the 9,000 years since stripped Attica to "the bones of a sick man".

poseidon-cleito-hill.label: Poseidon married Cleito, the only daughter of the native Evenor, and walled her hill with rings; the hill stood about 50 stades from the plain's centre.

ringed-city.label: Poseidon cut the hill into rings: three of sea and two of land, alternating and equally spaced, so that nobody could cross.

ring-widths.label: Water rings are 3, 2 and 1 stades wide, land rings 3 and 2, around a central island 5 stades across.

central-island-diameter.label: The island with the royal palace was five stades across.

canal-to-sea.label: A canal 3 plethra wide, 100 feet deep and 50 stades long ran from the sea to the outermost ring, wide enough for the largest ships.

bridges-and-trireme-channels.label: Bridges one plethron wide crossed the water rings; a roofed channel through each land ring let a single trireme pass.

stone-walls-and-metals.label: The rings and the island were enclosed by a stone wall with towers and gates; the walls were coated with brass, tin and orichalcum.

red-white-black-stone.label: The stone for the buildings was white, black and red, quarried from under the central island and the rings; the quarries became roofed double docks.

outer-wall-50-stades.label: A wall began at the sea, ran round the whole city at a constant 50 stades from the largest ring, and closed on the mouth of the canal; it was crowded with houses and harbour traffic.

temple-of-poseidon.label: The temple of Poseidon, on the central island, was a stade long and three plethra wide, covered in silver and gold, with a golden statue of the god in a six-horse chariot.

hot-and-cold-springs.label: There were two springs, one warm and one cold, with baths and a sacred grove.

race-course-and-gardens.label: The ring islands had temples, gardens and exercise grounds; the larger land ring held a race-course a stade wide running all the way round.

fleet-and-harbours.label: The shipyards were full of triremes; the harbour was crowded night and day; the military levy supplied 1,200 ships.

lofty-coast.label: The whole region rose high and steep out of the sea.

great-plain.label: Beside the city lay a smooth, level, oblong plain, 3,000 stades one way and 2,000 stades inland from the sea at its middle, ringed by mountains that ran down to the sea.

mountains-shelter-north.label: This region faced south and was sheltered from the north; the mountains around it were more numerous and beautiful than any now.

mountains-around-plain.label: The mountains around the plain held rich villages, streams, lakes and meadows, and much timber.

plain-ditch.label: A man-made ditch ran round the whole plain, a stade wide and a plethron (100 feet) deep, 10,000 stades long, collecting the mountain streams and emptying into the sea by the city.

plain-canals.label: Straight canals about 100 feet wide cut across the plain, 100 stades apart, ran into the ditch on the seaward side and carried timber and crops to the city.

two-harvests.label: The land gave two harvests a year, using winter rain and summer irrigation from the canals.

forests-and-animals.label: The island supplied timber and plenty of tame and wild animals.

elephants.label: There were very many elephants on the island, with food for every other animal.

orichalcum-and-metals.label: The island yielded every kind of metal, including orichalcum, which was dug in many places and was the most precious metal after gold.

fruits-and-scents.label: Scented plants, cultivated grains and pulses, tree fruits and orchard fruits all grew in great variety.

ten-kings.label: Ten kings, descended from Poseidon and Cleito through five pairs of twin sons, each ruled a tenth of the island; Atlas, the eldest, was the overlord.

bull-ritual.label: Every fifth and sixth year the ten kings met at the temple, hunted bulls with staves and nooses, and cut the throat of one over the orichalcum pillar of laws.

army-and-allotments.label: The plain was split into 60,000 allotments of 10 by 10 stades; the royal city's levy was 10,000 chariots and 1,200 ships.

critias-breaks-off.label: The Critias ends as Zeus calls the gods together to punish the decayed kings; Plato gives no account of the war or the sinking there.

legends.name: Doggerland
legends.summary: Doggerland was the plain that joined Britain to mainland Europe when Ice Age seas were low. Mesolithic hunters lived on it until rising water drowned it about 8,000 years ago. It is a real, mapped landscape under the southern North Sea, known from trawled finds and from seismic survey data.
legends.when: Dry land from the last Ice Age until about 6200 BCE

origin.text: National Geographic Magazine, "Searching for Doggerland" (L. Spinney, 2012)

legends.look_for: River valleys, lake basins and old coastlines buried under seabed mud, visible in seismic reflection data and fine bathymetry. Finds come from peat and from stone and bone tools caught in trawls or washed on to beaches.

places.name: Doggerland plain (southern North Sea)
places.claim: Teams led by Vincent Gaffney have used seismic data gathered for oil and gas to map the rivers, lakes and coasts of the drowned plain. A 2020 study found the first deposits of the Storegga tsunami of about 8150 BP in the southern North Sea and argued that the wave did not end Doggerland on its own.

sources.title: J. Walker, V. Gaffney et al., "A great wave: the Storegga tsunami and the end of Doggerland?", Antiquity 94 (2020)
National Geographic Magazine, "Searching for Doggerland" (2012)

places.name: Dogger Bank
places.claim: The bank was the high ground of Doggerland; a barbed antler point trawled up east of the Wash in 1931 first showed that people had lived on what is now seabed. Models of the Storegga tsunami suggest the wave overran what was left of it.

sources.title: BBC News, "Prehistoric North Sea 'Atlantis' hit by 5m tsunami" (2014)
Wikipedia, "Doggerland"

legends.name: Sundaland
legends.summary: Sundaland is the shelf that joined Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula into one landmass when Ice Age seas were low. It flooded as the ice melted, in steps that sediment cores from the shelf record in detail. It is a real drowned land; claims that it was Atlantis have no support.
legends.when: Exposed during the last glacial period; flooded as the ice melted, from about 21,000 years ago

origin.text: T. Hanebuth, K. Stattegger and P. Grootes, "Rapid Flooding of the Sunda Shelf: A Late-Glacial Sea-Level Record", Science 288 (2000)

legends.look_for: Drowned river valleys running across the shelf between the islands, visible in bathymetry and seismic data. Mangrove peat and shoreline deposits in cores date each stage of the flooding.

places.name: Sunda Shelf
places.claim: Cores from the shelf give a sea-level record from 21,000 to 14,000 years ago. They show the sea rising as much as 16 m in 300 years about 14,600 years ago, which drowned wide lowlands between the islands.

sources.title: T. Hanebuth et al., "Rapid Flooding of the Sunda Shelf: A Late-Glacial Sea-Level Record", Science 288 (2000)
Wikipedia, "Sundaland"

legends.name: Beringia
legends.summary: Beringia is the land that joined Siberia and Alaska when Ice Age seas were low. People and animals crossed it into the Americas. The central part now lies under the shallow Bering and Chukchi seas.
legends.when: Exposed during glacial periods, when sea level was 100 m or more lower

origin.text: US National Park Service, "Beringia: Lost World of the Ice Age"

legends.look_for: Old river channels, lake basins and shorelines on the shallow seabed, seen in bathymetry and sonar. Pollen, insects and plant remains in seabed cores show what grew on the bridge.

places.name: Bering Strait
places.claim: During glacial periods sea level fell by 100 m or more and the shallow floor of the Bering and Chukchi seas became dry land. Seabed cores hold the remains of the tundra plants and insects that lived on it.

sources.title: US National Park Service, "Beringia: Lost World of the Ice Age"
S. Elias et al., "Life and times of the Bering land bridge", Nature 382 (1996)

places.name: Bering Land Bridge National Preserve
places.claim: This preserve on the Seward Peninsula in Alaska protects a part of Beringia that stayed above water.

sources.title: US National Park Service, Bering Land Bridge National Preserve
US National Park Service, Shared Beringian Heritage Program

legends.name: Lemuria
legends.summary: The zoologist Philip Sclater proposed Lemuria in 1864 as a sunken land bridge in the Indian Ocean, to explain why lemur-like fossils and animals occur in both Madagascar and India. Continental drift explained the pattern better and geologists dropped the idea. Occult writers and Tamil nationalists later remade it as a lost homeland of humankind.
legends.when: Proposed in 1864; abandoned by science by the 1960s

origin.text: P. L. Sclater, "The Mammals of Madagascar", Quarterly Journal of Science (1864); history of the idea in S. Ramaswamy, The Lost Land of Lemuria (2004)

legends.look_for: Nothing: ocean floor is young basalt, not drowned continent. The real traces of the old link between India and Madagascar are matching rocks and fossils on land, and scraps of continental crust under volcanic islands.

places.name: Madagascar
places.claim: Sclater started from the lemurs of Madagascar and their relatives in India, and supposed a continent had once joined the two.
places.against: Madagascar and India were once joined, but plate movement carried them apart tens of millions of years ago; no land bridge sank.

sources.title: S. Ramaswamy, The Lost Land of Lemuria (2004)
Wikipedia, "Lemuria"

places.name: Mauritia (under Mauritius)
places.claim: In 2013 geologists reported zircons between 600 and 1,970 million years old in the beach sand of Mauritius, a volcanic island only about 9 million years old. They take them as proof of a buried scrap of continent, which they named Mauritia.
places.against: Mauritia broke up by about 85 million years ago, long before there were people or lemurs; it is not the Lemuria of legend.

sources.title: T. Torsvik et al., "A Precambrian microcontinent in the Indian Ocean", Nature Geoscience 6 (2013)
BBC News, "Fragments of ancient continent buried under Indian Ocean" (2013)

legends.name: Mu
legends.summary: Augustus Le Plongeon invented Mu in the 1800s from a mistaken reading of a Maya book. James Churchward moved it to the Pacific in a series of books from 1926 and said an advanced civilisation lived there until 12,000 years ago. No geologist or archaeologist accepts it: the Pacific floor holds no sunken continent.
legends.when: Named in the 19th century; popularised from 1926

origin.text: A. Le Plongeon, after a mistaken reading of the Madrid Codex; J. Churchward, The Lost Continent of Mu (1926), reviewed in The Geographical Journal (1932)

legends.look_for: Nothing: seafloor mapping and drilling show the Pacific basin is ocean crust. Monuments that fans link to Mu, such as those on Easter Island or Pohnpei, were built by Polynesians and Micronesians within the last 1,500 years.

places.name: Central Pacific Ocean
places.claim: Churchward claimed a continent once filled the central Pacific from Hawaii to Easter Island and Fiji, and that the islands are its mountain tops.
places.against: The Pacific islands are volcanoes and atolls on ocean crust, and the tablets Churchward said he read have never been produced.

sources.title: Review of J. Churchward, The Lost Continent of Mu, The Geographical Journal 79 (1932)
Wikipedia, "Mu (mythical lost continent)"

legends.name: Kumari Kandam
legends.summary: Medieval commentaries on Tamil literature tell of Pandya lands south of Cape Comorin that the sea swallowed, along with the first two Tamil literary academies. In the late 1800s and 1900s Tamil writers joined this to Lemuria and described a lost continent called Kumari Kandam, the home of the Tamils. Historians treat the continent as a modern myth built on older flood legends.
legends.when: Flood legends in commentaries of about the 8th to 14th centuries CE; the continent idea dates from the 1890s on

origin.text: Medieval commentaries on Tamil literature; the modern continent is traced in S. Ramaswamy, "History at Land's End", Journal of Asian Studies 59 (2000)

legends.look_for: Rising seas did drown a strip of the south Indian shelf after the Ice Age, so drowned shorelines and river mouths exist offshore in bathymetry. There is no sunken continent in the deep ocean south of India.

places.name: Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin)
places.claim: The legend places the lost land south of this cape, the southern tip of India. Tamil revivalists drew maps of a continent reaching from here towards Madagascar and Australia.
places.against: Plate tectonics rules out a sunken continent, and the texts speak of lost territory, not a continent; the scale was added in modern times.

sources.title: S. Ramaswamy, "History at Land's End: Lemuria in Tamil Spatial Fables", Journal of Asian Studies 59 (2000)
Wikipedia, "Kumari Kandam"

legends.name: Lyonesse
legends.summary: Lyonesse is the home of Tristan in Arthurian romance; the name first appears in Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur in the late 15th century. William Camden gave the name in 1586 to a land between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly that tradition said the sea had drowned. The romance kingdom is fiction, but the Isles of Scilly really were a single larger island that rising seas broke up over thousands of years.
legends.when: Named by Malory in the late 15th century; drowned land called Lyonnesse by Camden, 1586

origin.text: Thomas Malory, Le Morte Darthur (late 15th century), for the name; William Camden, Britannia (1586), for the drowned land

legends.look_for: Field walls, hut circles and cists that run down the beach and under the sea between the Scilly islands, visible at low tide, in bathymetry and in air photos. Peat and tree stumps in the intertidal zone date the flooding.

places.name: Isles of Scilly
places.claim: Prehistoric field walls and houses lie under the shallow water between the islands. A 2020 study of Scilly in Science Advances rebuilt 12,000 years of sea level and coastline there and found that land was lost at an uneven rate as one large island broke into many.
places.against: The drowning took centuries and happened long before the Middle Ages; it was not one night.

sources.title: R. Barnett, D. Charman et al., "Nonlinear landscape and cultural response to sea-level rise", Science Advances 6 (2020)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Lyonnesse"
Wikipedia, "Lyonesse"

places.name: Seven Stones Reef
places.claim: Cornish tradition names this reef between Land's End and Scilly as the site of the chief town of Lyonesse, and fishermen told of hauling up pieces of doors and windows there.
places.against: The reef is bare rock; no survey has found any building.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Lyonesse"
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Lyonnesse"

legends.name: Ys
legends.summary: Breton legend tells of the city of Ys, built below sea level behind a dyke by King Gradlon. His daughter Dahut opened the sluice gates and the sea drowned it. The story is known from the late Middle Ages on and has no archaeological basis.
legends.when: Set in the 5th century CE; written versions from the 15th century on

origin.text: Breton tradition, written down from the late 15th century; retold in L. Spence, Legends and Romances of Brittany (1917)

legends.look_for: A real town would leave walls, quays or a dyke on the floor of a shallow bay, within reach of multibeam sonar. None has been found in the Bay of Douarnenez.

places.name: Bay of Douarnenez
places.claim: Most versions of the legend place the drowned city in this bay in Finistère, and local tradition points to old walls and roads near the shore as its remains.
places.against: No trace of a city has been found on the seabed, and the story took shape only between the 15th and 17th centuries.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Ys"
L. Spence, Legends and Romances of Brittany (1917), Project Gutenberg

legends.name: Cantre'r Gwaelod
legends.summary: Welsh legend tells of a rich lowland in Cardigan Bay, ruled by Gwyddno Garanhir, that the sea drowned when its dykes or its well were left unwatched. The oldest form is a poem in the 13th century Black Book of Carmarthen. Drowned forests on the shore and a medieval map suggest real memories of lost coast lie behind it.
legends.when: Set in about the 6th century CE; earliest text about 1250

origin.text: Poem in the Black Book of Carmarthen (13th century), where the land is called Maes Gwyddno

legends.look_for: Tree stumps and peat on beaches at low tide, and drowned islands or ridges in bathymetry of the bay. Shingle ridges that look like causeways are natural glacial moraines.

places.name: Borth and Ynyslas submerged forest
places.claim: Stumps of pine, oak, alder and birch, killed by rising water and peat thousands of years ago, stand in the beach here and show after storms. They are the most likely source of the story of a drowned land.
places.against: The forest drowned in prehistory, long before the time the legend describes.

sources.title: BBC Travel, "How a storm revealed a Welsh kingdom" (2020)
Wikipedia, "Cantre'r Gwaelod"

places.name: Lost islands of Cardigan Bay
places.claim: Simon Haslett and David Willis showed in 2022 that the Gough Map, a map of Britain from the 13th or 14th century, marks two islands in Cardigan Bay that no longer exist. They argue the islands were the last pieces of a low coast of glacial deposits, worn away by the 16th century.
places.against: The case rests on one medieval map and a model of erosion; no seabed remains of the islands have been found, and other scholars have challenged the reading of the map.

sources.title: S. Haslett and D. Willis, "The 'lost' islands of Cardigan Bay, Wales, UK", Atlantic Geoscience 58 (2022)
C. Delano-Smith et al., Discussion of "The 'lost' islands of Cardigan Bay", Atlantic Geoscience 58 (2022)
BBC News, "Map may show evidence of Wales' Atlantis off Ceredigion" (2022)

places.name: Sarn Badrig
places.claim: This shingle reef runs out to sea from the coast of Gwynedd. Folklore took it for one of the dykes of the drowned land.
places.against: It is made of glacial deposits left by retreating ice sheets at the end of the last Ice Age.

sources.title: BBC News, "Map may show evidence of Wales' Atlantis off Ceredigion" (2022)
Wikipedia, "Sarn Badrig"

legends.name: Vineta
legends.summary: North German and Polish legend tells of Vineta, a rich trading city on the Baltic that sank under the sea as a punishment for pride. Chroniclers of the 11th and 12th centuries describe a real great port on the south Baltic coast, called Jumne among other names. Most historians identify that port with the Viking Age town at Wolin; the sinking is legend.
legends.when: Port described by Adam of Bremen about 1075; said to have been destroyed in the 12th century

origin.text: Adam of Bremen, about 1075 to 1080, on a great trading town at the mouth of the Oder; later legend of the sunken city

legends.look_for: A Viking Age port leaves harbour timbers, ramparts, craft debris and coin hoards in waterlogged ground, found by coring, geophysics and excavation. Old river channels in lidar and historic maps show where the coast lay.

places.name: Wolin
places.claim: Adolf Hofmeister argued in 1931 and 1932 that Vineta, Jumne, Julin and Jomsborg are all names for the trading town at Wolin, at a mouth of the Oder. Excavations from the 1930s on uncovered a large early medieval settlement there, and his thesis is the mainstream view.
places.against: Wolin never sank; the chronicles report Danish campaigns against it, the last in 1170.

sources.title: C. Broich, "The Wasting of Wolin: Environmental Factors in the Downfall of a Medieval Baltic Town", Environment and History 7 (2001)
Wikipedia, "Vineta"

places.name: Barth
places.claim: Klaus Goldmann, a Berlin museum curator, and Günter Wermusch argued in 1999 that the Oder once had a western mouth and that Vineta lay in the lagoon near Barth.
places.against: No excavation has found a town there and most historians keep to Wolin.

sources.title: Archaeology, "Letter from Germany: Atlantis of the Baltic" (2003)
wissenschaft.de, review of K. Goldmann and G. Wermusch, Vineta (1999)
Wikipedia, "Vineta"

legends.name: Rungholt
legends.summary: Rungholt was a medieval trading settlement in North Frisia that a storm surge destroyed in January 1362. Legend made it a rich city sunk for its sins, and its site was argued over for a century. In 2023 the Rungholt Project, which includes archaeologists from Kiel University, found its main church and many dwelling mounds under the mudflats near Hallig Südfall.
legends.when: Destroyed by the storm surge of 1362 CE (the Grote Mandrenke); church located in 2023

origin.text: D. Wilken, H. Hadler et al., "The discovery of the church of Rungholt, a landmark for the drowned medieval landscapes of the Wadden Sea World Heritage", Scientific Reports 14 (2024)

legends.look_for: Dwelling mounds, drainage ditches, dykes and tide gates buried under tidal mud. They show in magnetic gradiometry, electromagnetic induction and seismic survey on the flats at low tide, and are checked by coring.

places.name: Tidal flats at Hallig Südfall
places.claim: Magnetic and electromagnetic survey of more than ten square km of mudflat, with cores and finds, mapped up to 64 dwelling mounds, a sea dyke, drains and the foundations of a church about 40 m long. The team identifies it as the main church of the Edomsharde district and its centre, Rungholt.

sources.title: D. Wilken, H. Hadler et al., "The discovery of the church of Rungholt", Scientific Reports 14 (2024)
D. Wilken, H. Hadler et al., "Lost in the North Sea: Geophysical and geoarchaeological prospection of the Rungholt medieval dyke system", PLOS ONE 17 (2022)
CBC Radio, "Scientists map medieval town that's been buried beneath the sea for 661 years" (2023)

legends.name: Hy-Brasil
legends.summary: Hy-Brasil is a phantom island that sea charts showed west of Ireland from about 1325 until 1865. Expeditions left Bristol in 1480 and 1481 to look for it and found nothing. Scholars see it as a map error that merged with Irish stories of an island in the western sea.
legends.when: On charts from about 1325 to 1865 CE

origin.text: Portolan chart of Angelino Dulcert, about 1325; history in B. Freitag, Hy Brasil: The Metamorphosis of an Island (2013)

legends.look_for: A real island would be a shoal in bathymetry. The shallowest ground in the mapped position, Porcupine Bank, is still about 200 m under water.

places.name: Porcupine Bank
places.claim: This bank about 200 km west of Ireland, found in 1862, has been suggested as the origin of the island on the charts.
places.against: The bank lies about 200 m deep and has not been land in historic times; scholars see the island as a map error mixed with Celtic otherworld lore.

sources.title: B. Freitag, Hy Brasil: The Metamorphosis of an Island (2013)
Wikipedia, "Hy Brasil"
Wikipedia, "Porcupine Bank"

legends.name: Thule
legends.summary: The Greek explorer Pytheas of Massalia reported about 325 BCE a land called Thule, six days' sail north of Britain, near a frozen sea, where the summer sun hardly set. His book is lost and we have only quotations by later writers such as Strabo, who thought him a liar. Thule was a real report of a far northern land, but scholars still disagree on which one.
legends.when: Voyage of Pytheas about 325 BCE

origin.text: Strabo, Geography 1.4.2 (quoting Pytheas on Thule)

legends.look_for: This is a question of ancient texts and latitudes, not of remains: no site would prove it. Greek or Massaliote objects of the 4th century BCE in the far north would help, and none has been found.

places.name: Smøla and the coast of central Norway
places.claim: Fridtjof Nansen argued in 1911 that Thule was the coast of Norway, where Pytheas could have met farmers who threshed grain indoors and made mead. In 2010 a team at the Technical University of Berlin corrected the distortions in Ptolemy's map and placed his Thule at the island of Smøla.
places.against: Pytheas called Thule an island, and a six day crossing from Britain fits Iceland as well.

sources.title: F. Nansen, In Northern Mists, vol. 1 (1911), ch. 2, Project Gutenberg
Review of A. Kleineberg et al., Germania und die Insel Thule (2010), Isis 103 (2012)
Wikipedia, "Thule"

places.name: Iceland
places.claim: Iceland lies about six days' sail north-west of Britain, close to the Arctic Circle and to drift ice, as Pytheas described. The Irish monk Dicuil, writing about 825, described clerics who had stayed on Thule and seen the midnight sun, and this is usually taken to be Iceland.
places.against: Pytheas spoke of people who farmed and kept bees, and Iceland had no known inhabitants before the 9th century CE.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Ultima Thule"
Wikipedia, "Thule"

places.name: Shetland
places.claim: Tacitus says that the Roman fleet that sailed round Britain under Agricola conquered the Orkneys and sighted Thule, which can only be Shetland or Fair Isle. Some scholars think this is also the Thule of Pytheas.
places.against: Shetland is one day north of Orkney, not six days from Britain, and has no midnight sun.

sources.title: Tacitus, Agricola 10 ("Thule was sighted")
Wikipedia, "Thule"

legends.name: Dwarka (Dvaraka)
legends.summary: The Mahabharata and the Puranas say that Krishna's city of Dvaraka on the coast of Gujarat was swallowed by the sea after his death. Marine archaeologists have found stone structures and many stone anchors in shallow water off modern Dwarka and Bet Dwarka. Their age is disputed: the finds show a harbour of the historical and medieval periods, and nothing proves a city of Krishna's legendary time.
legends.when: Legend set in the age of the Mahabharata; underwater surveys since 1983

origin.text: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva (book 16), where Arjuna sees the sea cover Dvaraka

legends.look_for: Dressed stone blocks, walls and stone anchors on the seabed in 3 to 12 m of water, seen by divers and side-scan sonar. Dates need pottery or organic material sealed under the stones, which is what is still missing.

places.name: Seabed off Dwarka
places.claim: The Marine Archaeology Unit of India's National Institute of Oceanography dug under water here from 1983 to 1990, and S. R. Rao, who led the work, took the stone structures on the seabed for a city of about 1500 BCE. Later seasons found many stone anchors in 10 to 14 m of water.
places.against: The 1500 BCE date rests on a single radiocarbon sample, and the institute's own later study dates the grapnel anchors to Indo-Arab trade of the 8th to 16th centuries CE.

sources.title: A. S. Gaur, Sundaresh, S. Tripati et al., "A group of 20 stone anchors from the waters of Dwarka, on the Gujarat Coast, India", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 30 (2001)
Wikipedia, "Dvārakā"

places.name: Bet Dwarka
places.claim: Work on this island in the 1980s found pottery of the Late Harappan period. In 5 to 8 m of water near the jetty lie stone and lead anchors, amphora sherds and a lead ingot of about the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, which show an old anchorage.
places.against: The finds are a small coastal settlement, not the great city of the epic.

sources.title: A. S. Gaur, Sundaresh and S. Tripati, "Evidence for Indo-Roman Trade from Bet Dwarka Waters, West Coast of India", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 35 (2006)
Wikipedia, "Bet Dwarka"

places.name: Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay)
places.claim: In 2001 and 2002 India's National Institute of Ocean Technology reported side-scan sonar images of geometric shapes about 36 m deep in the gulf, with dredged objects and a piece of wood dated to about 9,500 years ago. India's minister for ocean development presented it as a city older than any known.
places.against: The objects were dredged, not excavated, so nothing ties the dated wood to the sonar shapes, and critics say the stone "artefacts" may be natural; no site has been confirmed.

sources.title: S. Kathiroli et al., "New Archaeological sites in the Gulf of Cambay, India", Episodes 26 (2003)
BBC News, "Lost city 'could rewrite history'" (2002)
Wikipedia, "Marine archaeology in the Gulf of Khambhat"

legends.name: Yonaguni Monument
legends.summary: A terraced rock formation rises from about 25 m of water off Yonaguni, in the far south-west of Japan. Kihachiro Aratake, a local dive guide looking for sharks, found it in 1986. The marine geologist Masaaki Kimura says people carved it thousands of years ago; most geologists who have looked at it say the steps and flat faces are natural fractures in bedded sandstone.
legends.when: Found in 1986

origin.text: Found in 1986 by the diver Kihachiro Aratake; described in National Geographic (2007)

legends.look_for: Flat terraces and right angles in sandstone that splits along straight joints, seen by divers and in multibeam sonar. Tool marks, quarried blocks moved out of place or artefacts would show human work; natural joints explain the rest.

places.name: Yonaguni Monument
places.claim: Masaaki Kimura of the University of the Ryukyus has dived the site for years and reads it as a stepped monument with roads, a castle and carved faces, possibly sunk by an earthquake.
places.against: Robert Schoch of Boston University and others find that the sandstone breaks naturally along straight parallel joints, and neither Japan's cultural agency nor Okinawa Prefecture treats it as a cultural site.

sources.title: National Geographic, "Japan's Ancient Underwater 'Pyramid' Mystifies Scholars" (2007)
Wikipedia, "Yonaguni Monument"

legends.name: Helike
legends.summary: Helike was a Greek city on the Gulf of Corinth, destroyed in one winter night of 373 BCE by an earthquake and a wave from the sea. Ancient visitors said its ruins could be seen under water for centuries, then the site was lost. In 2001 the Helike Project found its buried remains on land, under the silt of a filled-in lagoon.
legends.when: Destroyed 373 BCE; located 2001 CE

origin.text: Strabo, Geography 8.7.2

legends.look_for: The city is not on the seabed, as searchers assumed for years, but under metres of river and lagoon silt on the coastal plain. Bore holes, ground-penetrating radar and magnetometry find walls and pottery layers under farmland.

places.name: Helike (near Rizomylos and Nikolaiika)
places.claim: Dora Katsonopoulou and Steven Soter began the search in 1988 and drilled bore holes across the delta. They found occupation layers from the Early Bronze Age to late antiquity, with signs that settlements here were drowned and raised again more than once.

sources.title: S. Soter and D. Katsonopoulou, "Submergence and uplift of settlements in the area of Helike, Greece, from the Early Bronze Age to late antiquity", Geoarchaeology 26 (2011)
BBC Horizon, "Helike: The Real Atlantis" (2002)

legends.name: Pavlopetri
legends.summary: Pavlopetri is a Bronze Age town that lies in 3 to 4 m of water off the coast of Laconia in southern Greece. Nicholas Flemming found it in 1967 and a Cambridge team mapped it in 1968. Work since 2009 has shown that people lived there about 5,000 years ago, which makes it the oldest known submerged town.
legends.when: Occupied from about 3000 BCE; found 1967

origin.text: A. Harding, G. Cadogan and R. Howell, "Pavlopetri: an Underwater Bronze Age Town in Laconia", Annual of the British School at Athens 64 (1969)

legends.look_for: Stone wall footings, streets, courtyards and cist graves on a sandy seabed a few metres deep, clear in air photos, sector-scan sonar and stereo photogrammetry. Shifting sand covers and uncovers them.

places.name: Pavlopetri
places.claim: A Greek and British team led by Jon Henderson of the University of Nottingham surveyed the town from 2009 and found pottery from the end of the Stone Age, which put its start some 1,200 years earlier than thought.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Lost Greek city that may have inspired Atlantis myth gives up secrets" (2009)
A. Harding, G. Cadogan and R. Howell, "Pavlopetri: an Underwater Bronze Age Town in Laconia" (1969)
Wikipedia, "Pavlopetri"

legends.name: Thonis-Heracleion
legends.summary: Thonis-Heracleion was Egypt's main port on the Mediterranean before Alexandria was founded. It stood at the Canopic mouth of the Nile and sank in stages, the last of it in the 8th century CE. It was known only from texts until Franck Goddio's team found it in 2000 under the Bay of Abu Qir, 6.5 km from the present shore.
legends.when: Founded about the 8th century BCE; sunk by the 8th century CE; found 2000

origin.text: Franck Goddio / IEASM, "Thonis-Heracleion"

legends.look_for: The city lies under metres of sand and silt in murky water, so it was found with towed magnetometers, side-scan sonar and sub-bottom profilers, then checked by divers. Temple blocks, statues, quays and dozens of ship hulls mark the old channels.

places.name: Thonis-Heracleion (Bay of Abu Qir)
places.claim: The European Institute for Underwater Archaeology (IEASM), led by Franck Goddio, located the city in 2000 after a geophysical survey of the bay. A stele found on the site showed that Greek Heracleion and Egyptian Thonis were one and the same town.

sources.title: Franck Goddio / IEASM, "Thonis-Heracleion"
The Guardian, "Lost cities #6: how Thonis-Heracleion resurfaced after 1,000 years under water" (2016)

legends.name: Canopus
legends.summary: Canopus was a town near the western mouth of the Nile, famous in Greek and Roman times for its temples of Osiris and Serapis and for its pleasure seekers. Its eastern part sank under the Bay of Abu Qir, like nearby Thonis-Heracleion. Franck Goddio's team has mapped the sunken remains east of the modern port of Abu Qir.
legends.when: Named by Solon in the 6th century BCE; sunk by the 8th century CE

origin.text: Franck Goddio / IEASM, "Canopus"

legends.look_for: Temple walls, statues and building rubble under sand in shallow, cloudy water, found by magnetometer and sonar survey and checked by divers.

places.name: East Canopus (Bay of Abu Qir)
places.claim: Two kilometres east of the port of Abu Qir the IEASM team identified a zone with many sunken remains, some of them matching what Prince Omar Toussoun recorded there in 1933. It identifies the zone as the eastern part of Canopus.

sources.title: Franck Goddio / IEASM, "Canopus"
Review of F. Goddio, Underwater Archaeology in the Canopic Region in Egypt: The Topography of Heracleion-Thonis and East Canopus 1996-2006, Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 95 (2009)

legends.name: Baiae
legends.summary: Baiae was the most fashionable seaside resort of the Roman rich, on the Bay of Naples. The ground there rises and falls with the volcanic activity of the Phlegraean Fields, and the lower part of the town has sunk under the bay. Its villas, mosaics and statues can be seen under shallow water.
legends.when: Resort from the 1st century BCE; deserted because of malaria in 1500 CE

origin.text: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Baiae"

legends.look_for: Mosaic floors, walls, fish ponds, roads and harbour moles under a few metres of clear water, visible in air photos and mapped by divers and photogrammetry.

places.name: Baiae
places.claim: More than 100 m of the old shore front now lies under the bay because of bradyseism, the slow sinking and rising of the ground over the magma chamber of the Phlegraean Fields.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Baiae"
Wikipedia, "Baiae"

legends.name: Port Royal
legends.summary: Port Royal in Jamaica was one of the richest English ports in the Americas and a base for privateers. On 7 June 1692 an earthquake turned the sand under it to liquid and much of the town slid under the harbour. The sunken streets are the best preserved 17th century English town site anywhere and became a World Heritage Site in 2025.
legends.when: Sunk 7 June 1692

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "The Archaeological Ensemble of 17th Century Port Royal"

legends.look_for: Brick buildings sunk upright with their contents in place, under a few metres of silt in the harbour. Found by probing, sonar and diver excavation.

places.name: Port Royal
places.claim: The 1692 earthquake put much of the town under water and sand. Excavations since the 1950s have recorded whole buildings and thousands of everyday objects from the moment of the disaster.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "The Archaeological Ensemble of 17th Century Port Royal"
Wikipedia, "Port Royal"

legends.name: Dunwich
legends.summary: Dunwich in Suffolk was one of the largest ports of medieval England. Storms in the 13th and 14th centuries blocked its harbour and the cliff has been falling into the sea ever since, taking the town with it. Sonar surveys led by David Sear have mapped the ruins of its churches on the seabed.
legends.when: Lost to the sea from the 13th century CE on; seabed surveys from 2008

origin.text: D. Sear et al., "Cartographic, Geophysical and Diver Surveys of the Medieval Town Site at Dunwich, Suffolk, England", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 40 (2011)

legends.look_for: Piles of worked stone and flint rubble where churches fell from the cliff, up to 10 m down in water with almost no visibility. Multibeam and side-scan sonar, sub-bottom profiling and acoustic imaging cameras find them; old maps say which building is which.

places.name: Dunwich seabed
places.claim: The Dunwich project matched historic maps to multibeam, side-scan and sub-bottom sonar and then to acoustic images, and located the remains of medieval buildings, churches and a priory among them, up to 10 m under the sea.

sources.title: D. Sear et al., "Cartographic, Geophysical and Diver Surveys of the Medieval Town Site at Dunwich" (2011)
BBC News, "Dunwich underwater images show 'Britain's Atlantis'" (2013)

legends.name: Ravenser Odd
legends.summary: Ravenser Odd was a medieval port on a sandbank at the mouth of the Humber, near Spurn Point. It grew rich in the 13th century, sent two members to the Model Parliament of 1295, and was then abandoned and destroyed by storms, the last in 1362. Its site has never been found.
legends.when: Founded in the 13th century CE; destroyed by 1362

origin.text: Medieval records of the port, which sent two members to the Model Parliament of 1295

legends.look_for: Stone footings of a sea wall, quays and buildings on or under the sandy seabed off Spurn, where the sand moves fast. High-resolution multibeam sonar is the tool being used.

places.name: Seabed off Spurn Point
places.claim: Daniel Parsons, a sedimentologist at the University of Hull, surveyed about 10 hectares of seabed off Spurn Point with high-resolution sonar in 2021. It did not find the town, but he believed the search was close and planned a second survey.
places.against: No remains have been confirmed, and the sands at the mouth of the Humber have shifted a great deal since the 14th century.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Yorkshire's lost 'Atlantis' nearly found, says Hull professor" (2022)
Wikipedia, "Ravenser Odd"

legends.name: Old Winchelsea
legends.summary: Old Winchelsea was one of the main ports of medieval Sussex, built on a shingle spit in Rye Bay. The sea wore the spit away through the 13th century and a great storm in 1287 destroyed what was left. Edward I laid out the present town of Winchelsea on a hill inland; the old site has not been found.
legends.when: Destroyed by the storm of 1287 CE

origin.text: University of Sussex, Coastview project, "Changes in the Rother Mouth"

legends.look_for: Building stone, wharf timbers and pottery under shingle, marsh clay or the bed of Rye Bay. The coast here has moved so much that the remains may be under land as easily as under sea; boreholes and seismic survey are the likely tools.

places.name: Rye Bay, south-east of Winchelsea
places.claim: The old town is believed to have stood on a sand and shingle spit that shielded the marshes between Fairlight and Dungeness. The pin is the present town, which replaced it; the lost site lies some way to the south-east.
places.against: The exact position is not known, and the shingle has been reworked many times since.

sources.title: University of Sussex, Coastview project, "Changes in the Rother Mouth"
Wikipedia, "Winchelsea"

legends.name: Saeftinghe
legends.summary: Saeftinghe was a district of farms, villages and a castle on the south bank of the Western Scheldt. Floods in the 14th and 16th centuries drowned it, and the dykes cut during the Dutch Revolt in 1584 finished it. It is now a 3,500 hectare tidal marsh on the Dutch and Belgian border, with the lost villages somewhere under the mud.
legends.when: Flooded in the 14th and 16th centuries CE; lost in 1584

origin.text: Stichting Het Zeeuwse Landschap, "Verdronken Land van Saeftinghe" (in Dutch)

legends.look_for: Brick foundations, dyke lines and field ditches under tidal mud and creeks. Electromagnetic and electrical surveys on the flats at low tide have been tried here; lidar shows the creek pattern.

places.name: Verdronken Land van Saeftinghe
places.claim: The body that manages the marsh records that villages and a castle stood here in the Middle Ages and that floods returned the land to the tides. Geophysicists have tested several survey methods on the flats to look for what is buried.

sources.title: Stichting Het Zeeuwse Landschap, "Verdronken Land van Saeftinghe" (in Dutch)
T. Missiaen et al., "Comparing Different Geophysical Methods in a Tidal Flat Area (Verdronken Land van Saeftinge, Westerschelde)", Near Surface 2006 (EAGE)
Wikipedia, "Saeftinghe"

legends.name: Atlit Yam
legends.summary: Atlit Yam is a Neolithic village on the seabed off the Carmel coast of Israel, 8 to 12 m under water. People lived there about 9,000 years ago and left houses, wells, graves and a ring of standing stones. Rising seas after the Ice Age covered it, and sand kept it whole until it was found in 1984.
legends.when: Occupied about 8100 to 7500 BP (late Pre-Pottery Neolithic); found 1984

origin.text: E. Galili et al., "Atlit-Yam: A Prehistoric Site on the Sea Floor off the Israeli Coast", Journal of Field Archaeology 20 (1993)

legends.look_for: Stone wall footings, stone-lined wells and upright stones on a clay seabed, exposed when storms strip the sand. Divers find them; they are too small and low for most sonar.

places.name: Atlit Yam
places.claim: Ehud Galili and colleagues describe it as the largest and most deeply submerged prehistoric settlement found on the Mediterranean coast: about 60,000 square metres, 8 to 12 m below sea level, dated to about 8100 to 7500 BP.

sources.title: E. Galili et al., "Atlit-Yam: A Prehistoric Site on the Sea Floor off the Israeli Coast", Journal of Field Archaeology 20 (1993)
Wikipedia, "Atlit Yam"

legends.name: Lake Titicaca underwater ruins
legends.summary: Andean tradition makes Lake Titicaca the place where the world began, and stories of drowned temples there are old. Underwater excavation on Khoa Reef, near the Island of the Sun, has proved that the Tiwanaku state made rich offerings in the lake between the 8th and 10th centuries CE. A claim in 2000 of a large temple on the lake bed has never been published in detail.
legends.when: Tiwanaku offerings of the 8th to 10th centuries CE

origin.text: C. Delaere, J. Capriles and C. Stanish, "Underwater ritual offerings in the Island of the Sun and the formation of the Tiwanaku state", PNAS 116 (2019)

legends.look_for: Offerings on a reef top: stone boxes, incense burners, gold sheet, shells and animal bones in lake mud, found by divers and excavated with suction dredges. Walls or terraces would show in multibeam sonar of the lake floor.

places.name: Khoa Reef, Island of the Sun
places.claim: The first systematic underwater excavation here found ceramic incense burners in the shape of cats, killed young llamas and ornaments of metal, shell and worked stone, left in repeated rituals by the Tiwanaku state between the 8th and 10th centuries CE.

sources.title: C. Delaere, J. Capriles and C. Stanish, "Underwater ritual offerings in the Island of the Sun and the formation of the Tiwanaku state", PNAS 116 (2019)

places.name: Lake bed near Copacabana (2000 claim)
places.claim: In August 2000 a team of divers backed by the group Akakor Geographical Exploring said it had found a temple about 200 m long, a crop terrace, a road and an 800 m wall under the lake, not far from Copacabana.
places.against: It was announced to the press with full results promised later; no scholarly report of a temple was found for this dataset, so treat it as unconfirmed.

sources.title: BBC News, "Ancient temple found under Lake Titicaca" (2000)

legends.name: Shicheng (Lion City)
legends.summary: Shicheng was a county town in Zhejiang, China. In 1959 the government flooded its valley to make the reservoir of the Xin'an River dam, now Qiandao Lake, and the town was forgotten. Divers found it again in 2001, with its Ming and Qing walls, gates and carved arches standing whole about 40 m down.
legends.when: Flooded 1959; explored by divers from 2001

origin.text: BBC Travel, "China's Atlantis of the East" (2014)

legends.look_for: A whole walled town standing upright in fresh water: city walls, five gates, streets and timber buildings, clear in sonar of the lake bed and to divers.

places.name: Shicheng, Qiandao Lake
places.claim: The town lies about 40 m under the lake that formed when the valley was dammed in 1959. Cold, still fresh water has kept its Ming and Qing dynasty stonework and woodwork in good order.

sources.title: BBC Travel, "China's Atlantis of the East" (2014)
Wikipedia, "Shicheng, Zhejiang"

legends.name: Olous
legends.summary: Olous was a Greek city state on the north coast of Crete, at the neck of land that joins the Spinalonga peninsula to the island. Part of it now lies under the shallow water of Elounda Bay. Its walls can be seen by swimmers, and geophysicists have used it to test survey methods for very shallow sea.
legends.when: City of the Classical and Hellenistic periods

origin.text: K. Simyrdanis, N. Papadopoulos and G. Cantoro, "Shallow Off-Shore Archaeological Prospection with 3-D Electrical Resistivity Tomography: The Case of Olous (Modern Elounda), Greece", Remote Sensing 8 (2016)

legends.look_for: Wall lines under less than 2 m of water and under the sand below it. Electrical resistivity tomography with cables laid on the sea floor maps buried walls where sonar and magnetometers do poorly.

places.name: Olous (Elounda)
places.claim: A team from the Institute for Mediterranean Studies ran 8.3 km of electrical resistivity lines over the shallow sea bed here and mapped buried and submerged structures of the ancient town.

sources.title: K. Simyrdanis, N. Papadopoulos and G. Cantoro, "Shallow Off-Shore Archaeological Prospection with 3-D Electrical Resistivity Tomography: The Case of Olous" (2016)
Wikipedia, "Olous"

legends.name: Phanagoria
legends.summary: Phanagoria was the largest Greek city on the Taman Peninsula, on the Asian side of the Kerch Strait, founded about 543 BCE by settlers from Teos. It was later the eastern capital of the Bosporan Kingdom. About a third of its 75 hectares is now under the sea.
legends.when: Founded about 543 BCE; lived in until the Middle Ages

origin.text: Wikipedia, "Phanagoria"

legends.look_for: Harbour works, streets and building stone in a few metres of water off the present beach, mapped by divers and sonar. The land part is a low mound with a large cemetery around it.

places.name: Phanagoria
places.claim: A survey in 1998 recorded the submerged remains of the city in Taman Bay. One third of the ancient town lies under water.

sources.title: C. Brandon and G. Tsetskhladze, "Notes on the Survey of the Submerged Remains of Phanagoria in the Taman Peninsula, 1998", Ancient West and East 1 (2002)
Wikipedia, "Phanagoria"

legends.name: Seven Pagodas of Mahabalipuram
legends.summary: European sailors called Mahabalipuram, on the coast of Tamil Nadu, the Seven Pagodas, and local tradition says six temples besides the Shore Temple lie under the sea. Divers reported man-made stonework offshore in 2002, and the tsunami of December 2004 stripped sand from buried temple remains on the beach. The offshore structures have not been dated, so how much of the legend is true is still open.
legends.when: Shore Temple built in the 8th century CE; offshore finds reported 2002 and 2005

origin.text: Local tradition of seven temples, six of them under the sea, known to European travellers as the Seven Pagodas

legends.look_for: Cut granite blocks, wall lines and steps on the seabed within a kilometre of the shore, seen by divers and side-scan sonar, and brick or stone temple bases under beach sand. Natural granite outcrops here split into block shapes too, so each feature needs a diver.

places.name: Seabed off the Shore Temple
places.claim: In April 2002 divers from India's National Institute of Oceanography and the British Scientific Exploration Society reported ruins spread over a wide area of seabed off Mahabalipuram. After the 2004 tsunami the Archaeological Survey of India and the navy found more remains close to shore.
places.against: The structures are not dated and some may be natural rock; Graham Hancock, who was on the 2002 team, used them to argue for a far older lost civilisation, which archaeologists do not accept.

sources.title: BBC News, "Lost city found off Indian coast" (2002)
Wikipedia, "Seven Pagodas of Mahabalipuram"

places.name: Temple remains uncovered by the 2004 tsunami
places.claim: After the tsunami the Archaeological Survey of India dug on the beach and found the remains of a brick temple under a later Pallava one, with layers of shells and debris showing that earlier tsunamis had twice flattened the complex.

sources.title: BBC News, "Tsunami reveals ancient temple sites" (2005)

legends.name: Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam)
legends.summary: Poompuhar was the great port of the early Chola kings at the mouth of the Kaveri, praised in Tamil poems of about 2,000 years ago and in the epics Silappathikaram and Manimekalai. Erosion and floods washed much of the old town away. Remains of the port lie on the shore and in shallow water; a claim that sonar shows a far older harbour 30 km out to sea is not accepted.
legends.when: Port of about 300 BCE to 300 CE; underwater surveys since the 1990s

origin.text: Tamil Sangam poems and the epics Silappathikaram and Manimekalai

legends.look_for: Brick structures, ring wells and pottery on the shore and in a few metres of water, found by divers. Claims from coarse global depth grids need multibeam survey and diving to check, because gridding makes false straight lines.

places.name: Poompuhar coast
places.claim: Underwater exploration by the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology in 2026 found ancient ring wells and a piece of a West Asian torpedo jar off the coast, more evidence of the early historic port.

sources.title: The Hindu, "Torpedo jar fragment, ring wells found in underwater archaeological exploration off the Poompuhar coast" (2026)
Wikipedia, "Poombuhar"

places.name: Claimed harbour 30 km offshore
places.claim: A paper in Current Science in 2020 reported that depth data (the GEBCO global grid and multibeam sonar) show a harbour and related structures on a drowned delta of the Kaveri about 30 km out to sea, a delta the authors put at 11,000 to 15,000 years old.
places.against: Nothing has been sampled or dated on the seabed; the shapes come from depth grids alone, and a harbour that old would predate any known port by thousands of years.

sources.title: S. M. Ramasamy et al., "Detection of submerged harbour using GEBCO and MBES data, in the offshore region of ancient port city Poompuhar, South India", Current Science 119 (2020)

legends.name: Rhapta
legends.summary: Rhapta was the last market town on the coast of East Africa known to Greek and Roman traders. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written in the 1st century CE, says it exported ivory and tortoise shell, and Ptolemy calls it a metropolis. It was somewhere on the coast of Tanzania and has never been found.
legends.when: Described in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE

origin.text: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 16 (1st century CE) and Ptolemy's Geography; discussed in L. P. Kirwan, "Rhapta, Metropolis of Azania", Azania 21 (1986)

legends.look_for: Roman glass, beads and pottery in a coastal or river mouth settlement of the early first millennium CE. River deltas here shift and bury sites, so coring and survey of old channels seen in satellite images matter more than surface finds.

places.name: Rufiji delta
places.claim: G. W. B. Huntingford listed five proposed sites and preferred the last: somewhere in the Rufiji delta, opposite Mafia Island. The sailing distances in the Periplus fit this stretch of coast.
places.against: No town of the right date has been excavated there; other scholars argue for sites near Dar es Salaam or Pangani.

sources.title: B. A. Datoo, "Rhapta: the Location and Importance of East Africa's first Port", Azania 5 (1970)
L. P. Kirwan, "Rhapta, Metropolis of Azania", Azania 21 (1986)
Wikipedia, "Rhapta"

legends.name: Bouldnor Cliff
legends.summary: Bouldnor Cliff is a Mesolithic site on the bed of the Solent, off the Isle of Wight, about 11 m under water. People lived there about 8,000 years ago, when the Solent was a wooded valley, and left worked timber, flint tools and hearths in peat. It was found in 1999 when divers saw a lobster throwing worked flints out of its burrow.
legends.when: Occupied about 6000 BCE; found 1999

origin.text: O. Smith, G. Momber et al., "Sedimentary DNA from a submerged site reveals wheat in the British Isles 8000 years ago", Science 347 (2015)

legends.look_for: A drowned land surface of peat and tree stumps at the foot of an underwater cliff, with flints and cut wood eroding out. Bathymetry finds the cliff; only divers find the finds.

places.name: Bouldnor Cliff
places.claim: Sediment from the old land surface held DNA of wheat about 8,000 years old, 2,000 years before farming is known in Britain, which the authors read as trade with farmers on the continent. Another scientist published a comment questioning the result.

sources.title: O. Smith, G. Momber et al., "Sedimentary DNA from a submerged site reveals wheat in the British Isles 8000 years ago", Science 347 (2015)
K. D. Bennett, Comment on "Sedimentary DNA from a submerged site reveals wheat in the British Isles 8000 years ago", Science 349 (2015)
Wikipedia, "Bouldnor Cliff"

legends.name: Alpena-Amberley Ridge hunting sites
legends.summary: About 9,000 years ago the water in Lake Huron stood far lower than now and a rocky ridge ran dry across the lake from Michigan to Ontario. Caribou crossed it and hunters built stone lanes and blinds to ambush them. John O'Shea's team found the structures on the lake bed, where nothing has disturbed them since.
legends.when: About 9,000 years ago; reported 2009 and 2014

origin.text: J. O'Shea et al., "A 9,000-year-old caribou hunting structure beneath Lake Huron", PNAS 111 (2014)

legends.look_for: Lines and rings of boulders on a drowned ridge: drive lanes, hunting blinds and caches. Side-scan and scanning sonar find them, then divers and remote vehicles look for stone flakes.

places.name: Alpena-Amberley Ridge, Lake Huron
places.claim: The Drop 45 Drive Lane is a stone structure built to channel migrating caribou towards waiting hunters. With the artefacts found beside it, it shows how early hunters organised the drives by season.

sources.title: J. O'Shea et al., "A 9,000-year-old caribou hunting structure beneath Lake Huron", PNAS 111 (2014)

legends.name: Zakynthos "lost city"
legends.summary: Snorkellers off the Greek island of Zakynthos reported what looked like paved floors and column bases on the seabed, and it was first taken for a lost harbour city. A study in 2016 showed they are natural: minerals that hardened around methane seeps in the sediment up to 5 million years ago. It is a useful example of how regular a natural rock can look.
legends.when: Explained as natural in 2016

origin.text: J. Andrews et al., "Exhumed hydrocarbon-seep authigenic carbonates from Zakynthos Island (Greece): Concretions not archaeological remains", Marine and Petroleum Geology 76 (2016)

legends.look_for: Ring-shaped and slab-shaped stone on a shallow seabed with no pottery, no tool marks and no mortar around it. Mineral and isotope tests show whether stone grew in place.

places.name: Alikanas Bay, Zakynthos
places.claim: Tourists and then Greek divers took the discs and slabs in 2 to 5 m of water for the remains of an ancient harbour city.
places.against: Geologists from the University of East Anglia and Athens found the "columns" are dolomite concretions formed by microbes around old methane seeps, and there is no pottery or other trace of people at the site.

sources.title: J. Andrews et al., "Exhumed hydrocarbon-seep authigenic carbonates from Zakynthos Island (Greece): Concretions not archaeological remains", Marine and Petroleum Geology 76 (2016)
University of East Anglia news release, "Underwater 'lost city' found to be geological formation" (EurekAlert, 2016)

legends.name: El Dorado
legends.summary: El Dorado, "the gilded one", began as a Spanish report of a Muisca ceremony in the highlands of Colombia: a new chief, covered in gold dust, rode a raft on to Lake Guatavita and threw gold into the water. Within decades the man had become a golden city, and explorers looked for it across the Amazon and the Guianas for two centuries. The ceremony was real; the city never existed.
legends.when: Ceremony reported in the 1530s CE; searches from 1541 into the 1700s

origin.text: Spanish chronicles of the Muisca ceremony of the gilded man, 16th and 17th centuries

legends.look_for: The real trace is small gold offerings in highland lakes and caves, found by divers, by draining and by chance. The lake that mapmakers called Parime was most likely seasonal flooding of savannah, which shows in radar and optical satellite images of wet and dry seasons.

places.name: Lake Guatavita
places.claim: This crater lake north-east of Bogotá is where chroniclers set the raft ceremony of the Muisca. Gold and silver offerings have come out of it, though every attempt to drain it since the 16th century has recovered little.
places.against: It is the source of the story, not a city or a hoard.

sources.title: BBC News, "El Dorado: The truth behind the myth" (J. Cooper, 2013)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Eldorado"
Wikipedia, "Lake Guatavita"

places.name: Pasca (find spot of the Muisca raft)
places.claim: In 1969 three villagers found a gold model of a raft carrying a chief and attendants in a small cave in the hills south of Bogotá. It shows the scene the chroniclers described and is now in the Gold Museum in Bogotá.

sources.title: BBC News, "El Dorado: The truth behind the myth" (2013)
Wikipedia, "Muisca raft"

places.name: Lake Parime and Manoa (Guiana)
places.claim: Walter Raleigh went up the Orinoco in 1595 to find Manoa, a golden city said to stand on a great lake called Parime. Maps showed the lake for two hundred years.
places.against: Later explorers, Alexander von Humboldt among them, showed there is no such lake; it was probably the seasonal flooding of the Rupununi savannah.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Eldorado"
Wikipedia, "Lake Parime"

legends.name: Lost City of Z
legends.summary: The British surveyor Percy Fawcett believed that the ruins of an old stone city, which he called Z, lay in the forest of Mato Grosso in Brazil. He went to look for it in 1925 with his son and a friend, and none of them came back. No stone city has been found, but archaeology in the Upper Xingu has since shown that large, planned settlements of earth and timber did exist in the region.
legends.when: Fawcett vanished in 1925

origin.text: Letters and notes of P. H. Fawcett, published by his son as Exploration Fawcett (1953)

legends.look_for: Not stone ruins but earthworks: ditches, raised roads, plaza rings and patches of dark fertile soil under forest. They show in lidar and, where forest is cleared, in satellite images.

places.name: Upper Xingu (Fawcett's last route)
places.claim: Fawcett wrote that his route would start from Dead Horse Camp, at 11°43' S, 54°35' W, and head east into the country of the Xingu headwaters. Many search parties have followed him there.
places.against: Fawcett's family later admitted that he gave false coordinates to throw off rivals, and no stone city of the kind he imagined has been found.

sources.title: The New Yorker, "The Lost City of Z" (D. Grann, 2005)

places.name: Kuhikugu
places.claim: Michael Heckenberger, working with the Kuikuro people, mapped a cluster of large settlements here with plazas, ditches and roads, lived in from about 1200 to 1600 CE. Stories of them may have reached Fawcett.
places.against: These were towns of earth and wood built by ancestors of the people who still live there, not the stone city of an unknown race that Fawcett described.

sources.title: M. Heckenberger et al., "Amazonia 1492: Pristine Forest or Cultural Parkland?", Science 301 (2003)
M. Heckenberger et al., "Pre-Columbian Urbanism, Anthropogenic Landscapes, and the Future of the Amazon", Science 321 (2008)
Wikipedia, "Kuhikugu"

legends.name: Paititi
legends.summary: Paititi is a legendary Inca refuge said to lie east of the Andes, in the rainforest where Peru, Bolivia and Brazil meet. Colonial reports spoke of a rich kingdom of that name, and Andean stories tell of the hero Inkarri withdrawing to it. Expeditions have found real Inca outposts in the forest, but no city.
legends.when: Reports from the 16th and 17th centuries CE; expeditions to the present

origin.text: Spanish colonial reports of the 16th and 17th centuries, and Andean stories of the hero Inkarri

legends.look_for: Inca stonework is regular (terraces, straight roads, rectangular platforms) and under cloud forest it shows best in lidar. Regular shapes in satellite images of this region have turned out before to be natural sandstone ridges.

places.name: Forests of Manú and the upper Madre de Dios
places.claim: Gregory Deyermenjian led expeditions here from 1984 to 2011 and recorded Inca remains at Mameria and elsewhere. Some versions of the legend place the city in the Pantiacolla hills of this region.
places.against: The finds are small outposts, and a set of pyramid shapes seen in satellite images of the area proved to be natural sandstone.

sources.title: BBC News, "Dundee explorer's search for 'lost city' of Paititi" (2011)
Wikipedia, "Paititi"

legends.name: Ciudad Blanca (White City)
legends.summary: Stories of a White City in the rainforest of La Mosquitia, in eastern Honduras, go back to the conquistadors and grew in the 20th century through explorers' tales. An airborne lidar survey in 2012 found real, unrecorded settlements in a remote valley there, and a ground team visited one in 2015. Archaeologists accept the sites but object to calling them the White City: the region holds many such sites, and no single legendary city.
legends.when: Legend from the 16th century CE; lidar survey 2012; ground visit 2015

origin.text: A letter of Hernán Cortés to Charles V, 1526, on rich towns in the region; explorers' tales of the 20th century

legends.look_for: Earthen mounds set around plazas, terraces, canals and roads under high rainforest canopy, visible only in lidar ground models. Stone sculpture lies on the surface at some sites.

places.name: Valley "T1" in La Mosquitia (location withheld)
places.claim: A lidar survey flown in 2012 for a project led by the film maker Steve Elkins mapped plazas, mounds and terraces in remote valleys, and Christopher Fisher's team published one, called T1, in 2016. What is confirmed is a group of ancient settlements, not the city of the legend; the pin is the biosphere reserve because the team does not publish coordinates.

sources.title: C. Fisher et al., "Identifying Ancient Settlement Patterns through LiDAR in the Mosquitia Region of Honduras", PLOS ONE 11 (2016)
The Guardian, "Archaeologists condemn National Geographic over claims of Honduran 'lost cities'" (2015)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve"
Wikipedia, "La Ciudad Blanca"

legends.name: Ciudad Perdida (Teyuna)
legends.summary: Ciudad Perdida is a Tairona town of stone terraces and stairways in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Colombia. Looters hunting for gold found it in 1972, and its objects on the black market led archaeologists to it; it was revealed to the world in 1975. The indigenous peoples of the Sierra say they always knew it, and call it Teyuna.
legends.when: Tairona town; looted from 1972; announced 1975

origin.text: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Lost City" (T. Muse, 2004)

legends.look_for: Round stone terraces, paved paths and long stairways on steep forested ridges. Under canopy they show in lidar; from the ground they are a day or more on foot from any road.

places.name: Ciudad Perdida (Teyuna)
places.claim: A gang of looters reached the terraces in 1972. Colombian archaeologists followed the trail of looted pieces, and the site was made public in 1975 as Ciudad Perdida.

sources.title: Archaeology, "Lost City" (2004)
Wikipedia, "Ciudad Perdida"

legends.name: Vilcabamba
legends.summary: Vilcabamba was the last capital of the Incas, a refuge in the forested foothills north-west of Cusco from which they held out against Spain until 1572. The Incas burned it when the Spanish came, and its place was forgotten. Hiram Bingham thought he had found it at Machu Picchu in 1911; in 1964 Gene Savoy showed it was the ruin at Espíritu Pampa, which Bingham had also seen.
legends.when: Inca refuge 1539 to 1572 CE; identified 1964

origin.text: The Guardian, "Peru's last Incan city reveals its secrets" (2018)

legends.look_for: Low Inca walls and platforms under tall forest, with burned layers from 1572. Little of it rises above the undergrowth, so lidar and clearing are needed to see the plan.

places.name: Espíritu Pampa
places.claim: Gene Savoy identified this ruin as Vilcabamba in 1964, and archaeologists widely accept it. Excavations have since found burned Inca buildings and, lower down, rich tombs of the much older Wari culture.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Peru's last Incan city reveals its secrets" (2018)
B. Bauer et al., Vilcabamba and the Archaeology of Inca Resistance (Cotsen Institute, 2015), "An Introduction to the Site of Espíritu Pampa"
Wikipedia, "Vilcabamba, Peru"

places.name: Machu Picchu (Bingham's mistake)
places.claim: Hiram Bingham, who was looking for Vilcabamba in 1911, was led to Machu Picchu and argued for years that it was the last Inca capital.
places.against: Machu Picchu is a royal estate of the 15th century in the wrong place; the Spanish accounts of the 1572 campaign fit Espíritu Pampa.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Vilcabamba, Peru"
R. Burger et al., "New AMS dates for Machu Picchu: results and implications", Antiquity 95 (2021)

legends.name: Machu Picchu
legends.summary: Machu Picchu is an Inca royal estate on a ridge 2,430 m above sea level, above the Urubamba river in Peru. The Spanish never recorded it, and it was known only to local farmers until one of them led Hiram Bingham there in 1911. Radiocarbon dates show it was in use from about 1420 to 1532 CE.
legends.when: In use about 1420 to 1532 CE; made known to the outside world 1911

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu"

legends.look_for: Fine cut-stone buildings and farming terraces on a ridge top. Before clearing, forest hid most of it; lidar surveys of the surrounding sanctuary are still finding terraces and paths.

places.name: Machu Picchu
places.claim: Hiram Bingham reached the ruins in 1911, guided by local people who knew them. New radiocarbon dates on burials published in 2021 show people lived there from about 1420, two decades earlier than the Spanish texts suggest.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu"
R. Burger et al., "New AMS dates for Machu Picchu: results and implications", Antiquity 95 (2021)
Wikipedia, "Machu Picchu"

legends.name: Seven Cities of Cíbola
legends.summary: Spanish stories told of seven rich cities to the north of Mexico. The friar Marcos de Niza claimed in 1539 to have seen one, called Cíbola, and in 1540 Francisco Vázquez de Coronado marched north to take it. He found the stone and adobe pueblos of the Zuni, which had no gold; they were the real places behind the tale.
legends.when: Reports of 1539 CE; Coronado expedition 1540 to 1542

origin.text: Report of the friar Marcos de Niza, 1539

legends.look_for: The ruins of the Zuni towns Coronado saw: rubble mounds of multi-storey room blocks on low rises, with Spanish metal such as crossbow points and nails from the 1540 fight. Metal detecting and surface survey have found such traces along his route.

places.name: Hawikuh
places.claim: Hawikuh was one of the Zuni pueblos that Coronado's army conquered in 1540; Spanish chroniclers called it Cevola or Cibola. Its ruin lies on the Zuni reservation in New Mexico, 19 km south-west of Zuni Pueblo.
places.against: It was a farming town of stone and mud, not a city of gold.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Seven Cities of Cíbola"
Wikipedia, "Hawikuh Ruins"

legends.name: Quivira
legends.summary: After Cíbola failed him, Coronado followed a guide's promise of a golden land called Quivira and crossed the plains to it in 1541. It turned out to be the country of the Wichita people in what is now Kansas, with large villages of grass houses and no gold. Archaeologists place it near the Great Bend of the Arkansas River in central Kansas.
legends.when: Reached by Coronado in 1541 CE and by Oñate in 1601

origin.text: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Quivira"

legends.look_for: Ancestral Wichita villages: storage pits, house floors, ditched circles and a scatter of Spanish chain mail and iron. Magnetic gradiometry, thermal imaging and drone lidar show the ditches and pits under pasture.

places.name: Wichita villages of central Kansas (Rice County)
places.claim: Coronado reached Quivira in 1541 and found the Wichita living there, without gold. Remains of several villages have been found near Lyons, in Rice County, along Cow Creek and the Little Arkansas River, together with objects of Spanish make.
places.against: No document fixes the name to one site; the match rests on the Spanish accounts of the route and on finds of Spanish make.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Quivira"
Wikipedia, "Quivira"

places.name: Etzanoa (Arkansas City, Kansas)
places.claim: Donald Blakeslee of Wichita State University matched the Spanish account of a "Great Settlement" seen in 1601 to sites at Arkansas City. In 2020 Jesse Casana's team used multi-sensor drone survey to find a large earthwork under a cattle pasture there.
places.against: The identification rests on fitting the Spanish descriptions to the ground; excavation is still at an early stage.

sources.title: J. Casana et al., "A Council Circle at Etzanoa? Multi-sensor Drone Survey at an Ancestral Wichita Settlement in Southeastern Kansas", American Antiquity 85 (2020)
Science News, "Drones find signs of a Native American 'Great Settlement' beneath a Kansas pasture" (2020)

legends.name: Norumbega
legends.summary: Norumbega appears on 16th century maps as a region, and then a rich city, on the coast of what is now New England. The name comes from Verrazzano's map of 1529. Samuel de Champlain sailed up the Penobscot in 1604 to look for it and found only a river and small native villages.
legends.when: On maps from 1529 CE; searched for in 1604

origin.text: Giovanni da Verrazzano's map of 1529, as "Oranbega"

legends.look_for: Nothing to find as a city. The lesson is in the maps: a native place name grew into a kingdom in the hands of European mapmakers.

places.name: Penobscot River (Bangor, Maine)
places.claim: Champlain looked for Norumbega in 1604 and took the Penobscot for its great river, sailing as far as the rapids near modern Bangor. Historians place the name in this region.
places.against: He found no city.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Norumbega"
Review of American Beginnings: Exploration, Culture, and Cartography in the Land of Norumbega (1995)

places.name: Norumbega Tower (Weston, Massachusetts)
places.claim: Eben Norton Horsford decided in the late 19th century that Norumbega was a Norse settlement on the Charles River and built a stone tower in 1889 to mark the spot.
places.against: There is no Norse site on the Charles; archaeologists and historians rejected his evidence then and since.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Norumbega Tower"
Wikipedia, "Norumbega"
Review of American Beginnings: Exploration, Culture, and Cartography in the Land of Norumbega (1995)

legends.name: Vinland
legends.summary: Icelandic sagas tell how Leif Eriksson and others sailed from Greenland about 1000 CE to a land of timber and wild grapes they called Vinland. For centuries nobody knew if it was true. In 1960 Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad found a Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, which proves the voyages; where the Vinland of the grapes lay, further south, is still open.
legends.when: Voyages about 1000 CE; Norse wood at the site cut in 1021 CE; found 1960

origin.text: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Vinland"

legends.look_for: Turf-walled halls show as low rectangular banks, which satellite images can flag, but only digging tells a Norse wall from a natural one. Proof needs Norse objects: iron boat rivets, slag from bog iron, a bronze cloak pin.

places.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
places.claim: Excavation after the discovery in 1960 uncovered eight timber-framed turf buildings like those of Norse Greenland and Iceland. In 2021 a marker left in tree rings by a solar storm in 993 CE dated wood cut with metal tools at the site to exactly 1021 CE.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site"
M. Kuitems et al., "Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021", Nature 601 (2022)

places.name: Point Rosee
places.claim: Sarah Parcak picked out this headland in south-west Newfoundland from satellite images in 2015. A test dig found what looked like a turf wall and a hearth with roasted bog iron, and the press announced a possible second Norse site.
places.against: Two summers of digging found no evidence of Norse activity; the team's own report to the province says so.

sources.title: CBC News, "Archeological quest for Codroy Valley Vikings comes up short" (2018)
National Geographic, "Discovery Could Rewrite History of Vikings in New World" (2016)

legends.name: Aztlán
legends.summary: Aztlán is the island homeland that the Mexica, the Aztecs, said they left to wander south and found Tenochtitlan. It is known only from their own histories, written down after the Spanish conquest. Scholars disagree on whether it was a real place in the north-west or a mythical mirror of Tenochtitlan itself.
legends.when: Migration set in the 11th or 12th century CE; recorded in the 16th century
