origin.text: Mexica migration histories written down in the 16th century, such as the Codex Mexicanus

legends.look_for: The histories describe an island town in a lagoon with reeds and herons. A real candidate would need a settlement of the right date with Aztatlán or early Mexica pottery; none has been tied to the story.

places.name: Mexcaltitán
places.claim: From the 1960s some Mexican scholars, Wigberto Jiménez Moreno among them, proposed that this small island town in a lagoon in Nayarit was Aztlán, because of its shape and setting.
places.against: No excavation supports it, and many scholars think it impossible to fix a mythical homeland on the map.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Aztlán"
The Codex Mexicanus (2018), ch. 5, "A History of the Mexica People: From Aztlan to Tenochtitlan to New Spain"

legends.name: Tollan
legends.summary: Tollan is the splendid city of the Toltecs in Aztec tradition, home of the priest-king Quetzalcoatl and the source of all fine craft. Most scholars identify the historical Tollan with the ruins at Tula in Hidalgo. The name also meant any great city, and some argue the first Tollan was Teotihuacan.
legends.when: Tula flourished about 850 to 1150 CE

origin.text: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Tula"

legends.look_for: A planned ceremonial centre with pyramids, colonnaded halls and ball courts, and a wide spread of houses around it, mapped by survey and air photos.

places.name: Tula (Hidalgo)
places.claim: The ruins at Tula, with their pyramid topped by warrior columns, are identified as Tollan, the Toltec capital.
places.against: The site is smaller and plainer than the city of the Aztec stories, which were part legend.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Tula"
Wikipedia, "Tula (Mesoamerican site)"

places.name: Teotihuacan
places.claim: Tollan was also a title for great cities, and Teotihuacan, far older and larger than Tula, seems to have been the first to bear it.
places.against: The Toltec dynasty of the histories belongs to the centuries after Teotihuacan fell.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Tollan"
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan"

legends.name: Lost Colony of Roanoke
legends.summary: In 1587 about 115 English settlers landed on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina. Their governor, John White, sailed home for supplies and could not return until 1590, when he found the settlement empty and the word CROATOAN carved on a post. Where the colonists went has never been settled.
legends.when: Settled 1587 CE; found abandoned 1590

origin.text: John White's account of his return to Roanoke in 1590

legends.look_for: Late 16th century English things in Native American settings: pottery, gun parts, copper. Ground-penetrating radar and magnetometry guide the digging, and the colony's own village may have eroded into the sound.

places.name: Roanoke Island (Fort Raleigh)
places.claim: The colonists lived on the north end of Roanoke Island. A small earthwork and a metalworking area from the 1585 expedition have been excavated here, but the village of 1587 has not been found.

sources.title: US National Park Service, Fort Raleigh National Historic Site
Wikipedia, "Roanoke Colony"

places.name: Hatteras Island (Croatoan)
places.claim: Croatoan was the name of Hatteras Island and of its people, who were friendly to the English. Digs at Native sites on the island have found English objects, among them a ring with a lion crest once thought to be the gold signet of a colonist.
places.against: Tests in 2017 showed the ring is plain brass, a common trade item; the other English objects could also have come by trade.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "The Mystery of Roanoke Endures Yet Another Cruel Twist" (A. Lawler, 2017)
National Geographic, "Newfound survivor camp may explain fate of the famed Lost Colony of Roanoke" (2020)

places.name: Sites X and Y, head of Albemarle Sound (Bertie County)
places.claim: A patch on John White's map in the British Museum hides a fort symbol 50 miles west of Roanoke. The First Colony Foundation dug there and found English pottery of the right kind on a bluff over Albemarle Sound, and argues a group of colonists moved inland.
places.against: Other archaeologists say the pottery could date from later English settlement in the area.

sources.title: National Geographic, "Newfound survivor camp may explain fate of the famed Lost Colony of Roanoke" (2020)
Wikipedia, "Roanoke Colony"

legends.name: Cahokia
legends.summary: Cahokia, across the Mississippi from modern St Louis, was the largest settlement north of Mexico before Europeans came. At its height between 1050 and 1150 CE it held 10,000 to 20,000 people and about 120 earthen mounds. It was abandoned by about 1400; its builders left no writing and its original name is unknown.
legends.when: Occupied about 800 to 1400 CE; peak 1050 to 1150

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site"

legends.look_for: Flat-topped and conical earth mounds around levelled plazas, borrow pits and the post holes of palisades and timber circles. Lidar shows mounds that ploughing has nearly flattened; magnetometry finds houses and pits.

places.name: Cahokia Mounds
places.claim: The site covered nearly 1,600 hectares. Monks Mound, its centre, is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas: it covers over 5 hectares and stands 30 m high.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site"

legends.name: City of the Caesars
legends.summary: Colonial Chile and Argentina believed in a rich city somewhere in Patagonia, founded by shipwrecked Spaniards or by refugees from the Inca empire, Reports of it went round for two hundred years, and the Jesuit Nicolás Mascardi spent the years 1666 to 1673 looking for it from Chiloé and Nahuel Huapi. No evidence shows that it ever existed.
legends.when: Reports from the 1520s CE; searches until the late 1700s

origin.text: R. Urbina, "La creencia en la ciudad de los Césares desde Chiloé en tiempos del jesuita Nicolás Mascardi, 1666-1673", Magallania 48 (2020)

legends.look_for: Nothing has been found. The real traces behind the story would be small: camps of shipwreck survivors on the Strait of Magellan and short-lived Spanish forts.

places.name: Nahuel Huapi Lake
places.claim: Mascardi crossed the Andes from Chiloé and set up a mission on the shore of this lake, from which he and other Jesuits made journeys across Patagonia in search of the city.
places.against: Two centuries of searching found nothing.

sources.title: R. Urbina, "La creencia en la ciudad de los Césares desde Chiloé en tiempos del jesuita Nicolás Mascardi, 1666-1673", Magallania 48 (2020)
Wikipedia, "Nicolás Mascardi"
Wikipedia, "City of the Caesars"

legends.name: La Navidad
legends.summary: When the Santa María ran aground on Christmas Day 1492, Columbus used her timbers to build a small fort on the north coast of what is now Haiti and left 39 men there. He came back a year later to find it burned and the men dead. It was the first European settlement in the Americas since the Norse, and its exact site is not yet proved.
legends.when: Built at Christmas 1492 CE; found destroyed on the second voyage

origin.text: Columbus's journal of the first voyage, December 1492

legends.look_for: Late 15th century European things inside a Taíno town: glass beads, hawk bells, Spanish pottery, pig and rat bones, and a burned structure with a well. Coring and magnetometry on the coastal plain guide the test pits.

places.name: En Bas Saline
places.claim: This large Taíno town near Cap-Haïtien, lived in from about 1200 to 1530 CE, is thought to be the town of the chief Guacanagarí, beside which Columbus built the fort. Kathleen Deagan of the Florida Museum excavated there and found European material of the contact years.
places.against: No structure that can be shown to be the fort itself has been found.

sources.title: Florida Museum of Natural History, "En Bas Saline"
Smithsonian Magazine, "The Lost Fort of Columbus" (2008)

legends.name: Mabila
legends.summary: Mabila was a fortified town in what is now Alabama where, in October 1540, warriors of Chief Tuskaloosa ambushed the army of Hernando de Soto. The Spanish burned the town and killed most of its defenders. The site of the battle, a turning point of the expedition, has been looked for since the 19th century and not found.
legends.when: De Soto reached Mabila on 18 October 1540 CE

origin.text: Chronicles of the Hernando de Soto expedition, 1540

legends.look_for: A small palisaded town with a thick burned layer and 16th century Spanish metal: crossbow bolt heads, chain mail links, horseshoe nails. Systematic metal detecting has been the method that works.

places.name: Marengo County, Alabama
places.claim: In late 2021 archaeologists announced Spanish objects from several Native American sites in this county and argued that they had found the province of Mabila, with the town itself within a few miles.
places.against: The town has not been found, and other researchers favour sites elsewhere in south-west Alabama.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mabila"
V. J. Knight Jr (ed.), The Search for Mabila (2009)

legends.name: Sak Tz'i'
legends.summary: Sak Tz'i', "White Dog", was a Classic Maya kingdom named in the inscriptions of its neighbours and on looted monuments, and every known mention of it came from other cities or from looted stones. Fieldwork in 2018 with the local community identified the site of Lacanjá Tzeltal, in Chiapas, as its capital.
legends.when: Classic period Maya kingdom; identified 2018, published 2020

origin.text: C. Golden, A. Scherer et al., "Centering the Classic Maya Kingdom of Sak Tz'i'", Journal of Field Archaeology 45 (2020)

legends.look_for: A royal centre with monumental buildings and carved monuments. What settled the identification was epigraphy: inscriptions on stones still at the site that name the kingdom.

places.name: Lacanjá Tzeltal (Lacandon forest, Chiapas)
places.claim: Charles Golden, Andrew Scherer and colleagues worked with the local community in 2018 and identified the site as the capital of the kingdom, known until then only from looted inscriptions. The pin is the region; the site is on private land.
places.against: The identification rests on inscriptions read at the site by the team that found it, and excavation has only begun.

sources.title: C. Golden, A. Scherer et al., "Centering the Classic Maya Kingdom of Sak Tz'i'", Journal of Field Archaeology 45 (2020)

legends.name: Site Q (La Corona)
legends.summary: In the 1960s finely carved Maya panels from an unknown city appeared on the art market. Scholars called their source Site Q and looked for it for decades. It proved to be La Corona, a small ruin in northern Guatemala: in 2005 Marcello Canuto found a panel still in place there that matched the looted ones.
legends.when: Looted in the 1960s; located 1996; confirmed 2005

origin.text: M. Canuto and T. Barrientos Q., "La Corona", in Approaches to Monumental Landscapes of the Ancient Maya (University Press of Florida, 2020)

legends.look_for: Looters' trenches cut into small pyramids are the mark of a plundered Maya site, clear in lidar. The proof came from inscriptions: place names and royal names on a panel in the ground that matched pieces in museums.

places.name: La Corona
places.claim: La Corona was located in 1996, and Ian Graham and David Stuart of Harvard's Peabody Museum went to study the heavily looted site; Stuart saw that its texts matched the Site Q panels. Canuto's find of a matching panel in the ground in 2005 confirmed it.

sources.title: M. Canuto and T. Barrientos Q., "La Corona" (2020)
Wikipedia, "La Corona"

legends.name: Iram of the Pillars (Ubar)
legends.summary: The Quran speaks of Iram of the Pillars, a city of the people of Ad that God destroyed, and Arab tradition tells of a lost trading town called Ubar or Wabar in the sands of southern Arabia. In 1992 a team that had studied space shuttle radar and satellite images dug at Shisr in Oman and found an old fort and caravan station on the frankincense route. The team called it Ubar; scholars accept the site but mostly not the name.
legends.when: Quranic story of the 7th century CE; NASA gives the site a life from about 2800 BCE to 300 CE; found 1992

origin.text: Quran 89:6-8, on Iram of the people of Ad

legends.look_for: Old caravan tracks worn into the desert floor, which converge on water and show in radar and multispectral satellite images even where dunes have since crossed them. The site itself is too small to see from orbit; the tracks that lead to it are not.

places.name: Shisr (Wubar), Oman
places.claim: Space shuttle radar and other satellite images showed old tracks, some running under later dunes, converging near the well of Shisr. Excavation there from 1992 uncovered a fortress on the frankincense route, which NASA and the expedition announced as the lost city of Ubar.
places.against: The identification of Ubar with Shisr, and of either with Quranic Iram, is not generally accepted: Ubar in the old sources may be a region or a people, and Shisr is a small fort.

sources.title: NASA/JPL Photojournal, "Space Radar Image of the Lost City of Ubar" (PIA01721)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Land of Frankincense"
R. Blom, R. Crippen, C. Elachi, N. Clapp, G. Hedges and J. Zarins, "Southern Arabian Desert Trade Routes, Frankincense, Myrrh, and the Ubar Legend", in Remote Sensing in Archaeology (Springer, 2006)
Wikipedia, "Iram of the Pillars"

legends.name: Zerzura
legends.summary: Zerzura is a white city or oasis said to lie hidden in the desert west of the Nile, full of treasure and guarded by a sleeping king. It appears in medieval Arabic writings, among them a lost treasure hunters' manual, the Kitab al-Kanuz. In the 1920s and 1930s British and Hungarian desert explorers made a sport of looking for it and mapped the Gilf Kebir plateau on the way.
legends.when: Named in medieval Arabic texts; expeditions 1929 to 1934 CE

origin.text: Medieval Arabic writings, including the lost treasure hunters' manual Kitab al-Kanuz

legends.look_for: Dry valleys with living trees in a plateau that is otherwise bare, which show as dark threads in satellite images. Rock art in the region records a time when the Sahara was green.

places.name: Wadis of the Gilf Kebir
places.claim: Flights by the expedition of László Almásy and Patrick Clayton in 1932 found two valleys with trees in the northern Gilf Kebir, and Almásy later reached a third. He argued that these three green wadis were the Zerzura of the legend.
places.against: They are seasonal pastures, not a city, and the treasure of the Arabic texts is fable.

sources.title: O. Wingate, "In Search of Zerzura", The Geographical Journal 83 (1934)
N. B. de Lancey Forth, "More Journeys in Search of Zerzura", The Geographical Journal 75 (1930)
Wikipedia, "Zerzura"

legends.name: Ophir
legends.summary: The Hebrew Bible says the ships of King Solomon and Hiram of Tyre sailed from the Red Sea to Ophir and came back with gold, precious stones and almug wood. A potsherd of the 8th century BCE found at Tell Qasile, inscribed "gold of Ophir", shows the name was real to people of the time. Where it was is unknown; Arabia, East Africa and India have all been argued.
legends.when: Voyages set in the 10th century BCE; inscription of the 8th century BCE
legends.look_for: Ancient gold workings: open cuts, shafts, grinding stones and slag near quartz veins, datable by pottery and charcoal. A Red Sea or Indian Ocean port of the right date with Levantine goods would be the other half of the proof.

places.name: Tell Qasile (the "gold of Ophir" ostracon)
places.claim: A potsherd found here in 1946, dated to the 8th century BCE, reads "gold of Ophir for Beth-Horon, 30 shekels". It is the only mention of Ophir outside the Bible.

sources.title: B. Maisler (Mazar), "Two Hebrew Ostraca from Tell Qasile", Journal of Near Eastern Studies 10 (1951)
Wikipedia, "Ophir"

places.name: Mahd adh Dhahab, Saudi Arabia
places.claim: In 1976 the US Department of the Interior announced that a joint US and Saudi geological team thought this ancient gold mine, in the Medina province of the Hejaz, could be the source of Solomon's gold. It was worked in antiquity and lies within reach of the Red Sea.
places.against: Nothing at the mine names Ophir, and old workings alone cannot settle a biblical place name.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Ophir"
R. Worl, "Ore controls at the Mahd adh Dhahab gold mine, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia", US Geological Survey Open-File Report 78-778 (1978)
Wikipedia, "Mahd Al-Dhahab"

places.name: Great Zimbabwe and Sofala
places.claim: Portuguese writers of the 16th century reasoned that Great Zimbabwe, the centre of the southern African gold trade, was Ophir. The German explorer Karl Mauch came upon the ruins while searching for Ophir.
places.against: Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestors of the Shona between the 11th and 15th centuries CE, two thousand years after Solomon.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Great Zimbabwe National Monument"
Wikipedia, "Ophir"

legends.name: King Solomon's Mines
legends.summary: The Bible credits Solomon with great wealth but names no mines; the phrase comes from H. Rider Haggard's adventure novel of 1885, set in southern Africa. In the 1930s the archaeologist Nelson Glueck linked the copper district of Timna, in the Arabah valley, to Solomon. Radiocarbon dating has since shown that copper was indeed produced there on an industrial scale in the 10th century BCE, though by whom is argued.
legends.when: Solomon is dated to the 10th century BCE; the novel is from 1885 CE

origin.text: H. Rider Haggard, King Solomon's Mines (1885)

legends.look_for: Black slag heaps, smelting furnaces, mine shafts and walled camps in a desert valley, plain in satellite images. Short-lived seeds and charcoal inside the slag layers give the dates.

places.name: Timna Valley
places.claim: The Timna mines were long dated to the Egyptian New Kingdom. Erez Ben-Yosef's team redated the main smelting camps and showed that work peaked in the Iron Age, around the 10th century BCE.
places.against: The dates fit Solomon's century but nothing links the mines to Jerusalem; they may have been run by the local kingdom of Edom.

sources.title: E. Ben-Yosef et al., "A New Chronological Framework for Iron Age Copper Production at Timna (Israel)", BASOR 367 (2012)
Wikipedia, "Timna Valley"

places.name: Khirbat en-Nahas, Jordan
places.claim: Thomas Levy's excavation of this very large smelting site in the Faynan district produced high-precision radiocarbon dates showing industrial copper production in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE.
places.against: As at Timna, who controlled the work is disputed.

sources.title: T. Levy, T. Higham et al., "High-precision radiocarbon dating and historical biblical archaeology in southern Jordan", PNAS 105 (2008)

legends.name: Land of Punt
legends.summary: For more than a thousand years the Egyptians sent ships to a land they called Punt and brought back incense, gold, ebony and live baboons. Queen Hatshepsut had her expedition carved on her temple at Deir el-Bahari in the 15th century BCE. Punt was real, but the Egyptians left no map; most scholars now place it on the African side of the southern Red Sea.
legends.when: Expeditions from the 25th century BCE (Sahure) to the New Kingdom

origin.text: Egyptian records from Sahure (25th century BCE) to the reliefs of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari

legends.look_for: Egyptian pottery and inscriptions at a harbour on the southern Red Sea or the Horn of Africa would mark Punt itself. Chemistry already helps: isotopes in the teeth of baboons mummified in Egypt point to where the animals were born.

places.name: Mersa/Wadi Gawasis (the Egyptian port for Punt)
places.claim: Kathryn Bard and Rodolfo Fattovich excavated this Middle Kingdom harbour on the Red Sea and found ship timbers, rope, cargo boxes and inscriptions that name expeditions to Punt and Bia-Punt in the 12th Dynasty.

sources.title: K. Bard and R. Fattovich, "The 12th Dynasty Punt/Bia-Punt Expeditions from Mersa/Wadi Gawasis" (2018)
Wikipedia, "Mersa Gawasis"

places.name: Eritrea and the Horn of Africa
places.claim: Oxygen and strontium isotopes in two hamadryas baboons mummified in New Kingdom Egypt show they were born in a region covering much of present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti and parts of Somalia and Yemen. The authors take this as evidence for where Punt lay.
places.against: The isotope region is wide and includes part of Yemen, so it does not settle between Africa and Arabia on its own.

sources.title: N. Dominy, S. Ikram et al., "Mummified baboons reveal the far reach of early Egyptian mariners", eLife 9 (2020)

legends.name: Great Zimbabwe
legends.summary: Great Zimbabwe is the largest ancient stone building complex in Africa south of the Sahara, the capital of a Shona state that traded gold to the Indian Ocean coast. It was built from the 11th century CE and abandoned in the 15th. European settlers long refused to believe that Africans had built it and gave it to Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba; excavation in 1929 settled the matter.
legends.when: Built 11th to 15th centuries CE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Great Zimbabwe National Monument"

legends.look_for: Curving dry-stone walls up to several metres thick on a granite hill and in the valley below, with the remains of clay houses between them. The wider town shows as low platforms and middens in lidar and air photos.

places.name: Great Zimbabwe
places.claim: Gertrude Caton Thompson's excavation in 1929 confirmed that the builders were African, and later work dates the main building to between the 11th and 15th centuries CE.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Great Zimbabwe National Monument"
S. Chirikure and I. Pikirayi, "Inside and outside the dry stone walls: revisiting the material culture of Great Zimbabwe", Antiquity 82 (2008)
Wikipedia, "Great Zimbabwe"

legends.name: Troy
legends.summary: Troy is the city of Homer's Iliad, which by the 18th century many thought pure legend. Frank Calvert and then Heinrich Schliemann, who dug from 1870, showed that the mound of Hisarlık near the Dardanelles holds a walled city rebuilt many times over 4,000 years, and that is accepted as Troy. Whether there was a Trojan War is a separate question.
legends.when: Occupied about 3000 BCE to 500 CE; excavated from 1870 CE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Archaeological Site of Troy"

legends.look_for: A tell: a mound built of one town on top of another. Later excavations found a lower town of Troy VI and VII beyond the citadel, ringed by a wide defensive ditch.

places.name: Hisarlık
places.claim: Excavations begun by Heinrich Schliemann in 1870 found a fortified citadel with many building levels. The levels of the Late Bronze Age, Troy VI and VII, are the ones usually linked to the Troy of the epic.
places.against: Nothing found on the mound names it as Troy; the identification rests on its place, size and dates, and nearly all scholars accept it.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Archaeological Site of Troy"
Wikipedia, "Troy"

legends.name: Akkad (Agade)
legends.summary: Akkad was the capital that Sargon built about 2300 BCE for the first empire in Mesopotamia. Its name is on thousands of tablets and it gave its name to the Akkadian language, but the city itself has never been found. Texts place it near the Tigris and the Diyala, within about 30 km of modern Baghdad.
legends.when: Capital of Sargon (reigned about 2334 to 2279 BCE) and his successors

origin.text: Mesopotamian royal inscriptions and later copies that name Agade

legends.look_for: A large tell with Akkadian period brick and inscriptions, perhaps buried under river silt or under greater Baghdad. Old river courses traced in declassified CORONA images and radar elevation data narrow down where a capital could have stood.

places.name: Tigris and Diyala confluence (Tell Muhammad)
places.claim: Texts put Akkad near Eshnunna and Sippar, not far from Kish, near the Tigris and not far from the Diyala. Tell Muhammad, in the south-eastern suburbs of Baghdad near the confluence, is one of the mounds proposed.
places.against: No inscription from any candidate site names it as Akkad.

sources.title: B. Foster, "Akkad (Agade)", The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (2019)
H. Weiss, "Kish, Akkad and Agade", Journal of the American Oriental Society 95 (1975)
Wikipedia, "Akkad (city)"

legends.name: Washukanni
legends.summary: Washukanni was the capital of Mitanni, the Hurrian kingdom that ruled northern Syria and Mesopotamia about 1500 to 1300 BCE and wrote to the pharaohs as an equal. The Hittites sacked it and the Assyrians took it over. Its site is not proved; the leading candidate is Tell Fekheriye at the head of the Khabur river.
legends.when: Capital about 1500 to 1300 BCE

origin.text: Hittite and other cuneiform texts of the Late Bronze Age

legends.look_for: A large mound with a Mitanni period palace and, with luck, an archive of clay tablets that names the city. Clay analysis of Mitanni royal letters found in Egypt has been used to test candidate sites.

places.name: Tell Fekheriye
places.claim: This largely unexcavated mound near Tell Halaf, at the head of the Khabur, was proposed as Washukanni in the early 20th century. Excavations by a German team led by Mirko Novák and Dominik Bonatz from 2006 gave the idea new support.
places.against: Many seasons of digging have not produced proof, and the claim is unconfirmed; many scholars have opposed it.

sources.title: D. Bonatz, "Tell Fekheriye", in Archaeological Explorations in Syria 2000-2011 (Archaeopress, 2018)
Wikipedia, "Waššukanni"
Wikipedia, "Tell Fekheriye"

legends.name: Tarhuntassa
legends.summary: In the early 13th century BCE the Hittite king Muwatalli II moved his capital from Hattusa to a new city in the south called Tarhuntassa. It later became the seat of a rival line of kings. Treaties describe its borders, but the city has not been found; it lay somewhere in south-central Turkey.
legends.when: Hittite capital in the early 13th century BCE

origin.text: M. Massa, C. Bachhuber et al., "A landscape-oriented approach to urbanisation and early state formation on the Konya and Karaman plains, Turkey", Anatolian Studies 70 (2020)

legends.look_for: A very large mound with a lower town, Late Bronze Age pottery on the surface and Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions. Regional survey, satellite images of old water courses and magnetic survey of the lower town are the tools in use.

places.name: Türkmen-Karahöyük
places.claim: A survey of the Konya plain found this mound to be a major Bronze and Iron Age centre, and in 2019 a farmer's tip led the team to a stone carved with a Luwian inscription of the Great King Hartapu. The surveyors tentatively suggest the city was Tarhuntassa in the Late Bronze Age.
places.against: The authors themselves call the identification tentative; other scholars place Tarhuntassa nearer the Mediterranean coast.

sources.title: M. Massa, C. Bachhuber et al., "A landscape-oriented approach to urbanisation and early state formation on the Konya and Karaman plains, Turkey", Anatolian Studies 70 (2020)
P. Goedegebuure, T. van den Hout et al., "Türkmen-Karahöyük 1: a new Hieroglyphic Luwian inscription from Great King Hartapu", Anatolian Studies 70 (2020)
University of Chicago News, "OI archaeologists discover lost city that may have conquered the kingdom of Midas" (2020)

legends.name: Thinis
legends.summary: Thinis was the home town of the first kings of a united Egypt, according to the historian Manetho, and the capital of its province for three thousand years. The kings were buried nearby at Abydos. The town itself has never been located; Egyptologists place it at or near modern Girga.
legends.when: Capital of the first two dynasties, about 3100 to 2700 BCE

origin.text: Manetho, Aegyptiaca (3rd century BCE), who calls the first two dynasties Thinite

legends.look_for: An Early Dynastic town mound, probably buried under Nile silt or a modern town. Deep coring, and satellite mapping of where the river ran 5,000 years ago, are the realistic ways to find it.

places.name: Girga and El-Birba
places.claim: The mainstream view places Thinis close to Abydos, at modern Girga or the neighbouring village of El-Birba.
places.against: Nothing has been excavated that proves it; the Nile has moved and the old town may lie under metres of silt.

sources.title: A. Othman, "Tni (Thinis), the lost capital of Egypt: a study of its history, civilizational role, and possible location" (2023)
Wikipedia, "Thinis"

legends.name: Pi-Ramesses
legends.summary: Pi-Ramesses was the great capital that Ramesses II built in the eastern Nile delta in the 13th century BCE. When its branch of the Nile silted up, later kings carried its statues and obelisks to Tanis, and for years archaeologists took Tanis for the lost capital. In the 1960s Manfred Bietak worked out where the vanished Nile branch had run, and digging and magnetic survey at Qantir showed the real city lies there under farmland.
legends.when: Capital of Ramesses II (13th century BCE); abandoned as a residence during the 20th Dynasty

origin.text: M. Bietak and E. Pusch, "Piramesse", The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (Wiley, 2012)

legends.look_for: Almost nothing shows on the surface. Mud-brick walls of palaces, temples, stables and whole street grids appear in caesium magnetometer maps of the fields, because fired and unfired Nile mud differ in magnetism from the soil around them.

places.name: Qantir
places.claim: Excavations and pottery survey at Qantir and nearby Tell el-Dab'a located the Ramesside capital. Nothing of it stood above ground; its plan is known mainly from geophysics.

sources.title: M. Bietak and E. Pusch, "Piramesse", The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (2012)
Wikipedia, "Pi-Ramesses"

places.name: Tanis (the earlier identification)
places.claim: Pierre Montet, who dug Tanis in the 1930s, found masses of stonework with the names of Ramesses II and identified the site as Pi-Ramesses.
places.against: It was later recognised that none of the Ramesside monuments at Tanis began there: they had been brought from elsewhere for reuse.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Pi-Ramesses"
M. Bietak and E. Pusch, "Piramesse", The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (2012)

legends.name: Avaris
legends.summary: Avaris was the capital of the Hyksos, kings of Levantine origin who ruled northern Egypt about 1650 to 1550 BCE until the Theban pharaoh Ahmose drove them out. Egyptian texts name it but its place was forgotten. Austrian excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, led by Manfred Bietak from 1966, proved the site and found wall paintings like those of Minoan Crete.
legends.when: Hyksos capital about 1650 to 1550 BCE; excavated from 1966 CE

origin.text: Review of M. Bietak, Avaris, the Capital of the Hyksos: Recent Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 84 (1998)

legends.look_for: Low mounds in delta farmland, with houses and tombs of Levantine type under them. Magnetic survey maps the mud-brick town and its harbour basins; old Nile branches show in satellite images and cores.

places.name: Tell el-Dab'a
places.claim: Excavation showed a large town of the Middle Bronze Age with Levantine houses, temples and burials, and above it a palace district of the early 18th Dynasty.

sources.title: Review of M. Bietak, Avaris, the Capital of the Hyksos: Recent Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a (1998)
Wikipedia, "Avaris"

legends.name: Sodom and Gomorrah
legends.summary: Genesis tells how God destroyed Sodom, Gomorrah and the other cities of the plain with fire and brimstone for their wickedness. The story may keep a memory of real ruined towns near the Dead Sea, but no site has been shown to be either city. Most scholars treat it as a moral tale, and the archaeological evidence for any candidate is inconclusive.
legends.when: Set in the age of Abraham, traditionally the early 2nd millennium BCE

origin.text: Genesis 18-19

legends.look_for: Walled Bronze Age towns near the Dead Sea with thick burned destruction layers. Claims of a cosmic airburst need shocked quartz and melt glass that stand up to independent testing, and so far they have not.

places.name: Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira
places.claim: These two walled towns on the south-east shore of the Dead Sea were destroyed and abandoned in the Early Bronze Age, with burned layers and a vast cemetery. The excavators Walter Rast and Thomas Schaub suggested they lie behind the story.
places.against: They fell centuries before the usual date for Abraham, and nothing at either site names it.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Sodom and Gomorrah"
Wikipedia, "Bab edh-Dhra"
L. Gasperetti and S. Sheridan, "Cry Havoc: Interpersonal Violence at Early Bronze Age Bab edh-Dhra'", American Anthropologist 115 (2013)

places.name: Tall el-Hammam
places.claim: Steven Collins of Trinity Southwest University, who has dug here since 2005, argues that this large Bronze Age city north-east of the Dead Sea is Sodom. In 2021 members of his team published a paper in Scientific Reports claiming that a cosmic airburst destroyed it.
places.against: Scientific Reports retracted the airburst paper on 24 April 2025, after an expert in research misconduct showed that images in it had been altered, and most archaeologists do not accept the site as Sodom.

sources.title: T. Bunch et al., "RETRACTED ARTICLE: A Tunguska sized airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam a Middle Bronze Age city in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea", Scientific Reports 11 (2021)
Wikipedia, "Tell el-Hammam"

legends.name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
legends.summary: Greek and Roman writers describe a terraced garden at Babylon, watered by machines, and count it among the Seven Wonders. It is the only one whose place has never been found: no Babylonian text mentions it and no remains have been identified in the ruins. Some think it a fiction; Stephanie Dalley argues it was real but stood at Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib.
legends.when: Attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605 to 562 BCE); Sennacherib reigned 705 to 681 BCE

origin.text: Berossus, about 290 BCE, as quoted by Josephus; later Greek and Roman writers

legends.look_for: Vaulted terraces with waterproofing and a water supply raised from a river or brought by canal. At Nineveh the aqueduct at Jerwan and the canal system are real and mapped; the garden itself is not.

places.name: Babylon
places.claim: The classical writers, drawing on the Babylonian priest Berossus, place the gardens at Babylon and credit them to Nebuchadnezzar II.
places.against: No surviving Babylonian text mentions them and no definite archaeological evidence has been found at Babylon.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Babylon"
Wikipedia, "Hanging Gardens of Babylon"

places.name: Nineveh
places.claim: Stephanie Dalley of Oxford argues that the gardens were the palace garden of Sennacherib at Nineveh, which his own inscriptions describe along with the canals and aqueduct that fed it, and that later writers confused the two cities.
places.against: The classical sources all say Babylon, and the garden at Nineveh has not been excavated.

sources.title: S. Dalley, "Nineveh, Babylon and the Hanging Gardens: Cuneiform and Classical Sources Reconciled", Iraq 56 (1994)
The Guardian, "Babylon's hanging garden: ancient scripts give clue to missing wonder" (2013)

legends.name: Xanadu (Shangdu)
legends.summary: Xanadu is the English name, from Marco Polo and Coleridge, for Shangdu, the summer capital that Kublai Khan founded in 1256 on the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. The site was abandoned in 1430. Its walls and mounds were never truly lost, and the site became a World Heritage Site in 2012.
legends.when: Founded 1256 CE; abandoned 1430

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Site of Xanadu"

legends.look_for: Three nested rectangles of earth walls, with palace platforms and a grid of streets, plain in satellite images of open steppe.

places.name: Site of Xanadu
places.claim: The remains cover 25,000 hectares north of the Great Wall: the palace city, imperial city and outer city of Kublai Khan's capital, laid out in 1256.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Site of Xanadu"

legends.name: Karakorum
legends.summary: Karakorum was the first capital of the Mongol Empire, built in the Orkhon valley in the 13th century and visited by envoys from across Eurasia. After the empire moved its centre to China the city declined, and the monastery of Erdene Zuu was built from its stones. Nikolai Yadrintsev identified the site in 1889, and a survey published in 2021 mapped the whole city for the first time.
legends.when: A town from 1220 CE; built up as capital from 1235

origin.text: J. Bemmann, S. Linzen et al., "Mapping Karakorum, the capital of the Mongol Empire", Antiquity 96 (2022)

legends.look_for: Faint earthworks of streets and house plots on steppe grassland, too low to see on the ground. Magnetic survey and a fine elevation model showed roads and buildings well beyond the old city wall.

places.name: Karakorum (Kharkhorin)
places.claim: A German and Mongolian team made new magnetic and topographic surveys of the walled city and the land around it. The maps show the city in a detail not seen before and show that it spread well beyond its walls.

sources.title: J. Bemmann, S. Linzen et al., "Mapping Karakorum, the capital of the Mongol Empire", Antiquity 96 (2022)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape"
Wikipedia, "Karakorum"

legends.name: Sarai
legends.summary: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the Mongol state that ruled Russia and the western steppe, founded by Batu Khan (ruled 1227 to 1255) on the lower Volga. Timur sacked it in the winter of 1395 to 1396. Two great ruin fields on the Akhtuba river, at Selitrennoye and Tsarev, have both been claimed for it, and which was Old Sarai and which New is still argued.
legends.when: Founded under Batu Khan (died 1255 CE); sacked 1395 to 1396

origin.text: M. Favereau and R. Pochekaev, "The Golden Horde, c. 1260-1502", The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire (2023)

legends.look_for: Spreads of brick rubble, glazed tile and kiln waste over several square km of river terrace, with no standing walls. Air and satellite images show the street pattern as soil marks.

places.name: Selitrennoye
places.claim: The ruin field at Selitrennoye, on the Akhtuba branch of the lower Volga, is one of the two great sites identified with Sarai.
places.against: Since the 19th century Sarai has also been sought at Tsarev, some 250 km upstream, and the written sources do not match the two sites neatly.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Sarai (city)"
M. Favereau and R. Pochekaev, "The Golden Horde, c. 1260-1502", The Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire (2023)

legends.name: Tartessos
legends.summary: Greek writers knew Tartessos as a kingdom rich in silver beyond the Pillars of Heracles, ruled by the long-lived king Arganthonios, and some speak of a city of that name at the mouth of a great river. The Tartessian culture of south-west Spain in the early first millennium BCE is real and well dug. No single capital city has been found, and many archaeologists doubt there was one.
legends.when: Culture of the early first millennium BCE

origin.text: Herodotus, Histories 1.163

legends.look_for: Mud-brick buildings deliberately buried under mounds, hoards of gold jewellery, and Phoenician imports. River mouths here have silted up by many kilometres, so the old coast must be mapped by coring before the search for a port can start.

places.name: Huelva
places.claim: Finds under the modern port city, including great quantities of early Phoenician and Greek pottery, led J. M. Luzón and others to identify Huelva with the trading town of Tartessos.
places.against: The remains lie under a living city and no palace or city wall has been found.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Tartessos"
Review of S. Celestino and C. López-Ruiz, Tartessos and the Phoenicians in Iberia (Oxford, 2016), American Journal of Archaeology 123 (2019)

places.name: Mouth of the Guadalquivir (Doñana)
places.claim: The German historian Adolf Schulten, whose publications from 1922 drew attention to Tartessos, held that the city lay buried under the shifting wetlands at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, the ancient Baetis.
places.against: No Tartessian city has been found in the marshes, then or since.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Tartessos"
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Tartessus"

places.name: Casas del Turuñuelo
places.claim: Excavation of this large Tartessian building in the Guadiana valley began in 2015. It has a courtyard used for animal sacrifice, and in April 2023 the excavators announced five carved busts of the 5th century BCE, the first human images known from the culture.

sources.title: S. Celestino Pérez and E. Rodríguez González, "Un espacio para el sacrificio: el patio del yacimiento tartésico de Casas del Turuñuelo (Guareña, Badajoz)", Complutum 30 (2019)
Wikipedia, "Turuñuelo"

legends.name: Shambhala and Shangri-La
legends.summary: Shambhala is a hidden kingdom in Tibetan Buddhist texts, a pure land ringed by snow mountains from which a future king will ride out. James Hilton borrowed the idea for Shangri-La, the valley monastery of his 1933 novel Lost Horizon. Neither is a real place, though several towns in the Himalaya have claimed the name for the sake of visitors.
legends.when: Shambhala in texts from about the 10th century CE; Lost Horizon published 1933

origin.text: Tibetan Buddhist tradition of Shambhala; J. Hilton, Lost Horizon (1933)

legends.look_for: Nothing: these are a religious ideal and a novel. The lesson is how a story can be pinned to a real town by decree.

places.name: Shangri-La City (Zhongdian), Yunnan
places.claim: In 2001 the Chinese government renamed Zhongdian county, in the Tibetan part of Yunnan, as Shangri-La (Xianggelila) after a campaign that argued it was the place Hilton had in mind.
places.against: Hilton's valley is an invention in a novel; the renaming was a tourism policy.

sources.title: Å. Kolås, "Tourism and the Making of Place in Shangri-La", Tourism Geographies 6 (2004)
Wikipedia, "Shangri-La City"

legends.name: Camelot
legends.summary: Camelot, the court of King Arthur, first appears in passing in a French romance by Chrétien de Troyes in the 1170s, six hundred years after the time Arthur is supposed to have lived. Earlier Welsh and Latin sources give Arthur other courts. Most scholars regard Camelot as a literary invention, and no site can be shown to be it.
legends.when: First named in the 1170s CE; Arthur is set about 500 CE

origin.text: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart (1170s)

legends.look_for: What can be tested is whether a given hillfort or Roman town was a seat of power about 500 CE: rebuilt ramparts, a large timber hall, and wine jars and tableware imported from the Mediterranean.

places.name: Cadbury Castle, Somerset
places.claim: John Leland wrote in 1542 that local people held this Iron Age hillfort to be Camelot. Leslie Alcock's excavation of 1966 to 1970 showed that it was refortified on a grand scale after the Romans left, with a great hall and pottery from the eastern Mediterranean: the stronghold of a major British ruler.
places.against: It proves a powerful lord of the right date, not Arthur, and the name Camelot is later fiction.

sources.title: L. Alcock, "Excavations at Cadbury-Camelot, 1966-70", Antiquity 46 (1972)
Wikipedia, "Camelot"
Wikipedia, "Cadbury Castle, Somerset"

places.name: Caerleon
places.claim: Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, set Arthur's court at Caerleon, where the ruins of a Roman legionary fortress and amphitheatre still stood. It is Arthur's court in the Welsh tradition and may lie behind the later Camelot.
places.against: The ruins are Roman military buildings of the 1st to 3rd centuries CE.

sources.title: Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain, book 9 (trans. A. Thompson and J. A. Giles), Wikisource
Wikipedia, "Camelot"
Wikipedia, "Caerleon"

places.name: Winchester
places.claim: Thomas Malory, in the 15th century, said firmly that Camelot was Winchester, where a great Round Table hangs in the castle hall.
places.against: Tree-ring dating shows the table is medieval, far later than Arthur, and its paintwork was done for Henry VIII; Winchester has no claim older than the romances.

sources.title: T. Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, vol. 1 (1485), Project Gutenberg
Wikipedia, "Camelot"
Wikipedia, "Winchester Round Table"

legends.name: Avalon and the grave of King Arthur
legends.summary: Avalon is the island where Arthur was taken to be healed of his wounds, in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th century history. In 1191 the monks of Glastonbury Abbey announced that they had dug up the bodies of Arthur and Guinevere, with a lead cross naming the place as Avalon. Historians regard the find as staged: the abbey had burned down in 1184 and needed pilgrims.
legends.when: Avalon first named about 1136 CE; "grave" found 1191

origin.text: Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain, book 11 (about 1136)

legends.look_for: A pit in a monastic cemetery would prove that monks dug, not what they found, and the lead cross they described is lost. Re-study of the abbey's excavation archive gives no support to an Arthurian burial.

places.name: Glastonbury Abbey
places.claim: The monks said they found two skeletons in their cemetery in 1191, under a stone with a lead cross that named King Arthur and the Isle of Avalon. Glastonbury has been equated with Avalon ever since.
places.against: A full re-study of the abbey excavations of 1904 to 1979, published in 2015, overturned older readings of the site; the link with Arthur was promoted by the medieval monks.

sources.title: R. Gilchrist and C. Green, Glastonbury Abbey: Archaeological Investigations 1904-79 (Society of Antiquaries, 2015)
Wikipedia, "Glastonbury Abbey"

legends.name: Vijayanagara (Hampi)
legends.summary: Vijayanagara was the capital of the last great Hindu empire of south India, a city that amazed Persian and Portuguese visitors in the 15th and 16th centuries. An alliance of sultanates defeated its army in 1565, sacked the city and left it empty. Its ruins at Hampi cover a wide granite landscape and were surveyed from the 19th century on.
legends.when: Capital from the 14th century CE; sacked 1565

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Group of Monuments at Hampi"

legends.look_for: Temples, palace platforms, market streets, aqueducts and miles of fortification wall spread among boulder hills. The wider suburbs and canals show in satellite images and lidar.

places.name: Hampi
places.claim: The site holds more than 1,600 surviving remains of the capital, among them forts, temples, shrines, pillared halls and water works.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Group of Monuments at Hampi"

legends.name: Mohenjo-daro
legends.summary: Mohenjo-daro, on the Indus in Sindh, was one of the largest cities of the Indus civilisation, built of fired brick in the 3rd millennium BCE with a street grid, drains and a great bath. The civilisation was wholly forgotten until the 1920s. R. D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India visited the mound in 1919 and 1920, and the excavations that followed from 1922 revealed a civilisation as old as those of Egypt and Mesopotamia.
legends.when: Built in the 3rd millennium BCE; found 1922 CE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro"

legends.look_for: A high citadel mound and a lower town of baked brick on a river plain. Much of the city is still unexcavated and lies below the water table; drilling and geophysics show it is far larger than the dug area.

places.name: Mohenjo-daro
places.claim: The ruins, found in 1922, are the best preserved city of the Indus civilisation, built entirely of unbaked and baked brick in the 3rd millennium BCE.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro"

legends.name: Loulan
legends.summary: Loulan was an oasis kingdom on the Silk Road, beside the lake of Lop Nur in what is now Xinjiang; the Han renamed it Shanshan in 77 BCE. When the rivers shifted and the lake dried, the town was abandoned to the desert. The Swedish explorer Sven Hedin found its ruins, and wooden tablets and silks in the sand have since told much of its story.
legends.when: Kingdom renamed Shanshan in 77 BCE; ruins found about 1900 CE

origin.text: Wikipedia, "Loulan"

legends.look_for: Wind-scoured mud-brick and timber ruins on a dead lake plain, with dry river channels leading to them. The old channels are clear in optical and radar satellite images and show where water, and so people, once were.

places.name: Loulan ruins, Lop Nur
places.claim: Sven Hedin discovered the ruined city and dug some of its houses. Remote sensing studies have since mapped the river system that fed the town in its lifetime.

sources.title: L. Zhu et al., "Analysis of the ancient river system in Loulan period in Lop Nur region", SPIE Proceedings (2010)
Wikipedia, "Loulan"

legends.name: Yamatai
legends.summary: The Chinese Records of Wei, written in the 3rd century CE, describe a country in the Japanese islands called Yamatai, ruled by a shaman queen named Himiko, who led a league of more than 30 small states. The directions in the text cannot be followed on a map. Scholars have argued for three hundred years over whether Yamatai was in northern Kyushu or in the Kinai region around Nara.
legends.when: Described for the 3rd century CE

origin.text: Chinese chronicles of the 3rd century CE (the Records of Wei)

legends.look_for: A large planned settlement of the early 3rd century with a palace-like compound, goods from all over Japan, Chinese bronze mirrors and a great mound tomb. Tree-ring and radiocarbon dates for the earliest keyhole tombs are the key evidence.

places.name: Makimuku and Hashihaka (Nara)
places.claim: Supporters of the Kinai theory point to the large settlement of Makimuku, which grew up suddenly in the early 3rd century, and to the nearby Hashihaka mound, which some propose as the tomb of Himiko.
places.against: The Imperial Household Agency does not allow Hashihaka to be excavated, and the dating of the mound is disputed.

sources.title: J. E. Kidder, Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai (University of Hawaii Press, 2007), ch. 12, "Makimuku and the Location of Yamatai"
W. Edwards, "In Pursuit of Himiko: Postwar Archaeology and the Location of Yamatai", Monumenta Nipponica 51 (1996)
Wikipedia, "Hashihaka Kofun"

places.name: Yoshinogari (Saga, Kyushu)
places.claim: Supporters of the Kyushu theory point to large moated Yayoi settlements in the north of the island, of which Yoshinogari, under full excavation since 1986, is the best known. Kyushu is where the Wei envoys would have landed.
places.against: Yoshinogari was at its height earlier than Himiko, and nothing there names Yamatai.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Yamatai"
Wikipedia, "Yoshinogari site"

legends.name: Kapilavastu
legends.summary: Kapilavastu was the capital of the Shakya clan, where Prince Siddhartha, the future Buddha, grew up. It never became a great pilgrim centre like nearby Lumbini, and its place was forgotten. Two sites on either side of the border of Nepal and India now claim to be it: Tilaurakot in Nepal and Piprahwa in India.
legends.when: City of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE

origin.text: Early Buddhist texts on the home of the Shakya clan

legends.look_for: A walled and moated town of the mid first millennium BCE with a palace compound, and monastery remains with inscriptions naming the city. Geophysical survey at Tilaurakot has mapped a planned street grid under the grass.

places.name: Tilaurakot, Nepal
places.claim: Nepal identifies this fortified town, with brick walls, a moat and gateways, as the Shakya capital and has put it on its World Heritage tentative list.
places.against: No inscription found there names Kapilavastu.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List, "Tilaurakot, the archaeological remains of ancient Shakya Kingdom"
Wikipedia, "Kapilavastu (ancient city)"

places.name: Piprahwa, India
places.claim: William Claxton Peppé opened a large stupa here in 1898 and found reliquaries, one with an inscription that mentions the Buddha and the Shakyas. Later digs found monastery sealings whose legend names Kapilavastu.
places.against: The seals belong to a monastery "of Kapilavastu", which may mean a community from the city and not the city itself; no town has been found at the site.

sources.title: W. C. Peppé and V. A. Smith, "The Piprahwa Stupa, containing relics of Buddha", Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1898)
Wikipedia, "Piprahwa"
Wikipedia, "Kapilavastu (ancient city)"

legends.name: Capital of the Mali Empire (Niani)
legends.summary: The Mali Empire of the 13th to 15th centuries was one of the richest states of its age; its capital was a great centre of the trade in gold and salt under Mansa Musa (reigned 1307 to 1332). The traveller Ibn Battuta stayed in the capital in the 14th century, but his account does not make clear where it was. Excavations in the 1960s at the village of Niani in Guinea were taken to have found it, but the dating and the texts leave room for doubt.
legends.when: Capital in the 13th and 14th centuries CE

origin.text: Arabic accounts of the 14th century, above all that of Ibn Battuta; discussed in J. O. Hunwick, Journal of African History 14 (1973)

legends.look_for: A large settlement of the 13th and 14th centuries with a royal quarter and a separate Muslim merchants' quarter, a mosque of fired or mud brick, and North African imports such as glazed pottery, glass and copper.

places.name: Niani, Guinea
places.claim: Niani, on the Sankarani river, is named in tradition as the capital founded by Sundiata Keita. Excavations there in the mid 1960s found a medieval settlement, which was taken to confirm it.
places.against: J. O. Hunwick argued from Ibn Battuta's route that the 14th century capital lay elsewhere, further down the Niger, and later scholars have questioned the dates from Niani.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Niani"
J. O. Hunwick, "The mid-fourteenth century capital of Mali", The Journal of African History 14 (1973)

legends.name: Nan Madol
legends.summary: Nan Madol is a group of more than 100 artificial islets built of basalt columns and coral rubble on the reef of Pohnpei, in Micronesia. It was the ritual and political seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled the island until about 1628. It was never lost to the people of Pohnpei; writers on lost continents have often tried to claim it, with no basis.
legends.when: Megalithic building from about 1180 CE; seat of power until about 1628

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia"

legends.look_for: Walls of stacked basalt logs on rectangular islets divided by tidal canals, much of it under mangrove. Lidar through the canopy and uranium-thorium dating of coral fill gave its plan and its age.

places.name: Nan Madol, Pohnpei
places.claim: Uranium-thorium dating of coral used as building fill, with chemical sourcing of the basalt, puts the start of monument building here at 1180 to 1200 CE, centuries before similar works on other Pacific islands.

sources.title: M. McCoy, H. Alderson et al., "Earliest direct evidence of monument building at the archaeological site of Nan Madol (Pohnpei, Micronesia) identified using 230Th/U coral dating", Quaternary Research 86 (2016)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia"

legends.name: Hawaiki
legends.summary: Hawaiki is the homeland from which, in the traditions of the Māori and other Polynesian peoples, their ancestors set sail, and to which the spirits of the dead return. It is a mythical place and not one island: the name moved with the voyagers. But it has real roots, since Havai'i is the old name of Ra'iātea in the Society Islands, a centre from which eastern Polynesia was settled.
legends.when: Traditions of the settlement of East Polynesia, about 1000 to 1300 CE

origin.text: Polynesian oral tradition

legends.look_for: The evidence is in language, genetics and the dating of first settlement on each island group, not in ruins. Temple platforms (marae) share forms and names across thousands of kilometres of ocean.

places.name: Ra'iātea and Taputapuātea
places.claim: Havai'i is the old name for Ra'iātea, and the marae of Taputapuātea on its coast was a religious centre from which stones were carried to found marae of the same name on other islands. UNESCO describes it as the ancestral homeland of Polynesian culture.
places.against: Other island groups have their own Hawaiki; the name also survives in Savai'i in Samoa and in Hawai'i.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Taputapuātea"
Wikipedia, "Hawaiki"

legends.name: Dilmun
legends.summary: Sumerian texts speak of Dilmun as a trading partner across the sea and, in myth, as a pure land without sickness or death, the home of the flood hero. It was a real place: the trading kingdom of the Gulf, centred on the island of Bahrain. A Danish expedition that dug from 1954 to 1972 found its capital at Qal'at al-Bahrain.
legends.when: Named from about 3000 BCE; capital occupied from about 2300 BCE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Qal'at al-Bahrain: Ancient Harbour and Capital of Dilmun"

legends.look_for: A tell beside an old harbour, with stamp seals, weights and pottery that tie it to both Mesopotamia and the Indus. Tens of thousands of burial mounds across the north of Bahrain mark the kingdom in air photos.

places.name: Qal'at al-Bahrain
places.claim: The mound is a tell built up by continuous occupation from about 2300 BCE to the 16th century CE. It was the capital of Dilmun.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Qal'at al-Bahrain: Ancient Harbour and Capital of Dilmun"

legends.name: Lost City of the Kalahari
legends.summary: In 1885 the showman Guillermo Farini crossed part of the Kalahari and reported the ruins of a great walled city half buried in the sand. Dozens of expeditions went looking for it in the 20th century. In the 1960s A. J. Clement retraced Farini's route and concluded that he had seen a natural outcrop of weathered rock that looks like masonry.
legends.when: Reported 1885 CE; explained in the 1960s

origin.text: G. A. Farini, Through the Kalahari Desert (1886)

legends.look_for: Dolerite and similar rocks weather into flat-sided blocks that sit in rows like walls. On satellite images they follow the natural lines of the rock, and no pottery or other debris lies around them.

places.name: Southern Kalahari (Farini's route)
places.claim: Farini wrote, in the book of his journey, of the ruins of a walled city half buried in sand.
places.against: A. J. Clement found a rock formation on the route that matches the description and judged that the "city" exists only as a natural formation, about 180 million years old.

sources.title: E. Haldeman, "Lost City of the Kalahari", The South African Archaeological Bulletin 13 (1958)
G. A. Farini, Through the Kalahari Desert (1886), Smithsonian Libraries
Wikipedia, "Lost City of the Kalahari"

legends.name: Caracol lidar survey
legends.summary: Caracol is a large Classic Maya city in the forest of western Belize, first reported in 1937 and dug for decades by Arlen and Diane Chase. In 2009 they had it scanned by airborne lidar, the first time the method was used on a whole Maya city. In a few days of flying it showed the full extent of the city under the canopy, with its causeways, reservoirs and farming terraces.
legends.when: Classic Maya city, lived in until about 950 CE; lidar flown 2009

origin.text: A. Chase, D. Chase et al., "Airborne LiDAR, archaeology, and the ancient Maya landscape at Caracol, Belize", Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011)

legends.look_for: In a lidar ground model: thousands of low terraces following the hill contours, straight raised causeways joining plaza groups, and square reservoirs. None of it shows in satellite photos of the canopy.

places.name: Caracol
places.claim: The Chases had lidar flown over the city in the dry season of 2009. It gave a fast view of the whole site and its surroundings, about 200 square km, and became the model for lidar work across the Maya lowlands.

sources.title: A. Chase, D. Chase et al., "Airborne LiDAR, archaeology, and the ancient Maya landscape at Caracol, Belize", Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011)
Wikipedia, "Caracol"

legends.name: Angkor lidar surveys
legends.summary: The temples of Angkor in Cambodia were never lost, but the wooden cities around them rotted away and forest covered the ground. Airborne lidar flown in 2012 showed that Angkor Wat and the other temples stood inside a planned grid of streets, canals and house mounds. It confirmed that Angkor was the largest settlement complex of the pre-industrial world.
legends.when: Khmer capitals of the 9th to 15th centuries CE; lidar flown 2012

origin.text: D. Evans et al., "Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar", PNAS 110 (2013)

legends.look_for: Under forest, a grid of low banks and ditches: city blocks, each with a house mound and a pond. Also canals, dykes and the faint outlines of reservoirs and quarries.

places.name: Angkor
places.claim: Damian Evans and colleagues used lidar to make ground models under the forest and found a formally planned urban landscape, not recorded before, into which Angkor Wat and the other great temples were built.

sources.title: D. Evans et al., "Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar", PNAS 110 (2013)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Angkor"

places.name: Mahendraparvata (Phnom Kulen)
places.claim: Inscriptions said that an early capital of the Khmer Empire, Mahendraparvata, stood on the Kulen plateau north-east of Angkor. An expedition led by Jean-Baptiste Chevance and Damian Evans mapped it with lidar in 2012, and a 2019 paper set out its full plan.

sources.title: J.-B. Chevance, D. Evans et al., "Mahendraparvata: an early Angkor-period capital defined through airborne laser scanning at Phnom Kulen", Antiquity 93 (2019)
Wikipedia, "Mahendraparvata"

legends.name: PACUNAM lidar survey of the Maya lowlands
legends.summary: In 2016 the Guatemalan foundation PACUNAM paid for the largest lidar survey then flown for archaeology: 2,144 square km of forest in northern Guatemala. The results, published in Science in 2018, showed that the Classic Maya lowlands were a network of densely settled, defended cities fed by intensive farming, and gave new population estimates for the region.
legends.when: Classic Maya, about 250 to 900 CE; lidar flown 2016; published 2018

origin.text: M. Canuto, F. Estrada-Belli et al., "Ancient lowland Maya complexity as revealed by airborne laser scanning of northern Guatemala", Science 361 (2018)

legends.look_for: House platforms in their tens of thousands, raised causeways, defensive walls and ditches, canals and field grids in swampy ground. Looters' trenches show too, as notches cut into mounds.

places.name: Northern Petén (Maya Biosphere Reserve)
places.claim: The 2016 survey mapped the natural ground and the archaeological features across 2,144 square km of northern Guatemala. It gave population estimates, measures of farming and evidence of large works that reshaped the landscape.

sources.title: M. Canuto, F. Estrada-Belli et al., "Ancient lowland Maya complexity as revealed by airborne laser scanning of northern Guatemala", Science 361 (2018)

places.name: Tikal (hidden Teotihuacan-style compound)
places.claim: In the lidar of Tikal, one of the most studied Maya cities, researchers picked out a precinct that probably copies the Ciudadela and Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan, the great city of central Mexico.

sources.title: S. Houston, E. Román Ramírez et al., "A Teotihuacan complex at the Classic Maya city of Tikal detected by lidar", Antiquity 95 (2021)

legends.name: Aguada Fénix
legends.summary: Aguada Fénix, in Tabasco, Mexico, is the oldest and largest monumental structure known in the Maya area: a raised earthen platform 1,400 m long, built between 1000 and 800 BCE. Nobody knew it was there. It is so wide and low that from the ground it looks like natural terrain, and Takeshi Inomata's team saw it only in lidar.
legends.when: Built about 1000 to 800 BCE; reported 2020

origin.text: T. Inomata et al., "Monumental architecture at Aguada Fénix and the rise of Maya civilization", Nature 582 (2020)

legends.look_for: A long rectangle of raised ground, 10 to 15 m high, with straight causeways running out from it: too regular to be natural and too big to notice on foot. Low-resolution public lidar was enough to see it.

places.name: Aguada Fénix
places.claim: An airborne lidar survey and excavation found a previously unknown site with an artificial plateau 1,400 m long and 10 to 15 m high, with nine causeways radiating from it. Radiocarbon dates put its building between 1000 and 800 BCE.

sources.title: T. Inomata et al., "Monumental architecture at Aguada Fénix and the rise of Maya civilization", Nature 582 (2020)

legends.name: Casarabe settlements of the Llanos de Mojos
legends.summary: The Casarabe culture lived in the seasonally flooded savannah of the Bolivian Amazon between about 500 and 1400 CE. Mounds there had been dug for years, but lidar showed that the largest, Cotoca and Landívar, were centres of a planned settlement system with platforms, pyramids, causeways and canals. It was the first clear case of low-density urbanism in Amazonia.
legends.when: About 500 to 1400 CE; lidar published 2022

origin.text: H. Prümers et al., "Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon", Nature 606 (2022)

legends.look_for: Stepped platforms topped by U-shaped buildings and conical mounds, ringed by ramparts, with straight causeways and canals running for kilometres to smaller sites and reservoirs.

places.name: Cotoca and Landívar (near Casarabe)
places.claim: Lidar data for six areas showed two very large settlement sites, Cotoca and Landívar, each the hub of a network of smaller sites joined to it by causeways that still run straight across the savannah.

sources.title: H. Prümers et al., "Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon", Nature 606 (2022)

legends.name: Ocomtún
legends.summary: Ocomtún is a Maya city in the Balamkú ecological reserve in Campeche, Mexico, in a block of forest of some 3,000 square km that archaeologists had never entered. Ivan Šprajc's team reached it in 2023 after airborne lidar showed concentrations of buildings there. Mexico's heritage institute INAH announced it in June 2023.
legends.when: Pottery points to about 600 to 800 CE (Late Classic); found 2023

origin.text: BBC News, "Maya civilisation: Archaeologists find ancient city in jungle" (2023)

legends.look_for: Pyramid mounds more than 15 m high and plazas on a rise surrounded by wetlands, picked out in lidar and then reached on foot along cut trails.

places.name: Balamkú ecological reserve, Campeche
places.claim: INAH said that airborne laser scanning by the University of Houston helped the team spot many concentrations of pre-Hispanic structures. On the ground they found several pyramid-like buildings more than 15 m high and the many stone columns that gave the site its name, which means "stone column".

sources.title: BBC News, "Maya civilisation: Archaeologists find ancient city in jungle" (2023)
Wikipedia, "Ocomtún"

legends.name: Upano Valley sites
legends.summary: In the Upano valley of Amazonian Ecuador, at the foot of the Andes, lidar revealed a dense system of towns built on earthen platforms and joined by wide straight roads. Excavation had gone on there for years; the lidar showed the whole pattern. People lived there from about 500 BCE to between 300 and 600 CE, which makes it the oldest urban network known in the Amazon.
legends.when: About 500 BCE to 300 to 600 CE; published 2024

origin.text: S. Rostain et al., "Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon", Science 383 (2024)

legends.look_for: Clusters of rectangular earth platforms around plazas, drained fields between them, and dug roads that run dead straight for kilometres across ravines.

places.name: Upano Valley
places.claim: Fieldwork and lidar analysis showed clusters of monumental platforms, plazas and streets set among farm drainage, with a road system running over great distances.

sources.title: S. Rostain et al., "Two thousand years of garden urbanism in the Upper Amazon", Science 383 (2024)

legends.name: Valeriana
legends.summary: Valeriana is a Classic Maya city in Campeche, Mexico, that nobody had recorded. Luke Auld-Thomas, a doctoral student at Tulane, found it in 2024 in a lidar survey flown in 2013 by an environmental group to monitor forest. It has two centres with pyramids and plazas, causeways and a reservoir, and lies 15 minutes' walk from a main road.
legends.when: Classic Maya; lidar flown 2013; reported 2024

origin.text: L. Auld-Thomas, M. Canuto et al., "Running out of empty space: environmental lidar and the crowded ancient landscape of Campeche, Mexico", Antiquity 98 (2024)

legends.look_for: The lesson is where to look: in lidar already flown for forestry, carbon or flood mapping. In the ground model the city shows as pyramid mounds on plazas, house platforms, causeways and a dammed reservoir.

places.name: Valeriana (near Xpujil, Campeche)
places.claim: In a 2013 forest monitoring lidar dataset of 122 square km, Auld-Thomas and Marcello Canuto counted 6,764 buildings across three areas. One held a city of about 16.6 square km with two monumental centres 2 km apart, not yet excavated, which they named Valeriana after a nearby lagoon.

sources.title: L. Auld-Thomas, M. Canuto et al., "Running out of empty space: environmental lidar and the crowded ancient landscape of Campeche, Mexico", Antiquity 98 (2024)
BBC News, "PhD student finds lost city in Mexico jungle by accident" (2024)
The Guardian, "Lost Maya city with temple pyramids and plazas discovered in Mexico" (2024)

legends.name: Tugunbulak and Tashbulak
aka: Highland Silk Road cities of Uzbekistan
legends.summary: Tugunbulak and Tashbulak are two medieval towns high in the mountains of south-eastern Uzbekistan, at 2,000 to 2,300 m, where no one expected cities. A team led by Michael Frachetti and Farhod Maksudov mapped them with lidar carried on a drone. Tugunbulak covers 120 hectares, one of the largest highland towns known on the Silk Routes.
legends.when: Medieval Silk Routes, about the 8th to 11th centuries CE; published 2024

origin.text: M. Frachetti et al., "Large-scale medieval urbanism traced by UAV-lidar in highland Central Asia", Nature 634 (2024)

legends.look_for: Grass-covered mounds and lumps on a mountain pasture. Centimetre-scale drone lidar, processed to pick out wall lines, shows fortification walls, a citadel, terraces and hundreds of buildings.

places.name: Tugunbulak
places.claim: Drone lidar gave a detailed plan of monumental fortifications and buildings over 120 hectares, at an altitude where towns of this size were not thought to exist.

sources.title: M. Frachetti et al., "Large-scale medieval urbanism traced by UAV-lidar in highland Central Asia", Nature 634 (2024)

legends.name: Calakmul lidar survey
legends.summary: Calakmul, in the forest of southern Campeche, was the seat of the Snake kings, the great rivals of Tikal. A lidar survey released in 2022 by the Bajo Laberinto project and INAH showed how big it really was: a dense spread of large housing compounds, temples, canals and terraces under the canopy for kilometres around the known centre.
legends.when: At its height about 700 CE; lidar results announced 2022

origin.text: University of Calgary, "UCalgary research collaboration reveals new urbanization and landscape modifications at ancient Maya city" (2022)

legends.look_for: Apartment-like compounds of dozens of buildings round shared courtyards, grouped near temples and possible markets, with canals, terraces, walls and dams filling the land between.

places.name: Calakmul
places.claim: The survey, led by Kathryn Reese-Taylor with INAH Campeche, found large residential compounds throughout the scanned area, some with as many as 60 buildings, around temples, shrines and possible marketplaces. It makes Calakmul one of the largest cities in the Americas in 700 CE.

sources.title: University of Calgary, "UCalgary research collaboration reveals new urbanization and landscape modifications at ancient Maya city" (2022)
Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Lidar Survey Reveals Urban Sprawl of Ancient Maya City" (2022)

legends.name: El Mirador basin causeways
legends.summary: The forest around El Mirador, in the far north of Guatemala, hides some of the earliest and largest Maya cities, built between about 1000 BCE and 150 CE. Lidar published in 2022 by Richard Hansen's team identified more than 775 settlements in the basin, many joined by raised causeways into one web.
legends.when: Preclassic Maya, about 1000 BCE to 150 CE; lidar published 2022

origin.text: R. Hansen et al., "LiDAR analyses in the contiguous Mirador-Calakmul Karst Basin, Guatemala", Ancient Mesoamerica 34 (2022)

legends.look_for: White plaster causeways, now tree-covered ridges up to tens of metres wide, running straight between cities for many kilometres across seasonal swamp. Triadic pyramid groups and reservoirs mark the centres.

places.name: El Mirador
places.claim: The study identified more than 775 ancient Maya settlements in the basin and 189 more on the ridge around it, with a concentration of Preclassic sites connected by causeways. The authors read the web of causeways as a sign of early political union, a point other Maya archaeologists debate.

sources.title: R. Hansen et al., "LiDAR analyses in the contiguous Mirador-Calakmul Karst Basin, Guatemala", Ancient Mesoamerica 34 (2022)

legends.name: Geoglyphs of Acre
legends.summary: When cattle ranchers cleared forest in the Brazilian state of Acre from the 1970s on, perfect circles and squares of ditch and bank appeared in the pasture, some 300 m across. Hundreds are now known, most found in satellite images. A lidar study in 2023 found 24 more under standing forest and estimated that over 10,000 such earthworks remain hidden across Amazonia.
legends.when: Built about 2,000 to 700 years ago; recognised from the 1970s

origin.text: M. Pärssinen, D. Schaan and A. Ranzi, "Pre-Columbian geometric earthworks in the upper Purús: a complex society in western Amazonia", Antiquity 83 (2009)

legends.look_for: Ditches about 10 m wide laid out as exact circles, squares and octagons, joined by straight avenues. In cleared land they show in any satellite image; under forest only lidar finds them.

places.name: Eastern Acre
places.claim: Martti Pärssinen, Denise Schaan and Alceu Ranzi described the earthworks as the work of a previously unknown society that built precise geometric enclosures joined by straight roads. Brazil has put the geoglyphs on its World Heritage tentative list.

sources.title: M. Pärssinen, D. Schaan and A. Ranzi, "Pre-Columbian geometric earthworks in the upper Purús", Antiquity 83 (2009)
V. Peripato et al., "More than 10,000 pre-Columbian earthworks are still hidden throughout Amazonia", Science 382 (2023)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List, "Geoglyphs of Acre"

legends.name: Nazca geoglyphs found with AI
legends.summary: The Nazca lines of southern Peru have been studied for a century, in which time 430 figurative geoglyphs were found. In 2024 a team from Yamagata University and IBM Research reported 303 new figurative geoglyphs, found in six months of fieldwork after an AI model had flagged candidates in high-resolution aerial photographs. The new ones are small figures of animals and people beside old footpaths.
legends.when: Made about 2,000 years ago; AI survey published 2024

origin.text: M. Sakai et al., "AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose", PNAS 121 (2024)

legends.look_for: Faint relief-type figures about 9 m across, made by clearing dark stones from pale ground. They are too small and worn for the eye to find across 629 square km of desert; a model trained on few examples narrowed the search for people to check on the ground.

places.name: Nazca Pampa
places.claim: An AI system applied to the whole Nazca region led to the discovery of 303 new figurative geoglyphs within six months of field survey, nearly doubling the number known. Every candidate was checked on site by archaeologists.

sources.title: M. Sakai et al., "AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose", PNAS 121 (2024)
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa"
Wikipedia, "Nazca lines"

legends.name: Desert kites of Arabia
legends.summary: Desert kites are huge hunting traps: two low stone walls, sometimes kilometres long, that funnel gazelle into a walled pen. Royal Air Force pilots first saw them from the air in the 1920s and gave them their name. More than 6,000 are now known from Arabia to Central Asia, almost all found in satellite images, and the oldest are at least 9,000 years old.
legends.when: Oldest at least 9,000 years old; first seen from the air in the 1920s

origin.text: R. Crassard et al., "The oldest plans to scale of humanmade mega-structures", PLOS ONE 18 (2023)

legends.look_for: From above: a V or funnel of thin lines closing on an enclosure with small cells on its rim; on the ground the walls are a few stones high and almost invisible. Free satellite imagery is enough to map them.

places.name: Harrat al-Sham (Black Desert), Jordan
places.claim: The basalt desert of eastern Jordan and southern Syria holds the densest group of kites, the first to be seen from aircraft. In June 2015 a stone engraved with a plan of a kite, drawn to scale, was found on a site in south-eastern Jordan.

sources.title: R. Crassard et al., "The oldest plans to scale of humanmade mega-structures", PLOS ONE 18 (2023)
Wikipedia, "Desert kite"

places.name: Khaybar, Saudi Arabia
places.claim: Kites are thick on the lava fields of north-western Arabia, and the 2023 study illustrates plans of them from Khaybar. At Jebel az-Zilliyat, also in Saudi Arabia, the team found a boulder engraved with scale plans of kites.

sources.title: R. Crassard et al., "The oldest plans to scale of humanmade mega-structures", PLOS ONE 18 (2023)

legends.name: Mustatils of north-west Arabia
legends.summary: Mustatils are long rectangles of low stone wall, tens to hundreds of metres long, scattered in their hundreds across the lava fields and sandstone of north-western Saudi Arabia. They were noticed in satellite images and called "gates". Fieldwork in AlUla and Khaybar counties has shown that they are ritual monuments of the late sixth millennium BCE, linked to an early cult of cattle.
legends.when: Late sixth millennium BCE

origin.text: H. Thomas et al., "The mustatils: cult and monumentality in Neolithic north-western Arabia", Antiquity 95 (2021)
