legends.look_for: From above: a long narrow rectangle with a thicker platform at one end and a small entrance at the other, often in groups. Helicopter and satellite survey find them; excavation of the end chamber dates them.

places.name: AlUla and Khaybar counties
places.claim: Survey and excavation show the mustatils are more complex in build than was thought and served as ritual sites, with the earliest evidence for a cattle cult in the Arabian Peninsula.

sources.title: H. Thomas et al., "The mustatils: cult and monumentality in Neolithic north-western Arabia", Antiquity 95 (2021)

legends.name: Poverty Point
legends.summary: Poverty Point in Louisiana is a set of earthworks built by hunter-gatherers between 3,700 and 3,100 years ago: five mounds and six concentric half-rings of ridge around a plaza. People had farmed across the ridges for a century without seeing the pattern. Its design was recognised only when archaeologists looked at aerial photographs in the 1950s.
legends.when: Built 3700 to 3100 BP (about 1700 to 1100 BCE); pattern recognised in the 1950s CE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point"

legends.look_for: Curved ridges only a metre or two high and over a kilometre across: invisible from the ground, obvious from the air and in lidar hillshade.

places.name: Poverty Point
places.claim: The complex has five mounds, six concentric semi-elliptical ridges and a central plaza, made and used by a society of hunter fisher-gatherers. The ridges are so large that the geometric design was not recognised until researchers studied aerial photographs.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Monumental Earthworks of Poverty Point"
Wikipedia, "Poverty Point"

legends.name: Stonehenge Hidden Landscapes
legends.summary: Stonehenge is the most studied monument in Britain, yet the fields around it were largely unmapped. The Stonehenge Hidden Landscapes Project surveyed them with fast ground-based geophysics. Among the finds is a ring of huge pits, each 20 m or more across and at least 5 m deep, around the henge at Durrington Walls.
legends.when: Neolithic and Bronze Age monuments; project described 2012; pit ring published 2020

origin.text: C. Gaffney et al., "The Stonehenge Hidden Landscapes Project", Archaeological Prospection 19 (2012)

legends.look_for: Filled-in ditches, pits and post holes show as weak magnetic anomalies and radar reflections under grass. Very large features can be missed because they look like natural hollows until many are mapped together.

places.name: Durrington Walls pit ring
places.claim: A series of massive geophysical anomalies south of Durrington Walls, found in fluxgate gradiometer survey, proved on coring to be circular pits with a surface diameter of 20 m or more and a depth of at least 5 m. The authors read them as part of a late Neolithic circuit of pits around the henge.
places.against: The pits were tested by coring, not full excavation, and whether they form one planned monument has been questioned.

sources.title: V. Gaffney et al., "A Massive, Late Neolithic Pit Structure associated with Durrington Walls Henge", Internet Archaeology 55 (2020)
C. Gaffney et al., "The Stonehenge Hidden Landscapes Project", Archaeological Prospection 19 (2012)

legends.name: Kweneng
legends.summary: Kweneng is a large Tswana town of stone-walled homesteads, 30 km south of Johannesburg, lived in for several centuries up to the 1800s. Its ruins were known in part from air photos but thick bush hid most of them. Lidar studied by Karim Sadr of the University of the Witwatersrand showed a town with traces of about 900 homesteads.
legends.when: About the 15th to 19th centuries CE; lidar study published 2019

origin.text: K. Sadr, "Kweneng: A Newly Discovered Pre-Colonial Capital Near Johannesburg", Journal of African Archaeology 17 (2019)

legends.look_for: Clusters of dry-stone circles: cattle pens ringed by house enclosures, linked by walled cattle tracks, with ash heaps at the gates. Lidar strips away the bush and shows the whole street plan.

places.name: Kweneng (Suikerbosrand)
places.claim: Sadr describes Kweneng as a wide aggregation of stone-walled ruins that represent a pre-colonial Tswana capital, 30 km south of Johannesburg.

sources.title: K. Sadr, "Kweneng: A Newly Discovered Pre-Colonial Capital Near Johannesburg", Journal of African Archaeology 17 (2019)
The Guardian, "Laser technology shines light on South African 'lost city' of Kweneng" (2019)

legends.name: Garamantian towns of the Fezzan
legends.summary: The Garamantes were a Saharan people known to the Romans as desert raiders. Survey in the oases of the Libyan Fezzan, much of it with satellite images, has shown that they built real towns, fortified villages and underground water channels between the late first millennium BCE and the early first millennium CE. Their capital was Garama, modern Germa.
legends.when: Late first millennium BCE to early first millennium CE; satellite survey reported from 2011

origin.text: D. Mattingly and M. Sterry, "The first towns in the central Sahara", Antiquity 87 (2013)

legends.look_for: Mud-brick forts (qsur) with square towers, walled villages, field systems and long lines of shaft openings from foggara water tunnels. All show sharply in high-resolution satellite images of bare desert.

places.name: Germa (Garama) and the Fezzan oases
places.claim: David Mattingly and Martin Sterry show that the oasis settlements, though modest in size, meet the tests for towns, and argue that trans-Saharan trade and not farming alone called them into being.

sources.title: D. Mattingly and M. Sterry, "The first towns in the central Sahara", Antiquity 87 (2013)
Wikipedia, "Garamantes"

legends.name: Qalatga Darband
legends.summary: Qalatga Darband is a fortified town of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE at a mountain pass in Iraqi Kurdistan, on a route from Mesopotamia into Iran. It was first noticed in declassified Corona spy satellite photographs of the 1960s. A British Museum team confirmed it from 2016 with drone photographs of crop marks, geophysics and excavation.
legends.when: Mainly mid 2nd and 1st centuries BCE; investigated from 2016 CE

origin.text: British Museum, "Iraq Scheme: Darband-i Rania"

legends.look_for: Old spy satellite photos show sites before modern farming and building hid them. Here a large square feature in a Corona frame was followed up with drone images of crop marks, where wheat grows differently over buried walls.

places.name: Qalatga Darband
places.claim: Excavation of a square feature seen in the Corona image, with crop marks recorded by drone and geophysical mapping, confirmed a large fortified building. Pottery shows the site was mainly lived in during the early Parthian period.

sources.title: British Museum, "Iraq Scheme: Darband-i Rania"

legends.name: Falerii Novi radar survey
legends.summary: Falerii Novi is a Roman town in Lazio, north of Rome, now under fields. In 2020 a team from Cambridge and Ghent universities published the first high-resolution ground-penetrating radar survey of a complete Roman town. It showed the buried buildings of the whole town in depth, without digging.
legends.when: Founded after 241 BCE; radar survey published 2020 CE

origin.text: L. Verdonck, A. Launaro, F. Vermeulen and M. Millett, "Ground-penetrating radar survey at Falerii Novi: a new approach to the study of Roman cities", Antiquity 94 (2020)

legends.look_for: Radar time slices show wall footings, floors, drains and water pipes at each depth, so a town plan can be read level by level. Dry, stone-built sites under pasture give the clearest results.

places.name: Falerii Novi
places.claim: The survey is presented as the first high-resolution radar map of an entire Roman town, and as a method that could change how buried cities are studied.

sources.title: L. Verdonck et al., "Ground-penetrating radar survey at Falerii Novi: a new approach to the study of Roman cities", Antiquity 94 (2020)
Wikipedia, "Falerii Novi"

legends.name: Borgring
legends.summary: Borgring is a Viking Age ring fortress south of Copenhagen, one of the perfectly circular forts built in Denmark in the tenth century. Søren Sindbæk and Nanna Holm suspected a missing fort in the area and found a faint ring in a high-resolution lidar map. Geophysical survey and small trenches in 2014 confirmed it: the first such fortress found in Denmark in over six decades.
legends.when: Built in the 10th century CE; confirmed 2014

origin.text: H. Goodchild, N. Holm and S. Sindbæk, "Borgring: the discovery of a Viking Age ring fortress", Antiquity 91 (2017)

legends.look_for: A perfect circle 145 m across, ploughed almost flat, that shows as a faint rise in lidar. Excavation in 2014 found the north and east gates exactly where the standard plan of such forts puts them.

places.name: Borgring
places.claim: High-resolution lidar mapping, geophysical survey and targeted small excavation showed that the site is a Trelleborg-type ring fortress of the tenth century.

sources.title: H. Goodchild, N. Holm and S. Sindbæk, "Borgring: the discovery of a Viking Age ring fortress", Antiquity 91 (2017)
Wikipedia, "Borgring"

legends.name: Ahramat branch of the Nile
legends.summary: Most of Egypt's pyramids stand in a line along the edge of the desert, kilometres from the modern Nile. In 2024 Eman Ghoneim's team used radar satellite images, geophysics and deep soil cores to trace a silted-up branch of the river that once ran along the foot of that line. They named it the Ahramat Branch and argue that it was the waterway by which stone and workers reached the building sites.
legends.when: Active in the Old and Middle Kingdoms; published 2024 CE

origin.text: E. Ghoneim et al., "The Egyptian pyramid chain was built along the now abandoned Ahramat Nile Branch", Communications Earth & Environment 5 (2024)

legends.look_for: A buried river channel under farmland and sand, which radar from orbit can trace and cores then confirm. Pyramid causeways that end at the channel bank mark the old harbours.

places.name: Pyramid fields from Lisht to Giza
places.claim: The team combined radar satellite imagery with geophysical data and deep soil coring to trace the buried channel. Many Old and Middle Kingdom pyramids have causeways that lead to it and end at valley temples, which may have served as river harbours.
places.against: Independent teams still need to date the channel along its whole length to show it flowed at each pyramid's time.

sources.title: E. Ghoneim et al., "The Egyptian pyramid chain was built along the now abandoned Ahramat Nile Branch", Communications Earth & Environment 5 (2024)

legends.name: Roman forts in Cold War spy photographs
legends.summary: In the 1920s Father Antoine Poidebard recorded hundreds of Roman forts in the Near East from the air and took them for a line of defence against attack from the east. In 2023 Jesse Casana's team searched declassified CORONA and HEXAGON spy satellite photographs and found 396 more. Their wide spread does not fit a single defensive line.
legends.when: Roman period forts; study published 2023

origin.text: J. Casana, D. Goodman and C. Ferwerda, "A wall or a road? A remote sensing-based investigation of fortifications on Rome's eastern frontier", Antiquity 97 (2023)

legends.look_for: Square enclosures 50 to 200 m across with corner towers, pale against steppe soil in old black and white satellite film. Many have since been ploughed out or built over, so the old photographs are the only record.

places.name: Northern Fertile Crescent (Syria and Iraq)
places.claim: Using declassified CORONA and HEXAGON images the authors identified a further 396 forts spread widely across the northern Fertile Crescent, and question Poidebard's idea that the forts formed a defensive line.

sources.title: J. Casana, D. Goodman and C. Ferwerda, "A wall or a road? A remote sensing-based investigation of fortifications on Rome's eastern frontier", Antiquity 97 (2023)

legends.name: Tongatapu lidar survey
legends.summary: Tongatapu was the seat of an archaic state whose influence reached across the south-west Pacific between the 13th and 19th centuries CE. Lidar of the whole island has mapped thousands of earth mounds, roads and ditches. Phillip Parton and Geoffrey Clark used it to argue that the island was a low-density city long before Europeans arrived.
legends.when: State of the 13th to 19th centuries CE; lidar study published 2024

origin.text: P. Parton and G. Clark, "Low-Density Urbanisation: Prestate Settlement Growth in a Pacific Society", Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 31 (2024)

legends.look_for: Round and rectangular earth mounds, some faced with coral slabs, sunken roads between raised banks, and the big ditch and bank of the royal centre at Mu'a. They are low and under gardens, so lidar counts what ground survey cannot.

places.name: Tongatapu
places.claim: The study joins lidar mapping with methods from urban science to read the built landscape of Tongatapu, home of an archaic state, as low-density urbanisation.

sources.title: P. Parton and G. Clark, "Low-Density Urbanisation: Prestate Settlement Growth in a Pacific Society", Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 31 (2024)

legends.name: Tanis
legends.summary: Tanis, in the north-east Nile delta, was the capital of Egypt in the 21st and 22nd Dynasties. Its mounds were always known; Pierre Montet dug there from 1929 and in 1939 found royal tombs with their gold and silver intact. In 2011 Sarah Parcak showed that infrared satellite images reveal the street plan of the buried mud-brick town around the temples.
legends.when: Capital in the 21st and 22nd Dynasties (11th to 8th centuries BCE); royal tombs found 1939 CE; satellite plan 2011

origin.text: BBC News, "Egyptian pyramids found by infra-red satellite images" (2011)

legends.look_for: Mud-brick is denser than the soil around it and holds water differently, so buried walls show as lines in near-infrared satellite images taken at the right season. Houses, streets and suburbs appear without digging.

places.name: Tanis (San el-Hagar)
places.claim: An infrared satellite image shows the streets and houses of ancient Tanis, which cannot be seen on the ground. The same survey of Egypt, led by Sarah Parcak, reported 17 possible lost pyramids, more than 1,000 tombs and 3,000 ancient settlements.

sources.title: BBC News, "Egyptian pyramids found by infra-red satellite images" (2011)
Wikipedia, "Tanis"

legends.name: Itjtawy
legends.summary: Itjtawy was the capital founded by Amenemhat I, who ruled from about 1991 to 1962 BCE, and the seat of the kings of the 12th Dynasty. The pyramids of its first kings stand at Lisht, so the city must be near, under the fields of the Nile flood plain. It has never been excavated; satellite mapping and coring have narrowed down where it lies.
legends.when: Founded in the 20th century BCE; capital during the Middle Kingdom

origin.text: Egyptian texts of the 12th Dynasty, which name the residence Amenemhat-itj-tawy

legends.look_for: A buried town under several metres of Nile silt. NASA elevation data shows where the river ran and where a slight rise marks old settlement; cores then bring up pottery and worked stone from the right period.

places.name: Flood plain east of Lisht
places.claim: Sarah Parcak's team used NASA topography data to map the flood plain and work out where the Nile once flowed, then cored a likely spot with Egyptian colleagues and found a layer of pottery under thick mud. The cemetery at Lisht, where a joint mission mapped 802 tombs, belongs to the city.
places.against: A layer of pottery in a core is not a city plan; no buildings of Itjtawy have been uncovered.

sources.title: TED Ideas, "Gallery: Archaeological mysteries hidden in satellite images" (2016)
National Geographic, "More Than 800 Ancient Egyptian Tombs Mapped in Lisht Necropolis" (2018)

legends.name: Amber Room
legends.summary: The Amber Room was a chamber lined with several tons of carved amber, given by Prussia to Peter the Great in 1716 and installed in the Catherine Palace near St Petersburg. German troops took it down in 1941 and put it on show in Königsberg Castle, where it was crated at the end of 1943 and never seen again after the castle was bombed in August 1944. Many think the amber burned in the castle; a replica was finished in 2003.
legends.when: Made in the early 18th century; looted 1941; lost by 1945

origin.text: Smithsonian Magazine, "A Brief History of the Amber Room" (J. Blumberg, 2007)

legends.look_for: Amber burns, so what could remain is the stone mosaics that were set in the panels. One of the four, "Feel and Touch", turned up in Germany in 1997.

places.name: Catherine Palace, Tsarskoye Selo
places.claim: The room stood here from the 18th century until German soldiers took it down within 36 hours in 1941 and shipped it west in 27 crates. A reconstruction begun in 1979 and finished 25 years later is in the same hall.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "A Brief History of the Amber Room" (J. Blumberg, 2007)

places.name: Königsberg Castle (Kaliningrad)
places.claim: The panels were reinstalled in the castle museum, and in late 1943 the museum director was advised to take them down and crate them. In August 1944 Allied bombing destroyed the city and left the castle museum in ruins, and there the trail ends.
places.against: The simplest reading is that the amber was destroyed in the castle, whose ruins the Soviet government demolished in 1968; no search has found the crates.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "A Brief History of the Amber Room" (J. Blumberg, 2007)
Wikipedia, "Amber Room"

places.name: Wreck of the steamer Karlsruhe (off Ustka, Poland)
places.claim: Divers of the Baltictech group found the wreck of the Karlsruhe in 2020. She sailed from Königsberg in 1945 with a heavy cargo and was sunk by Soviet aircraft; the divers saw military vehicles and many unopened crates in her holds and suggested the Amber Room could be among them.
places.against: Nothing from the Amber Room has been recovered from the wreck.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Nazi shipwreck found off Poland may solve Amber Room mystery" (2020)

legends.name: Yamashita's gold
legends.summary: A persistent story in the Philippines says that Japanese forces under General Tomoyuki Yamashita buried a vast hoard of looted gold in caves and tunnels there before their surrender in 1945. It has drawn treasure hunters for eighty years, some of whom have died digging. Most experts and Filipino historians say there is no credible evidence that the hoard exists.
legends.when: Said to have been buried in 1944 to 1945

origin.text: Rumours in the Philippines since the end of the Second World War

legends.look_for: Wartime tunnels and caves are real and show in lidar and ground radar, but so do unexploded bombs. No survey has produced evidence of bullion.

places.name: Luzon
places.claim: Most digging has been in the mountains and old military sites of Luzon, where Yamashita's army made its last stand.
places.against: Historians such as Ricardo Jose of the University of the Philippines doubt the story, and the digging is dangerous: in 1998 a wartime Japanese bomb killed five treasure hunters who had dug it up.

sources.title: BBC News, "WWII Japanese bomb kills Philippines treasure hunters" (1998)
Wikipedia, "Yamashita's gold"

legends.name: Oak Island Money Pit
legends.summary: In 1795 a boy named Daniel McGinnis found a hollow in the ground on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, and with two friends dug into what seemed to be a filled-in shaft. Syndicates have dug there ever since, in the belief that pirates, Templars or others buried something below. The digging has cratered the island and cost lives, and no treasure has been found.
legends.when: Digging began in 1795 CE and continues

origin.text: Accounts of digging on the island from 1795

legends.look_for: Two centuries of shafts, tunnels and backfill have destroyed any original layers, so nothing dug up now can be tied to an early deposit. The island lies over water-filled cavities in anhydrite rock, which may explain both the "pit" and its flooding as natural sinkholes.

places.name: Oak Island, Nova Scotia
places.claim: The first diggers reported a shaft with layers of logs. Later companies reported flood tunnels from the shore and scraps of chain and parchment brought up by drills.
places.against: Four treasure hunters died in an accident in 1965, millions have been spent, and no treasure has been found.

sources.title: The Canadian Encyclopedia, "Oak Island"
Wikipedia, "Oak Island mystery"

legends.name: Montezuma's treasure
legends.summary: When the Spanish fled Tenochtitlan on the night of 30 June 1520, they carried the gold they had taken from the palace of the emperor Moctezuma, and much of it was lost in the canals as they were cut down. Legends say the Aztecs hid the rest. One piece of the lost loot is real: a gold bar found in Mexico City in 1981, which tests in 2020 matched to that night.
legends.when: Lost on the Noche Triste, 30 June 1520 CE

origin.text: Spanish accounts of the flight from Tenochtitlan on the Noche Triste, 1520

legends.look_for: The Spanish melted Aztec goldwork into bars for carrying, and such a bar, from the bed of an old canal on the line of their retreat, is what was found. Analysis of its mix of gold, silver and copper lets it be compared with dated Aztec finds.

places.name: Mexico City (the 1981 gold bar)
places.claim: A gold bar weighing 1.93 kg was found in Mexico City in 1981, where a canal of Tenochtitlan once ran. In 2020 Mexico's heritage institute INAH reported that its composition matches other Aztec gold of the period and confirmed it as loot dropped in the Spanish retreat of 1520.

sources.title: AFP via Phys.org, "Gold bar found in Mexico was Aztec treasure: study" (2020)

legends.name: Treasure of Lima
legends.summary: The story goes that in 1820, with rebel armies closing on Lima, the Spanish authorities loaded the city's church and state treasure on to the ship Mary Dear, and that her captain, William Thompson, killed the guards, sailed to Cocos Island off Costa Rica and buried it. Expeditions have gone to the island to dig since at least the 1850s and none is known to have found it. No document from the time proves the treasure was ever shipped.
legends.when: Said to have been buried in 1820 CE

origin.text: Treasure hunters' tales of the 19th century about the ship Mary Dear

legends.look_for: The island is steep, wet and prone to landslides, so a pit dug in 1820 would be hard to find and easy to lose. It is now a national park where treasure hunting needs permission.

places.name: Cocos Island
places.claim: Cocos Island, far off the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, is where the legend puts the hoard. UNESCO notes that the island is also known as Treasure Island and that pirates, whalers and sailors long used it for shelter and water.
places.against: Generations of searches have recovered nothing, and the story rests on tales told long afterwards.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Cocos Island National Park"
Wikipedia, "Treasure of Lima"

legends.name: Copper Scroll treasure
legends.summary: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is one unlike the rest: a list, punched into sheets of copper, of 64 places where gold and silver were hidden. Archaeologists found it in 1952 at the back of Cave 3 at Qumran. Scholars disagree on whether it records a real treasure, perhaps from the Jerusalem Temple, or an imaginary one; none of its hiding places has been identified for certain.
legends.when: Written about the 1st century CE; found 1952

origin.text: The Copper Scroll (3Q15), found in Cave 3 at Qumran in 1952

legends.look_for: The entries give directions such as "in the cistern", "under the steps", "at the tomb", with depths in cubits. Matching them needs ancient place names tied to real ruins, tombs and water systems around Jerusalem, Jericho and the Judaean desert.

places.name: Qumran, Cave 3 (where the scroll was found)
places.claim: The scroll, in two rolls of copper, was found on 14 March 1952 and is now in the Jordan Museum in Amman. It is a list of 64 places where items of gold and silver were buried or hidden.

sources.title: J. Høgenhaven, The Cave 3 Copper Scroll: A Symbolic Journey (Brill, 2020), "Translation of 3Q15"
Wikipedia, "Copper Scroll"

legends.name: Nazi gold train
legends.summary: A local legend in Lower Silesia says that in 1945 a German armoured train full of gold and looted goods was hidden in a tunnel near Wałbrzych. In August 2015 two men said they had found it with ground-penetrating radar, and a Polish deputy minister said he was "99% convinced". A university survey that December found no train, and a dig in 2016 hit only natural ground.
legends.when: Said to have been hidden in 1945; claim made 2015; dig 2016

origin.text: Local legend in Lower Silesia since 1945

legends.look_for: A buried train would be a huge mass of iron and should show strongly in magnetic survey, not only as a radar reflection. The geological survey by the Kraków team found no train, and the dig showed the radar "image" was natural ground.

places.name: Wałbrzych
places.claim: Piotr Koper and Andreas Richter told the authorities in 2015 that they knew the place and had radar images of a train with gun turrets. Deputy culture minister Piotr Żuchowski said the images had left him 99% sure.
places.against: A geological survey by Professor Janusz Madej of the AGH University of Science and Technology in Kraków found no train, and the excavation of 2016 was stopped when the anomaly proved to be natural geology.

sources.title: BBC News, "Nazi gold train: 'No evidence' of discovery in Poland" (2015)
Wikipedia, "Nazi gold train"

legends.name: Beale ciphers
legends.summary: A pamphlet printed in Virginia in 1885 tells of a man named Thomas Beale who buried gold and silver in Bedford County about 1820 and left three coded messages. One, solved with the Declaration of Independence as its key, describes the hoard; the other two, said to give the place and the heirs, have never been read. Many cryptographers think the whole story is a hoax by the pamphlet's author.
legends.when: Story set in 1819 to 1822; published 1885

origin.text: The Beale Papers (1885), Wikisource

legends.look_for: Nothing has ever been found. The tests are textual: analysis of the writing style points to the pamphlet's own author as the writer of the "Beale" letters.

places.name: Bedford County, Virginia
places.claim: The solved cipher says the vault is "in the county of Bedford, about four miles from Buford's", and treasure hunters have dug around the old Buford tavern site for over a century.
places.against: No treasure has been found, no record of Beale exists, and studies of the wording argue that the pamphlet is fiction.

sources.title: The Beale Papers (1885), Wikisource
Wikipedia, "Beale ciphers"

legends.name: Forrest Fenn's treasure
legends.summary: Forrest Fenn, an art dealer in Santa Fe, said he hid a chest of gold and jewels in the Rocky Mountains and put the clues in a 24-line poem in his 2010 memoir. Hundreds of thousands of people searched, and at least four died. In June 2020 Fenn announced that it had been found; the finder, Jack Stuef, said it was in Wyoming and has not revealed the spot.
legends.when: Hidden about 2010; found June 2020

origin.text: The Guardian, "$1m treasure in Rocky Mountains has been found, says Forrest Fenn" (2020)

legends.look_for: This was a puzzle hunt, solved by reading the poem, not by survey. It is in the dataset as a rare modern case of a hidden treasure that was real and was found.

places.name: Wyoming (exact spot not public)
places.claim: Fenn confirmed the find in June 2020 and died that September. The finder was later named as Jack Stuef, who has refused to say where in Wyoming the chest lay.

sources.title: The Guardian, "$1m treasure in Rocky Mountains has been found, says Forrest Fenn" (2020)
Wikipedia, "Fenn treasure"

legends.name: Captain Kidd's treasure
legends.summary: William Kidd, a privateer turned pirate, buried part of his loot on Gardiners Island off Long Island in 1699 as he sailed to New York to bargain for a pardon. The governor had it dug up within weeks and used it as evidence; Kidd was hanged in London in 1701. The rumour that he hid more has fed treasure hunts ever since.
legends.when: Buried and recovered 1699 CE

origin.text: J. F. Jameson (ed.), Privateering and Piracy in the Colonial Period: Illustrative Documents (1923), Project Gutenberg

legends.look_for: Documents, not maps: the inventory of what was dug up on Gardiners Island survives. Claims of more Kidd treasure have rested on metal bars and wrecks, which chemistry and timber dating can test.

places.name: Gardiners Island, New York
places.claim: Kidd left part of his treasure on the island in 1699, hoping to use it to bargain. The Earl of Bellomont, the governor who had first commissioned him, had him arrested in Boston that July and sent for the treasure; the papers, with John Gardiner's statement, survive.

sources.title: J. F. Jameson (ed.), Privateering and Piracy in the Colonial Period: Illustrative Documents (1923), Project Gutenberg
Wikipedia, "William Kidd"

places.name: Île Sainte-Marie, Madagascar (2015 claim)
places.claim: In May 2015 the American explorer Barry Clifford raised a 50 kg bar from a wreck off this former pirate base and presented it to the president of Madagascar as silver from Kidd's ship Adventure Galley.
places.against: A UNESCO scientific and technical advisory body reported in July 2015 that tests showed the ingot was lead, not silver.

sources.title: BBC News, "Pirate Captain Kidd's 'treasure' found in Madagascar" (2015)
Wikipedia, "William Kidd"

legends.name: Florentine Diamond
legends.summary: The Florentine Diamond is a 137 carat yellow stone that probably belonged to the Medici before it came to the Habsburgs. It vanished when the last emperor, Charles I, left Vienna about 1918, and for a century it was thought stolen or recut. In November 2025 members of the Habsburg family told the New York Times that it had lain all along in a bank vault in Canada, put there on the orders of Empress Zita.
legends.when: Missing from about 1918; revealed November 2025

origin.text: Euronews, "Habsburg family's Florentine diamond found in bank vault after a century" (2025)

legends.look_for: A case solved by family papers, not by search. The lesson for other lost jewels is that "lost" can mean kept quiet in a safe deposit box.

places.name: Vienna (Habsburg treasury)
places.claim: The diamond was part of the Habsburg jewels in Vienna until the end of the monarchy. It disappeared when Charles I fled abroad about 1918.

sources.title: Euronews, "Habsburg family's Florentine diamond found in bank vault after a century" (2025)

places.name: Bank vault in Canada (place not public)
places.claim: Three Habsburg relatives confirmed to the New York Times in 2025 that the stone had been kept in a Canadian bank vault for a century on Empress Zita's orders. The family said the jewels should now be exhibited.
places.against: The account comes from the family through the press; the dataset has not found a published gemmological report.

sources.title: Euronews, "Habsburg family's Florentine diamond found in bank vault after a century" (2025)

legends.name: Staffordshire Hoard
legends.summary: The Staffordshire Hoard is the largest find of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork ever made: more than 1,500 pieces at first count, almost all of them fittings stripped from swords and war gear of the 7th century. Terry Herbert found it with a metal detector in a ploughed field near Hammerwich in July 2009. It was buried in the kingdom of Mercia, for reasons nobody knows.
legends.when: Buried in the 7th century CE; found July 2009

origin.text: The Guardian, "Largest ever hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold found in Staffordshire" (M. Kennedy, 2009)

legends.look_for: Small gold and garnet fittings scattered in plough soil over a few square metres. A metal detector found them; archaeologists then dug the spot and later re-surveyed the field, finding more pieces in 2012.

places.name: Field near Hammerwich, Staffordshire
places.claim: Herbert, an amateur detectorist, found the first pieces in a farm field in July 2009; the hoard holds about 5 kg of gold, three times the amount in the Sutton Hoo ship burial. A second search of the same field in 2012 found more fragments.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Largest ever hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold found in Staffordshire" (2009)
BBC News, "Staffordshire Hoard: Gold fragments found in Hammerwich" (2012)
C. Fern, T. Dickinson and L. Webster (eds), The Staffordshire Hoard: An Anglo-Saxon Treasure (Society of Antiquaries, 2019)

legends.name: Hoxne Hoard
legends.summary: The Hoxne Hoard is the largest hoard of late Roman gold and silver found in Britain: 14,865 coins with jewellery, spoons and tableware, packed in a wooden chest and buried in Suffolk in the early 5th century. Eric Lawes found it in 1992 with a metal detector while looking for a friend's lost hammer. He reported it at once, and archaeologists excavated the whole hoard in a single day.
legends.when: Buried after 407 CE; found 16 November 1992

origin.text: The Guardian, "Golden hoard and silver too at British Museum" (M. Kennedy, 2003)

legends.look_for: A tight cluster of coins and plate that kept the shape of the rotted box around it. Because the finder left it in the ground, excavators could record the packing, the box fittings and even traces of straw and cloth.

places.name: Hoxne, Suffolk
places.claim: Lawes was hunting for a hammer dropped in a muddy field when his detector found the hoard, the largest treasure of late Roman gold and silver from Britain.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Golden hoard and silver too at British Museum" (2003)
Review of C. Johns, The Hoxne Late Roman Treasure: Gold Jewellery and Silver Plate (British Museum Press, 2010), American Journal of Archaeology 115 (2011)
Wikipedia, "Hoxne Hoard"

legends.name: Sutton Hoo ship burial
legends.summary: In the summer of 1939, on the eve of war, the largest barrow on a Suffolk estate was opened and found to hold the remains of a great ship with an untouched burial chamber at its centre. The helmet, gold buckle, shoulder clasps and silver in it make it one of the richest finds ever made in England. Coins date the burial to about 625, and the dead man is thought to be Rædwald, king of East Anglia.
legends.when: Buried about 625 CE; excavated 1939

origin.text: R. Bruce-Mitford, "The Sutton Hoo Ship-Burial", Nature 165 (1950)

legends.look_for: The ship survived only as rows of iron rivets and a hard crust of sand where its planks had been. Barrow cemeteries like this show as low mounds in lidar; robbers' pits in their tops show too.

places.name: Sutton Hoo
places.claim: The Great Ship Burial was found in 1939. Who lay in it cannot be proved; the leading theory is King Rædwald of East Anglia.

sources.title: National Trust, "History of Sutton Hoo"
R. Bruce-Mitford, "The Sutton Hoo Ship-Burial", Nature 165 (1950)

legends.name: Varna Necropolis gold
legends.summary: An excavator operator, Raycho Marinov, cut into a Copper Age cemetery at Varna, Bulgaria, in October 1972. Its graves held the oldest gold treasure in the world, most of it in a handful of very rich burials. Radiocarbon dates show the cemetery was in use from about 4560 to 4450 BCE.
legends.when: About 4560 to 4450 BCE; found 1972 CE

origin.text: T. Higham, J. Chapman et al., "New perspectives on the Varna cemetery (Bulgaria): AMS dates and social implications", Antiquity 81 (2007)

legends.look_for: Flat graves with no mound, found by chance in building work. Nothing marks such a cemetery on the surface; rescue excavation ahead of construction is how they come to light.

places.name: Varna Necropolis
places.claim: High-precision radiocarbon dating of the burials shows the cemetery in use from 4560 to 4450 BCE, with hints that the richest graves are among the earliest.

sources.title: T. Higham, J. Chapman et al., "New perspectives on the Varna cemetery (Bulgaria): AMS dates and social implications", Antiquity 81 (2007)
Wikipedia, "Varna Necropolis"

legends.name: Panagyurishte Treasure
legends.summary: Three brothers digging clay for bricks near Panagyurishte, Bulgaria, in December 1949 turned up nine vessels of solid gold: a great dish, an amphora with centaur handles and seven drinking horns shaped as animal heads and Amazons. They are thought to be a Thracian royal ceremonial set of about 300 BCE, 6.164 kg of gold in all.
legends.when: Made about the turn of the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE; found 1949 CE

origin.text: Review of I. Venedikov, The Panagyurishte Gold Treasure (Sofia, 1961), Journal of Hellenic Studies 84 (1964)

legends.look_for: A single buried cache with no building or grave around it, found by chance. Hoards like this are hidden in a hurry in open ground and leave nothing to see.

places.name: Panagyurishte
places.claim: The set was found at the Merul tile works near the town on 8 December 1949 by the brothers Pavel, Petko and Michail Deikov.

sources.title: Review of I. Venedikov, The Panagyurishte Gold Treasure (Sofia, 1961), Journal of Hellenic Studies 84 (1964)
Wikipedia, "Panagyurishte Treasure"

legends.name: Bactrian Gold (Tillya Tepe)
legends.summary: In 1978 the Soviet archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi dug six graves of nomad nobles at Tillya Tepe, "Golden Hill", in northern Afghanistan, and took out about 20,600 ornaments and other objects, most of gold, dating to around the 1st century BCE or CE. War followed and the hoard was thought lost or melted. In 2003 it was revealed that museum staff had hidden it in a vault under the presidential palace in Kabul and kept the secret through the civil war and Taliban rule.
legends.when: Graves of about the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE; found 1978; rediscovered 2003

origin.text: V. Sarianidi, "The Treasure of Golden Hill", American Journal of Archaeology 84 (1980)

legends.look_for: A low mound on a plain, the ruin of a much older temple, into which the graves were cut. Such mounds are common and are being looted across the region; satellite images show the pits.

places.name: Tillya Tepe
places.claim: Sarianidi published the find as "The Treasure of Golden Hill". The objects survived decades of war in a vault deep under the presidential palace, thanks to a few men who knew and said nothing, even at gunpoint; the store of 22,000 pieces was revealed in 2003.

sources.title: V. Sarianidi, "The Treasure of Golden Hill", American Journal of Archaeology 84 (1980)
BBC News, "Afghan gold: How the country's heritage was saved" (2011)
Wikipedia, "Tillya Tepe"

legends.name: Priam's Treasure
legends.summary: Heinrich Schliemann found a cache of gold diadems, cups and jewellery at Troy in 1873 and named it after Homer's King Priam, though it came from Troy II, a level many centuries older than any Trojan War. He smuggled it out of the Ottoman Empire, and it went to Berlin, where it vanished when the Red Army took the city. In 1994 the Pushkin Museum in Moscow admitted that it had the gold.
legends.when: Early Bronze Age (Troy II); found 1873 CE; lost 1945; revealed 1994

origin.text: D. F. Easton, "Priam's Gold: the Full Story", Anatolian Studies 44 (1994)

legends.look_for: The gold has been found twice. What is still argued is where exactly on the mound Schliemann dug it up and whether it was one deposit, which depends on his notebooks and plans.

places.name: Troy (where it was found)
places.claim: Schliemann found the hoard in 1873 beside the wall of the second city of Troy, an Early Bronze Age level.

sources.title: D. F. Easton, "Priam's Gold: the Full Story", Anatolian Studies 44 (1994)
Archaeology, "Calvert's Heirs Claim Schliemann Treasure" (1996)

places.name: Pushkin Museum, Moscow (where it is now)
places.claim: The gold was believed lost with the fall of Berlin until it was shown to be in the Pushkin Museum, where foreign archaeologists saw the Trojan objects in 1994.

sources.title: Archaeology, "Calvert's Heirs Claim Schliemann Treasure" (1996)
Wikipedia, "Priam's Treasure"

legends.name: Vinland Map
legends.summary: In 1965 Yale University announced a 15th century world map that showed "Vinland", part of the North American coast, drawn before Columbus sailed. In 2021 Yale's own analysis showed that the ink throughout the map contains a titanium compound first made in the 1920s. The map is a modern forgery.
legends.when: Announced 1965 CE; shown to be a forgery 2021

origin.text: Yale News, "Analysis unlocks secret of the Vinland Map: it's a fake" (2021)

legends.look_for: Chemistry of ink and parchment. X-ray fluorescence scans of the whole sheet show which elements are in every line, and a pigment invented in the 20th century cannot be in a 15th century drawing.

places.name: Beinecke Library, Yale University
places.claim: Yale caused a sensation in 1965 when it announced the map and published a scholarly book on it. The library still holds it.
places.against: Analysis found a titanium compound used in inks first made in the 1920s throughout the lines and text; the library's curator of early books says there is "no reasonable doubt" that the map is a fake.
places.wikipedia: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library

sources.title: Yale News, "Analysis unlocks secret of the Vinland Map: it's a fake" (2021)

legends.name: Bosnian "pyramids"
legends.summary: In October 2005 the businessman Semir Osmanagić announced that Visočica hill and other hills near Visoko in Bosnia are the largest and oldest pyramids on Earth. Geologists say they are natural: tilted layers of rock that erode into flat triangular faces. The European Association of Archaeologists called the project a cruel hoax on the public, and warned that the digging was damaging real medieval and Roman remains.
legends.when: Claim made in 2005 CE

origin.text: Smithsonian Magazine, "The Mystery of Bosnia's Ancient Pyramids" (C. Woodard, 2009)

legends.look_for: A hill with flat, triangular faces is a common landform called a flatiron, made where hard rock layers dip at an angle. The faces follow the bedding of the rock, and cut blocks, mortar and tools are absent.

places.name: Visočica hill, Visoko
places.claim: Osmanagić calls the 220 m hill the Pyramid of the Sun and says man-made blocks lie under its soil. More than 400,000 people visited in the first years after his announcement in October 2005.
places.against: Geologists identify the hill as a natural flatiron of layered rock; Anthony Harding, then president of the European Association of Archaeologists, and other scholars condemned the project.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "The Mystery of Bosnia's Ancient Pyramids" (2009)
Wikipedia, "Bosnian pyramid claims"

legends.name: Gunung Padang "pyramid"
legends.summary: Gunung Padang in West Java is a real megalithic site: terraces built of natural basalt columns on top of an old volcano, most likely within the last few thousand years. In 2023 a team led by the geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja published a paper claiming that the hill hides a man-made pyramid up to 27,000 years old. Archaeologists objected, the journal investigated, and the paper was retracted in March 2024.
legends.when: Terraces of the last few thousand years; pyramid claim published 2023 and retracted 2024

origin.text: Nature News, "A 27,000-year-old pyramid? Controversy hits an extraordinary archaeological claim" (2023)

legends.look_for: Radar, seismic and resistivity images show layers inside the hill, but layers alone do not show building. The claim failed because the dated soil samples held no artefacts or other sign of human work.

places.name: Gunung Padang, West Java
places.claim: The 2023 paper used ground-penetrating radar, seismic tomography and drill cores to argue that the hill was sculpted and built up by people in stages starting in the last Ice Age.
places.against: Wiley and the journal's editors retracted the paper in March 2024 because the radiocarbon dates came from soil with no artefacts or man-made features; the megalithic terraces on the summit are real and much younger.

sources.title: D. H. Natawidjaja et al., "RETRACTED: Geo-archaeological prospecting of Gunung Padang buried prehistoric pyramid in West Java, Indonesia", Archaeological Prospection (2023)
Nature News, "A 27,000-year-old pyramid? Controversy hits an extraordinary archaeological claim" (2023)
Wikipedia, "Gunung Padang"

legends.name: Galleon San José
legends.summary: The San José was the flagship of a Spanish treasure fleet, carrying gold, silver, gems and jewellery from the South American colonies, when a British squadron sank her off Cartagena in June 1708. Almost all of her crew of about 600 died. Colombia announced in December 2015 that the wreck had been found, and has kept the position secret while Colombia, Spain, a salvage company and indigenous groups dispute who owns the cargo.
legends.when: Sunk 8 June 1708; found November 2015

origin.text: BBC News, "Colombia treasure-laden San Jose galleon 'is found'" (2015)

legends.look_for: A scatter of bronze cannon, ceramics and coins on the seabed 600 m down. She was found with a REMUS 6000 autonomous underwater vehicle running side-scan sonar, and identified from photographs of her cannon.

places.name: Off Cartagena, near the Rosario Islands (position secret)
places.claim: President Juan Manuel Santos announced the find on 5 December 2015; the wreck had been located the month before, 600 m down, by a REMUS 6000 robot submarine operated by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. It is said to lie close to the Rosario Islands, and officials will not reveal the position.

sources.title: BBC News, "Colombia treasure-laden San Jose galleon 'is found'" (2015)
BBC Travel, "A shipwreck worth billions off the coast of Cartagena" (2019)
Wikipedia, "Spanish galleon San José"

legends.name: Merchant Royal
legends.summary: The Merchant Royal was an English ship that sank in rough weather off Land's End on 23 September 1641, when her pumps failed on the way home from Cádiz with bullion on board. She has not been found. When a salvage firm raised half a million coins from a secret Atlantic site in 2007, many guessed it was her; it was a Spanish frigate.
legends.when: Sunk 23 September 1641 CE

origin.text: Reports of the loss in 1641

legends.look_for: A 17th century wooden hull is long gone; what is left is anchors, iron guns and a low mound of concreted cargo. The western approaches to the Channel are deep, tidal and crowded with later wrecks, so each sonar target needs a camera.

places.name: Atlantic off the Isles of Scilly and Land's End
places.claim: The shipwreck historian Richard Larn told the BBC in 2007 that the Merchant Royal, a Dartmouth-based ship laden with bullion, sank off the Isles of Scilly in 1641.
places.against: The sinking position is known only roughly from the accounts of survivors, and no wreck has been identified.

sources.title: BBC News, "Record wreck 'found off Cornwall'" (2007)
Wikipedia, "Merchant Royal"

legends.name: Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes ("Black Swan")
legends.summary: The Spanish frigate Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes blew up in a British attack off the south coast of Portugal in October 1804, with the loss of about 250 lives and half a million silver and gold coins. In 2007 the American firm Odyssey Marine Exploration secretly raised the coins and flew them to Florida under the code name Black Swan. Spain sued in the US courts and won; the treasure went to Spain in 2012.
legends.when: Sunk 5 October 1804; salvaged 2007; returned to Spain 2012

origin.text: BBC News, "True-life treasure hunt that turned into a comic book" (J. Badcock, 2018)

legends.look_for: A debris field of coins in clumps on a deep seabed, with no hull. The case is in the dataset for its outcome: a warship stays the property of its flag state however deep it lies.

places.name: Off Cape Santa Maria, Portugal (wreck site)
places.claim: A British squadron opened fire on four Spanish frigates here in 1804 and the Mercedes exploded. Odyssey found the scattered wreck and took about half a million coins to Florida in 2007, refusing to say where the site was.

sources.title: BBC News, "True-life treasure hunt that turned into a comic book" (J. Badcock, 2018)
BBC News, "Record wreck 'found off Cornwall'" (2007)

places.name: National Museum of Underwater Archaeology, Cartagena (where the coins are)
places.claim: After Spain won its case in the US courts the coins were flown home. They are now in the national underwater archaeology museum in Cartagena, on the south-east coast of Spain.

sources.title: BBC News, "True-life treasure hunt that turned into a comic book" (J. Badcock, 2018)
Wikipedia, "Black Swan Project"

legends.name: Whydah Gally
legends.summary: The Whydah Gally was a slave ship that the pirate Samuel Bellamy captured on her first voyage and made his flagship. On 26 April 1717 a storm drove her on to a sandbar off Cape Cod and she broke up; only two of her crew lived. Barry Clifford found the wreck in 1984 under several metres of sand.
legends.when: Wrecked 26 April 1717; found 1984

origin.text: Wikipedia, "Whydah Gally"

legends.look_for: Iron guns, coins and tools locked in hard lumps of concretion under 3 to 15 m of shifting sand in the surf zone. Magnetometers find the iron; X-rays show what is inside each lump.

places.name: Off Marconi Beach, Wellfleet, Cape Cod
places.claim: The ship was driven aground at what is now Marconi Beach at Wellfleet, Massachusetts, on 26 April 1717. The wreck was found in 1984, buried under 3 to 15 m of sand.

sources.title: Review of K. Kinkor and G. Binder, The Treasures of the Pirate Ship "Whydah", The Public Historian 15 (1993)
Wikipedia, "Whydah Gally"

legends.name: Queen Anne's Revenge
legends.summary: Queen Anne's Revenge, the flagship of the pirate Blackbeard, had been the French slave ship La Concorde until he took her in 1717. In May 1718 he ran her aground at what is now Beaufort Inlet in North Carolina. A private firm found the wreck in 1996 and the state has been excavating it since.
legends.when: Run aground May 1718; found 1996

origin.text: North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, Queen Anne's Revenge Project, "History"

legends.look_for: Cannon, anchors and ballast stones in a pile on a sandy sea floor in 8.5 m of water, a mile offshore. Dates on a cannon and a bronze bell, and a French medical syringe, helped to confirm the ship.

places.name: Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina
places.claim: Before the pirates took her the ship was La Concorde and carried 1,265 African men, women and children into slavery. The wreck site off Beaufort was discovered in 1996 and is the second oldest shipwreck found in North Carolina.

sources.title: North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, Queen Anne's Revenge Project, "History"
M. Wilde-Ramsing and L. Carnes-McNaughton, "Blackbeard's Queen Anne's Revenge and Its French Connection", in Pieces of Eight (University Press of Florida, 2016)
Wikipedia, "Queen Anne's Revenge"

legends.name: Antikythera wreck
legends.summary: In 1900 sponge divers sheltering at the Greek island of Antikythera found a Roman period ship on the seabed, loaded with bronze and marble statues. Among the finds was a lump of corroded bronze gears, the Antikythera mechanism, a geared device that modelled the motions of the sun and moon and predicted eclipses. It is technically more complex than any device known for at least a thousand years afterwards.
legends.when: Sank in the 1st century BCE; found 1900 CE

origin.text: T. Freeth et al., "Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism", Nature 444 (2006)

legends.look_for: Statues, pottery and hull timbers on a steep rocky slope at the limit of early diving. Pottery in the cargo dates the voyage, and X-ray tomography reads the text inside the mechanism.

places.name: Antikythera wreck
places.claim: Sponge divers discovered the wreck off Point Glyphadia in 1900. It gave up statues, coins and the remains of the mechanism, which X-ray study shows was an astronomical calculator that could predict eclipses.

sources.title: T. Freeth et al., "Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism", Nature 444 (2006)
T. Freeth, "Eclipse Prediction on the Ancient Greek Astronomical Calculating Machine Known as the Antikythera Mechanism", PLOS ONE 9 (2014)
Wikipedia, "Antikythera wreck"

legends.name: Uluburun shipwreck
legends.summary: The Uluburun ship sank off the south coast of Turkey about 1320 BCE with a rich cargo: copper and tin ingots, glass, ivory, gold jewellery and luxury goods from many lands. A Turkish sponge diver saw the "metal biscuits with ears" in 1982, and the Institute of Nautical Archaeology dug the wreck from 1984 to 1994. It is the richest picture we have of trade in the Late Bronze Age.
legends.when: Sank about 1320 BCE; found 1982 CE; excavated 1984 to 1994

origin.text: Institute of Nautical Archaeology, "Uluburun Late Bronze Age Shipwreck Excavation"

legends.look_for: Rows of four-handled copper ingots, stone anchors and big storage jars on a steep rocky slope. A sponge diver's report led to it; excavation took more than 22,000 dives to depths of over 150 feet (45 m).

places.name: Uluburun, near Kaş
places.claim: A sponge diver reported the wreck in 1982 near Kaş. Excavation from 1984 to 1994 recovered a cargo of raw materials and finished luxury goods from across the eastern Mediterranean, dated to about 1320 BCE.

sources.title: Institute of Nautical Archaeology, "Uluburun Late Bronze Age Shipwreck Excavation"
C. Pulak, "The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 27 (1998)

legends.name: RMS Titanic
legends.summary: The liner Titanic struck an iceberg and sank on 15 April 1912 on her first voyage, and more than 1,500 people died. The wreck lay unfound for 73 years. A joint American and French expedition led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel found it on 1 September 1985, 3,800 m down.
legends.when: Sank 15 April 1912; found 1 September 1985

origin.text: NOAA, "R.M.S. Titanic: History and Significance"

legends.look_for: A ship that breaks up on the way down strews a field of wreckage far wider than the hull, which is easier to cross with a towed camera or sonar than the hull itself. The wreck lies in two main pieces, 3,800 m down.

places.name: Wreck of the Titanic
places.claim: The wreck was discovered on 1 September 1985 by an expedition led by Robert Ballard of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and Jean-Louis Michel of the French institute IFREMER. It lies in international waters off Newfoundland at a depth of 12,500 feet (3,800 m).

sources.title: NOAA, "R.M.S. Titanic: History and Significance"
J.-L. Michel and R. Ballard, "The RMS Titanic 1985 discovery expedition", Proceedings of OCEANS'94 (IEEE)

legends.name: Endurance
legends.summary: Endurance was the ship of Ernest Shackleton's Antarctic expedition. Sea ice in the Weddell Sea crushed her and she sank in 1915; Shackleton and his men escaped on foot and in small boats. In March 2022 an expedition found her almost intact, 3,008 m deep.
legends.when: Sank 1915; found March 2022

origin.text: BBC News, "Endurance: Shackleton's lost ship is found in Antarctic" (J. Amos, 2022)

legends.look_for: An intact wooden ship on the deep sea floor under sea ice, found by submersibles launched from an icebreaker that swept a set search area. No wood-eating worms live there, which is why she is whole.

places.name: Weddell Sea
places.claim: The Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust mounted the search from the South African icebreaker Agulhas II, and its submersibles combed a set search area for more than two weeks before finding the ship 3,008 m down. The wreck is a designated monument under the Antarctic Treaty and must not be disturbed.

sources.title: BBC News, "Endurance: Shackleton's lost ship is found in Antarctic" (2022)

legends.name: HMS Erebus and HMS Terror
legends.summary: Sir John Franklin sailed in 1845 with two ships and 129 men to find the Northwest Passage, and none came back. Searches went on for 170 years. Parks Canada found Erebus in 2014 with side-scan sonar, in the area where Inuit testimony had always said a ship sank, and Terror was found in 2016 in Terror Bay after a tip from an Inuk crew member.
legends.when: Abandoned 1848; Erebus found September 2014; Terror found September 2016

origin.text: Parks Canada, "Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror National Historic Site"

legends.look_for: Two wooden ships sitting upright in cold Arctic water. Side-scan sonar towed in the few ice-free weeks found the first; Inuit oral history said where to tow it.

places.name: HMS Erebus (Wilmot and Crampton Bay)
places.claim: Sonar images from the waters off King William Island showed a ship on the sea floor in September 2014; it was identified as Erebus. The site is the first national historic site managed jointly by Inuit and Parks Canada.

sources.title: BBC News, "Sir John Franklin: Fabled Arctic ship found" (2014)
Parks Canada, "Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror National Historic Site"
Wikipedia, "HMS Erebus (1826)"

places.name: HMS Terror (Terror Bay)
places.claim: A team from the Arctic Research Foundation found Terror on 3 September 2016 in the middle of Terror Bay, on the south-west coast of King William Island, with her hatches closed. They went there on the word of an Inuk crew member who had once seen a mast standing out of the ice.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Ship found in Arctic 168 years after doomed Northwest Passage attempt" (P. Watson, 2016)

legends.name: Mary Rose
legends.summary: The Mary Rose was a warship of Henry VIII that sank in the Solent on 19 July 1545, in sight of the king, as she went out to fight a French invasion fleet. Divers salvaged guns from her in the 1830s and she was lost again. She was found in 1971 after years of search, and in 1982 half of her hull, kept whole by the silt, was raised.
legends.when: Sank 19 July 1545; found 1971; raised 11 October 1982

origin.text: Mary Rose Trust, "History of the Mary Rose"

legends.look_for: A wooden hull buried on its side in soft mud, so that only the side that sank into the silt survives. A sonar scan by Harold Edgerton in 1967 and 1968 showed a buried feature before divers found timbers.

places.name: Mary Rose Museum, Portsmouth (the Solent wreck site is close by)
places.claim: The wreck was located in 1971 and raised on 11 October 1982 by the Mary Rose Trust. The hull and thousands of objects found in her are in the museum at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard.

sources.title: Mary Rose Trust, "History of the Mary Rose"
Wikipedia, "Mary Rose"

legends.name: Vasa
legends.summary: The Swedish warship Vasa heeled over and sank in Stockholm harbour in 1628, minutes into her first voyage; she was built too tall and too narrow. Her guns were salvaged in the 17th century and the wreck was forgotten. Anders Franzén found her again in the 1950s, and in 1961 the hull was raised almost whole after 333 years.
legends.when: Sank 10 August 1628; raised 1961

origin.text: Review of C. O. Cederlund and F. Hocker (eds), Vasa I: The Archaeology of a Swedish Warship of 1628, International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 36 (2007)

legends.look_for: The Baltic is too cold and too fresh for shipworm, so wooden wrecks there stand whole for centuries. Anders Franzén reasoned this in the early 1950s and went looking for old wrecks in Stockholm harbour.

places.name: Vasa Museum, Stockholm (she sank in the harbour here)
places.claim: The ship was salvaged in 1961 with her hull largely intact after 333 years on the seabed of a busy shipping lane in Stockholm harbour, and is shown in a museum built for her.

sources.title: Review of C. O. Cederlund and F. Hocker (eds), Vasa I: The Archaeology of a Swedish Warship of 1628 (2007)
Wikipedia, "Vasa (ship)"

legends.name: Batavia
legends.summary: The Dutch East India Company ship Batavia struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos, off Western Australia, in June 1629. While her commander sailed for help, a group of mutineers murdered more than 100 of the survivors on the islands. A lobster fisherman first sighted the wreck in 1963, it was excavated in the 1970s, and graves of the victims are still being found on Beacon Island.
legends.when: Wrecked 4 June 1629; found 1963

origin.text: J. Green, "The VOC ship Batavia wrecked in 1629 on the Houtman Abrolhos, Western Australia", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 4 (1975)

legends.look_for: Cannon, anchors and a section of hull under coral on a reef flat, and on the nearby islands shallow graves and the stone shelters of the survivors. Old journals gave the latitude; local fishermen knew the reef.

places.name: Morning Reef and Beacon Island, Houtman Abrolhos
places.claim: The ship was wrecked on the reef in 1629. Archaeologists working on Beacon Island have uncovered burials from the massacre that followed, in which more than 100 survivors were killed by mutineers.

sources.title: J. Green, "The VOC ship Batavia wrecked in 1629 on the Houtman Abrolhos, Western Australia" (1975)
BBC News, "Australia dig unearths Batavia mutiny skeleton" (2015)
Wikipedia, "Batavia (1628 ship)"

legends.name: Santa María
legends.summary: The Santa María, the largest of Columbus's three ships, ran on to a reef off the north coast of Hispaniola on 25 December 1492, and her timbers were stripped to build the fort of La Navidad. What was left has never been found. In 2014 the explorer Barry Clifford said a wreck off Cap-Haïtien was the ship; a UNESCO mission examined it and said it was not.
legends.when: Wrecked 25 December 1492 CE

origin.text: Columbus's journal for 25 December 1492

legends.look_for: Little would be left: ballast stones, a few iron fittings and no fastenings of copper, which ships did not use until centuries later. Columbus's own log gives distances from the wreck to the shore that any candidate must fit.

places.name: Reefs off Cap-Haïtien
places.claim: Columbus's journal puts the wreck on a bank off this coast, close to the village of the chief Guacanagarí. Barry Clifford announced in May 2014 that a ballast pile he had found here was the Santa María.
places.against: UNESCO's experts reported that the wreck Clifford identified is of a later date: its fastenings show a way of building ships that belongs to the late 17th or 18th century, and it lies further from the shore than the accounts allow.

sources.title: The Guardian, "Haiti shipwreck is not Columbus's Santa Maria, says Unesco" (2014)
Wikipedia, "Santa María (ship)"

legends.name: Kublai Khan's lost fleet
legends.summary: Kublai Khan sent fleets against Japan in 1274 and 1281, and Japanese tradition says a divine wind, the kamikaze, destroyed them. For a long time only the legend remained. Underwater archaeologists at the island of Takashima have since found the fleet's weapons, ceramic bombs and broken ship timbers.
legends.when: Fleet lost in the storm of 1281 CE

origin.text: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Relics of the Kamikaze" (J. Delgado, 2003)

legends.look_for: Timbers, stone-and-wood anchors, helmets and round ceramic shells buried a metre or more deep in bay mud. Sub-bottom profilers find the buried shapes; divers then dig by hand in near darkness.

places.name: Takashima, Imari Bay
places.claim: Underwater archaeologists led by Kenzo Hayashida excavated broken remains of the invasion fleet off Takashima, including a Mongol helmet, iron arrow tips and a tetsuhau, a ceramic bomb, the first proof that such weapons existed so early. Later surveys have searched the bay floor for the ships themselves.

sources.title: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Relics of the Kamikaze" (J. Delgado, 2003)
Y. Ikeda (Yoshifumi), R. Sasaki and J. Kimura, "Recent Underwater Investigations at Takashima: Searching for the Lost Fleet of the Mongol Empire", Current Science 117 (2019)

legends.name: SS Waratah
legends.summary: The British liner Waratah vanished in a storm off the east coast of South Africa in July 1909, between Durban and Cape Town, with all 211 people on board. No wreckage was ever identified. The wreck hunter Emlyn Brown searched for 22 years; a wreck reported as hers in 1999 proved to be a cargo ship sunk by a U-boat, and he gave up in 2004.
legends.when: Disappeared July 1909 CE

origin.text: Disappearance reported in July 1909

legends.look_for: A large steel hull on the seabed off the Wild Coast, where the strong Agulhas current makes survey slow. Sonar finds wrecks there; the hard part, as the 1999 mistake showed, is telling one steamer from another.

places.name: Off the Mbhashe River mouth, Wild Coast
places.claim: The last confirmed sighting of the Waratah was about ten miles off the delta of the Mbhashe (Bashee) River. Emlyn Brown led expeditions to this coast from 1983.
places.against: Brown's last expedition ended in failure in 2004 and he said he had no more ideas; where the ship lies is unknown.

sources.title: The Guardian, "'Titanic' hunt draws a blank" (2004)
Wikipedia, "SS Waratah"

legends.name: Bom Jesus (Oranjemund shipwreck)
legends.summary: The Bom Jesus was a Portuguese ship bound for India that left Lisbon in March 1533 and disappeared. In April 2008 a worker at a diamond mine on the coast of Namibia found copper ingots and ivory in sand that had been sea floor until the mine walled it off: her cargo of copper, elephant tusks and more than 2,000 gold and silver coins. It is the oldest known shipwreck found on the west coast of sub-Saharan Africa.
legends.when: Sailed 7 March 1533; found 1 April 2008

origin.text: E. Mowa, W. Engelbrecht et al., "Challenges in Rescue Excavation and Long-Term Conservation: The Case of the Oranjemund (Bom Jesus) Shipwreck, Namibia", International Journal of Historical Archaeology (2026)

legends.look_for: A wreck buried in beach sand, found only because miners had drained the shore behind a sea wall. A trident-shaped mark stamped on the copper ingots and the dates of the coins pointed to the ship.

places.name: Oranjemund, Namibia (restricted mining area)
places.claim: Kaapanda Shadika, a worker for the mining company Namdeb, found the first ingots and tusks on 1 April 2008. The rescue dig recovered 1,845 copper ingots, over 2,000 gold and silver coins and more than 100 elephant tusks.

sources.title: E. Mowa, W. Engelbrecht et al., "Challenges in Rescue Excavation and Long-Term Conservation: The Case of the Oranjemund (Bom Jesus) Shipwreck, Namibia" (2026)
Wikipedia, "Bom Jesus (ship)"

legends.name: Clotilda
legends.summary: The schooner Clotilda carried captive Africans from Dahomey to Alabama in 1860, long after the United States had banned the import of slaves, and her captain had her burned and sunk in the Mobile River delta to hide the crime. The freed survivors founded Africatown, and their descendants kept the story. The Alabama Historical Commission confirmed in May 2019 that the wreck had been found.
legends.when: Burned and sunk 1860; wreck confirmed May 2019

origin.text: Smithsonian Magazine, "The 'Clotilda,' the Last Known Slave Ship to Arrive in the U.S., Is Found" (A. Keyes, 2019)

legends.look_for: A burned wooden hull in river mud, one of many abandoned vessels in the delta. Sonar and magnetometer found candidates; the ship's recorded size, her rare hull design, the timber and nails, and signs of fire picked out the right one.

places.name: Mobile River delta, Alabama
places.claim: A wreck that a reporter found in 2018 proved too large to be the Clotilda, but the search it set off led archaeologists from the Alabama Historical Commission and SEARCH Inc. to the real ship, which they authenticated in 2019.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "The 'Clotilda,' the Last Known Slave Ship to Arrive in the U.S., Is Found" (2019)
US National Park Service, "Twelvemile Island Shipwreck"

legends.name: Belitung shipwreck
legends.summary: A ship of the 9th century CE, found off the Indonesian island of Belitung in 1998, carried some 60,000 pieces of Chinese pottery with gold and silver. Her planks were sewn together in the manner of Arab and Indian ships, the first hard evidence that such ships sailed direct between the Gulf and China. The cargo was raised by a commercial company, and the way it was dug drew criticism that led a museum to postpone its exhibition.
legends.when: Sank after 826 CE (a date written on one bowl); found 1998

origin.text: M. Flecker, "A ninth-century AD Arab or Indian shipwreck in Indonesia: First evidence for direct trade with China", World Archaeology 32 (2001)

legends.look_for: A low mound of stacked ceramics on a shallow reef flat, with hull planks pierced by stitch holes and no iron nails. In these waters fishermen find most wrecks, and cargoes are often sold before archaeologists hear of them.

places.name: Off Belitung island (Gelasa Strait)
places.claim: The well preserved wreck was excavated in 1998 and 1999. Her planks were joined by stitching, and the timber is of Arabian and Indian kinds; the cargo was almost all Chinese ceramics, mostly from the Changsha kilns.

sources.title: M. Flecker, "A ninth-century AD Arab or Indian shipwreck in Indonesia: First evidence for direct trade with China", World Archaeology 32 (2001)
Wikipedia, "Belitung shipwreck"

legends.name: Esmeralda (Vasco da Gama's fleet)
legends.summary: Esmeralda and São Pedro were two ships of Vasco da Gama's second fleet to India, commanded by his uncles Vicente and Brás Sodré. A storm wrecked them in May 1503 at an island off the coast of Oman, where they had gone to raid Arab shipping. A wreck site found there in 1998 and excavated in 2013 and 2014 is identified as probably Esmeralda.
legends.when: Wrecked May 1503; found 1998; excavated from 2013

origin.text: D. Mearns, D. Parham and B. Frohlich, "A Portuguese East Indiaman from the 1502-1503 Fleet of Vasco da Gama off Al Hallaniyah Island, Oman: an interim report", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 45 (2016)

legends.look_for: No hull, only heavy things caught in gullies of a shallow rocky bay: stone shot, lead and copper-alloy objects, coins and a ship's bell. Scientific dating and study of the finds made the identification.

places.name: Al Hallaniyah island, Oman
places.claim: David Mearns and Oman's Ministry of Heritage and Culture report a wreck off the north-east coast of the island that fits the ships lost there in May 1503, and identify it from its finds as Vicente Sodré's Esmeralda.
places.against: The paper is an interim report; the authors give the identification as probable, not proved.

sources.title: D. Mearns, D. Parham and B. Frohlich, "A Portuguese East Indiaman from the 1502-1503 Fleet of Vasco da Gama off Al Hallaniyah Island, Oman: an interim report", International Journal of Nautical Archaeology 45 (2016)

legends.name: Tomb of Genghis Khan
legends.summary: Genghis Khan died in 1227 and was buried in secret, by tradition near the sacred mountain Burkhan Khaldun in north-east Mongolia. No tomb has been found, and many Mongolians think it wrong to look for the grave at all. A crowdsourced search of satellite images flagged sites for checking on the ground without disturbing them.
legends.when: Died August 1227 CE

origin.text: Mongol tradition of a secret burial near Burkhan Khaldun

legends.look_for: Nobody knows what the grave looks like, which is the problem the satellite project took on: thousands of volunteers tagged anything that looked man-made, and agreement between them picked out real features such as old burial mounds. Mongolian law and custom rule out digging.

places.name: Burkhan Khaldun and the Khentii mountains
places.claim: UNESCO records that the mountain is believed to be the place of Genghis Khan's birth and burial. In the National Geographic "Valley of the Khans" project more than 10,000 online volunteers examined 6,000 square km of high-resolution satellite images of the region and tagged possible sites.
places.against: No burial has been identified, and searching is taboo for many Mongolians, who hold that he did not want to be found.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Great Burkhan Khaldun Mountain and its surrounding sacred landscape"
A. Lin et al., "Crowdsourcing the Unknown: The Satellite Search for Genghis Khan", PLOS ONE 9 (2014)
BBC Travel, "Why Genghis Khan's tomb can't be found" (2017)

legends.name: Tomb of Alexander the Great
legends.summary: Alexander the Great died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his body was brought to Egypt, where it lay in a mausoleum in Alexandria. The tomb drops out of the record in late antiquity and its site is lost under the modern city. Egypt's antiquities service has recognised more than 140 searches for it.
legends.when: Died 323 BCE; tomb lost in late antiquity

origin.text: Strabo, Geography 17.1.8, on the Sema in Alexandria

legends.look_for: A royal mausoleum in the palace quarter of ancient Alexandria, now 5 to 10 m under streets and buildings and partly under the harbour. Finds come from rescue digs and boreholes when buildings are replaced.

places.name: Central Alexandria
places.claim: Ancient writers place the tomb in the royal quarter of Alexandria. Searches have centred on the old crossroads of the city and on sites such as the Nabi Daniel mosque.
places.against: More than 140 officially recognised searches have failed; earthquakes, the sea, riots and rebuilding have destroyed or buried the ancient royal quarter.

sources.title: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Hunting Alexander's Tomb" (R. Bianchi)
A. Erskine, "Life after Death: Alexandria and the Body of Alexander", Greece and Rome 49 (2002)
Wikipedia, "Tomb of Alexander the Great"

places.name: Siwa Oasis (1995 claim)
places.claim: The Greek archaeologist Liana Souvaltzi dug from 1989 at a temple ruin at El Maraqi in the Siwa Oasis and announced in 1995 that she had found Alexander's tomb.
places.against: Greek officials doubted the claim at once and it has not been accepted; the American archaeological magazine that reviewed the searches lists it among "fanciful attempts".

sources.title: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), "Hunting Alexander's Tomb" (R. Bianchi)
Wikipedia, "Tomb of Alexander the Great"

legends.name: Tomb of Antony and Cleopatra
legends.summary: Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony died in Alexandria in 30 BCE, and ancient writers say Octavian let them be buried together in the mausoleum she had built there. It has never been found. Most scholars think it stood in the royal quarter, much of which is now under the harbour; since 2005 Kathleen Martínez has dug instead at the temple of Taposiris Magna, 45 km to the west.
legends.when: Died 30 BCE

origin.text: Plutarch, Life of Antony 86

legends.look_for: In Alexandria: masonry of a Ptolemaic royal building on the sunken shore, mapped by divers and sonar. At Taposiris Magna: rock-cut shafts and tunnels under a temple, traced by ground-penetrating radar and excavation.

places.name: Royal quarter of Alexandria (now partly under the harbour)
places.claim: When Octavian's army entered Alexandria in 30 BCE, Cleopatra shut herself in her mausoleum in the city, and that is where the sources say she and Antony were buried. The palace district has since sunk into the eastern harbour.
places.against: Nothing identified as the mausoleum has been found among the sunken ruins.

sources.title: National Geographic Magazine, "The Search for Cleopatra" (C. Brown, 2011)
Wikipedia, "Antirhodos"

places.name: Taposiris Magna
places.claim: Kathleen Martínez, a lawyer turned archaeologist from the Dominican Republic, proposed in 2004 that Cleopatra chose this temple of Osiris for her burial. Her digs have found coins with Cleopatra's name and image, a cemetery and, in 2022, a rock-cut tunnel about 1,300 m (4,300 feet) long under the temple.
places.against: Two decades of work have found no royal tomb, and the ancient accounts place the mausoleum in Alexandria.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine, "Archaeologists Discover 4,300-Foot-Long Tunnel Under Ancient Egyptian Temple" (2022)
National Geographic Magazine, "The Search for Cleopatra" (C. Brown, 2011)

legends.name: Tomb of Nefertiti
legends.summary: No tomb or mummy of Queen Nefertiti, wife of Akhenaten, has been identified for certain. In 2015 the Egyptologist Nicholas Reeves argued from laser scans of the walls of Tutankhamun's tomb that two sealed doorways lead to further rooms, and that Nefertiti lies behind one. A radar survey later that year seemed to show voids behind the walls, but follow-up radar surveys in 2016 and 2018 found none.
legends.when: Nefertiti died about 1330 BCE; claim made 2015; tested 2015 to 2018

origin.text: N. Reeves, "The Burial of Nefertiti?" (2015); tested in L. Sambuelli et al., Journal of Cultural Heritage 39 (2019)

legends.look_for: A void behind a plastered rock wall. Ground-penetrating radar should show a flat reflection where rock gives way to air, but cracks and natural cavities in limestone give false echoes, which is why three surveys were needed.

places.name: KV62, tomb of Tutankhamun (Valley of the Kings)
places.claim: Reeves read straight lines under the painted plaster of the north and west walls as blocked doorways, and proposed that the tomb was first made for Nefertiti and that her burial is still there, walled off.
places.against: Follow-up radar examinations in 2016 and 2018 found no such voids; Wikipedia reports a 2026 microgravity study that argues hidden chambers are still possible, which has not been checked for this dataset.

sources.title: L. Sambuelli et al., "The third KV62 radar scan: Searching for hidden chambers adjacent to Tutankhamun's tomb", Journal of Cultural Heritage 39 (2019)
Wikipedia, "Tomb of Tutankhamun"

legends.name: Tomb of Qin Shi Huang
aka: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor
legends.summary: Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a united China, died in 210 BCE and was buried under a great mound near Xi'an; the historian Sima Qian wrote that mercury was used in the tomb to model the rivers and seas of the empire. The pits of the Terracotta Army that guards it were found in 1974. The tomb mound itself has been explored by remote methods and remains largely unexcavated.
legends.when: Died 210 BCE; terracotta pits found 1974 CE

origin.text: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor"

legends.look_for: A great earth mound with a walled precinct and many buried pits around it; the Terracotta Army lies about 1.5 km east of the mound. A number of non-invasive techniques have been used to explore the underground palace without digging.

places.name: Mausoleum mound at Lintong, Xi'an
places.claim: The site was not discovered until 1974, and thousands of statues still wait to be unearthed. The emperor lies under a mound that remains largely unexcavated, so the account of what the tomb holds rests on Sima Qian.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor"
Wikipedia, "Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang"

legends.name: Tomb of Herod the Great
legends.summary: The historian Josephus says that Herod, king of Judea, was buried in 4 BCE at Herodium, the fortress palace he built south of Jerusalem. Ehud Netzer dug there from 1972 and searched for the tomb for more than thirty years.
